title: A research wiki on neurotechnology in the administration of justice, kept by language models on the library
source: Pages written by Claude Fable 5.1 agents from nine of the library's documents, each claim pinned to a passage and checked against it by tools/wiki_verify.py
schema:
# WIKI.md: schema and operating manual

A research wiki on **neurotechnology in the administration of justice**, kept by language models for the hands-on sessions of *AI for Human Rights Professionals* (Geneva Human Rights Hub and ITU, 4 December 2026). It follows the "LLM wiki" pattern: people choose the sources and ask the questions; the model reads the sources, writes and files the pages, and does the bookkeeping. Knowledge is compiled once and kept current, not rediscovered at every question.

Three layers:

1. **The library** (raw sources): `WORKSHOP_DATA.library`, ten documents passage by passage, each passage with the PDF page it starts on. Read-only: the wiki never changes a source.
2. **The wiki** (this folder): markdown pages written by the model, linked to each other and pinned to the library.
3. **This file** (the schema): what a page looks like, how a claim is pinned and checked, and what Ingest, Ask and Lint do.

Built on 2 November 2026 from nine documents. The tenth, A/HRC/57/61, waits in the inbox for the live ingest.

## The library and its registers

| id | cite as | register | kind |
|---|---|---|---|
| A/81/351 | A/81/351 | c | UN report (Secretary-General, 2026) |
| UNODC-INTERPOL-2025 | UNODC–INTERPOL 2025 | c | UN agency paper (2025) |
| A/HRC/57/61 | A/HRC/57/61 | c | UN report (Human Rights Council Advisory Committee, 2024), **inbox** |
| AHRC-2025 | AHRC 2025 | d | National human rights institution report (2025) |
| FuturesLab-2026 | Futures Lab 2026 | e | Civil-society submission (2026) |
| Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025 | Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025 | f | Journal article (2025) |
| Prainsack-et-al-2022 | Prainsack et al. 2022 | f | Journal article (2022) |
| CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4 | General Comment No. 22 | b | General Comment of the Human Rights Committee (1993) |
| CCPR/C/GC/32 | General Comment No. 32 | b | General Comment of the Human Rights Committee (2007) |
| CCPR/C/GC/34 | General Comment No. 34 | b | General Comment of the Human Rights Committee (2011) |

Six registers, never blurred:

- **(a) treaty law**: binding treaty text (the ICCPR). Not in the library: see *Treaty text* below.
- **(b) treaty-body interpretation**: General Comments of the Human Rights Committee.
- **(c) UN, agency and soft-law reports**: the Secretary-General, UNODC and INTERPOL, the Human Rights Council Advisory Committee, UNESCO.
- **(d) national human rights institution (NHRI)**: the Australian Human Rights Commission.
- **(e) civil society**: the Futures Lab submission.
- **(f) scholarship**: journal articles.

A claim has the register of the document that makes it. A report that quotes a General Comment does not become (b): pin the General Comment itself, and the report only for what the report adds.

## Page types

| type | folder | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| `source` | `sources/` | One page per ingested library document: what it says, in its own words, with pins. |
| `concept` | `concepts/` | An idea across documents (mental privacy, neuroprediction). The compounding core. |
| `entity` | `entities/` | A thing in the world: a treaty article, a General Comment as an authority, a report, a case, a law. Gathers what the library says about it. |
| `question` | `questions/` | An answered question, filed back as a page. |

A source page reads one document; an entity page follows one thing through all documents. So General Comment No. 34 has both: `sources/ccpr-c-gc-34` (what it says) and `entities/general-comment-34` (who in the library relies on it, for what).

The filename is the slug (kebab-case). `[[slug]]` links to a page in any folder.

## Frontmatter (every page)

```yaml
---
title: Mental privacy
type: concept                 # source | concept | entity | question
tags: [privacy, neural-data, art-17]
register: [b, c, d, f]        # see below
status: reviewed              # stub | draft | reviewed
updated: 2026-11-02
links: [[neural-data]], [[iccpr-art-17]]
sources: [A/81/351, AHRC-2025, Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025]
---
```

- `register`: a source page has its document's letter; an entity page the letter of the thing itself (an ICCPR article is `[a]`); a concept or question page every register its pins draw on.
- `sources`: the library ids the page pins. Never empty.
- `links`: the related pages, as `[[slug]]`.
- `stub`: a page that exists before its source is ingested (e.g. `a-hrc-57-61`).

## Pins: the direct-link rule

Every factual claim carries a **pin**: a link to one library document at one PDF page, which opens the PDF there (`studio.openSource(id, page)`). The syntax is a markdown link with a `pin:` address, the verbatim quote as its title, and a mark:

```
[LABEL](pin:DOC#pPAGE "QUOTE") ✓
```

- `DOC`: the library id (first column above).
- `PAGE`: the PDF page on which the quoted passage starts (`passage.page`), not the number printed on the page.
- `LABEL`: how a reader cites it: `<cite as>, para. <paragraph>` when the passage has a paragraph number, otherwise `<cite as>, p. <page_label>` (the printed page).
- `QUOTE`: words copied verbatim from that one passage. `…` joins fragments of the same passage, in order. Inside the quote, write double quotes as “ ”, never as `"`.
- Mark: `✓` verified, `⚠` unverified.

Example:

```
The Secretary-General records both views without choosing [A/81/351, para. 16](pin:A/81/351#p6 "While some contend that the challenges of neurotechnology may require development of new legal frameworks, others affirm that the risks of misuse or abuse of neurotechnology may be addressed within the existing international human rights law framework") ✓.
```

One regular expression finds every pin (JavaScript and Python alike):

```
\[([^\]]+)\]\(pin:([^#\s)]+)#p(\d+)(?: "([^"]*)")?\) ?(✓|⚠)
```

Groups: 1 label, 2 document id, 3 PDF page, 4 quote, 5 mark.

### Pin verification

A pin is **✓ verified** when the quote is found in a passage of that document that starts on that PDF page, and the label's paragraph or printed page is that passage's. Before comparing, both sides are normalised: Unicode NFKC; curly quotes and apostrophes made straight; dashes made hyphens; a hyphen and the space after it removed ("decision- making" = "decision-making" = "decisionmaking"); runs of whitespace made one space. Words and capitals must match.

A pin is **⚠ unverified** when it has no quote or has not been checked. A `✓` that fails is an error, not a warning. `python3 tools/wiki_verify.py` checks every pin; the target is 100% ✓.

What a pin cannot verify: the passages leave out footnotes, tables, captions and running heads. A claim about a footnote pins the paragraph that carries it and says so ("in its footnote 7, on the same page"); a reader checks the footnote by eye in the PDF.

**Treaty text.** The ICCPR is not in the library. An entity page for an article may quote it from the official text with a plain link, marked (a), e.g. `[ICCPR art. 14(3)(g)](https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-mechanisms/instruments/international-covenant-civil-and-political-rights)`. That link is not a pin; every other claim on the page is pinned.

**Inbox documents** are not pinned until they are ingested.

## Conventions

1. **Direct links.** Every factual claim carries a pin; every pin opens its page.
2. **Pin verification.** ✓ only after the check above; otherwise ⚠.
3. **Registers.** Name the register when it matters ("the Secretary-General, a (c) report, notes…"). Never present (c)–(f) as what the treaty requires.
4. **The document's own verb.** "Recommends", "is of the view", "proposes", "could": keep it. A recommendation is not an obligation; "may constitute" is not "constitutes".
5. **Caveats travel with the data.** A source page has a **How NOT to read this** section wherever the document misstates a provision, overstates the science, or speaks for one country only.
6. **Link, don't duplicate.** A page summarises and pins; the full text stays in the library, one click away.
7. **English, in UN terms**: "the Human Rights Committee", "General Comment No. 34", "the Secretary-General", "States parties".

## Contested claims and the authority ladder

Where documents disagree, the page records it in a `contested` block, shown as a card:

````
```contested
claim: Existing human rights law is enough to deal with neurotechnology in criminal justice.
verdict: leans-support
note: One line on where the real weight lies.
+ d | [AHRC 2025, p. 30](pin:AHRC-2025#p30 "these debates appear to be settling in favour of interpreting and adapting existing rights") ✓ | an NHRI reads the debate as settling | [[ahrc-2025]]
- e | [Futures Lab 2026, p. 7](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p8 "the United Nations needs to develop new human rights standards that reflect the emerging and rapidly evolving nature of neurotechnology") ✓ | calls for new UN standards | [[futures-lab-2026]]
```
````

- `verdict`: `settled-support` · `leans-support` · `contested` · `leans-contest` · `settled-contest`.
- A position line: sign (`+` supports, `-` contests, `~` mixed) · register letter · a pin · a short gloss · the wiki page. The register is the pinned document's.
- **Authority ladder.** Weights by register: (a) 5 · (b) 4 · (c) 3 · (d) 2 · (e) 1 · (f) ½. The lean bar shows support = (Σ`+` + ½Σ`~`) / Σ all. It is descriptive. The authored `verdict` and `note` lead: a higher register can decide the matter alone (one General Comment outweighs any number of reports), so never read the percentage as the answer.
- Every contested card is listed in `TENSIONS.md`.

## Page anatomy

**Source page.** `# <cite as>: <short title>` → **Full cite.** · **Register.** (the letter, and why) · **One-liner.** → `## Key takeaways` (each pinned) → `## How NOT to read this` (where needed) → `## Where it feeds the wiki` (the concepts and entities it informs) → `## Related`.

**Concept page.** `# Title` → **One-liner.** → `## What the library says`, highest register first → `## Contested claims` (if any) → `## Open questions` → `## Related`.

**Entity page.** `# Title` → **What it is.** (body, date, register; official link if outside the library) → `## In the library` (who relies on it, for what, pinned) → `## Related`.

**Question page.** `# The question?` → **Short answer.** → `## Reasoning` (pinned) → `## What the library cannot answer` → `## Related`.

## Operations

- **Ingest(document).** For a document with status `inbox`: read every passage; discuss the takeaways with the user; write `sources/<slug>.md`; update the concept and entity pages it touches (new pins, links both ways, a contested card where it disagrees with the wiki, a stub turned into a page); add its lines to `index.md`; append to `log.md`; run Lint. One document typically touches five to fifteen pages.
- **Ask(question).** Read `index.md` first, then the pages it points to, then the passages they pin. Answer with pins only. A good answer can be filed back as `questions/<slug>.md`.
- **Lint.** `python3 tools/wiki_verify.py` checks every pin, dangling `[[links]]`, orphan pages, pages without sources, registers, contested cards and the index. Then read for what code cannot see: contradictions between pages, claims a newer document has overtaken, concepts named but without a page.

## index.md, log.md, TENSIONS.md

- **`index.md`**: the catalog, by type, one line per page: `- [[slug]] — one-liner · (registers) · ✓N`. Read first on every Ask; updated on every Ingest.
- **`log.md`**: append-only, oldest first. Each entry starts `## [YYYY-MM-DD] ingest | <document>` (or `ask`, `lint`, `schema`), so `grep "^## \[" log.md` lists them.
- **`TENSIONS.md`**: the register of open disagreements, one `###` entry per contested card:

```
### do-existing-rights-suffice
title: Do existing rights suffice?
status: open                  # open | leaning | settled
card: [[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]]
poles: existing rights, interpreted (AHRC 2025) || new standards (Futures Lab 2026)
where: [[a-81-351]], [[ahrc-2025]], [[futures-lab-2026]]
```

## Tools

```bash
python3 tools/wiki_verify.py                      # verify every pin and lint the wiki
python3 tools/wiki_verify.py --check FILE …       # one or more pages: frontmatter, pins, cards
python3 tools/wiki_verify.py --find "regex" [--doc ID]   # passages matching, with the pin to paste
python3 tools/wiki_verify.py --doc ID             # every passage of one document
python3 tools/wiki_verify.py --pdf                # also look for each ✓ quote on the PDF page itself
```

pages.title: A/81/351: Secretary-General's report on human rights in the administration of justice (2026)

frontmatter.title: A/81/351: Secretary-General's report on human rights in the administration of justice (2026)

pages.body:
# A/81/351: Human rights in the administration of justice (Secretary-General, 2026)

**Full cite.** United Nations General Assembly, *Human rights in the administration of justice: report of the Secretary-General*, UN Doc. A/81/351, eighty-first session, agenda item 70 (b), 27 August 2026, 16 pages, https://docs.un.org/en/A/81/351. Prepared under General Assembly resolution 79/172 from submissions and research [A/81/351, para. 1](pin:A/81/351#p2 "submitted pursuant to General Assembly resolution 79/172 … The report draws on information received from Member States, United Nations entities, human rights mechanisms and civil society and on external research") ✓. Fifty paragraphs; the recommendations are para. 50 (a)–(j).

**Register.** (c): a report of the Secretary-General to the General Assembly, synthesising submissions, Special Procedures reports and the Committee's General Comments. Where it quotes the Committee, pin the General Comment ([[ccpr-c-gc-32]], [[general-comment-22]]); cite this report for the application to neurotechnology.

**One-liner.** The latest UN-level map of neurotechnology in the administration of justice: it names the uses, runs them through the Covenant rights, surveys regulation and recommends that Member States prohibit compulsory or coercive use.

## Key takeaways

**Neural data.** The definition comes from the UNESCO Recommendation (its footnote 6, on the same PDF page), and the report states a consensus [A/81/351, para. 5](pin:A/81/351#p3 "There is broad consensus that neural data are highly sensitive, providing unprecedented access to internal mental states, and that they require heightened ethical and legal protection") ✓. Its footnote 7, on the same PDF page, cites A/HRC/58/58, Szoszkiewicz and Yuste 2025 (the EMBO Reports article in the library, [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]]) and Genser, Damianos and Yuste 2024: the consensus is sourced to those three works. The conclusion repeats it [A/81/351, para. 49](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Neural data, as uniquely sensitive personal data, demand heightened protection") ✓.

**Uses.** "Brain-based deception detection" is the umbrella term; fMRI "lie detection" and concealed-information tests sold as "brain fingerprinting" are its species [A/81/351, para. 8](pin:A/81/351#p4 "The most discussed application is the use of functional magnetic resonance imaging for “lie detection”. Other related but distinct techniques are “guilty knowledge” or “concealed information” testing") ✓. Both terms recur: "deception detection" in paras. 8, 9, 20 and 50 (c), "lie detection" in paras. 8, 9, 28 and 32. None is court-ready [A/81/351, para. 9](pin:A/81/351#p4 "No brain-based deception detection method has achieved general acceptance for courtroom use") ✓. Whether decoding will ever be reliable enough for justice "is unknown" [A/81/351, para. 11](pin:A/81/351#p4 "Whether such approaches will, at some point, be able to produce information that is sufficiently reliable to be used in the administration of justice is unknown") ✓.

**New law or existing law.** Both positions are recorded, neither chosen [A/81/351, para. 16](pin:A/81/351#p6 "While some contend that the challenges of neurotechnology may require development of new legal frameworks, others affirm that the risks of misuse or abuse of neurotechnology may be addressed within the existing international human rights law framework") ✓. The conclusion leans to the second, with a caveat [A/81/351, para. 48](pin:A/81/351#p15 "International human rights law provides an applicable framework to address the risks of neurotechnology, but further clarification and consistent application are needed") ✓.

**Freedom of thought.** Applying General Comment No. 22 (its footnote 36, on the same PDF page), the report finds that deception detection and decoding "could reveal information that the person has not chosen to disclose" [A/81/351, para. 20](pin:A/81/351#p7 "through brain-based deception detection technology or decoding, could reveal information that the person has not chosen to disclose") ✓. The four pillars are attributed to experts, not to the Committee [A/81/351, para. 21](pin:A/81/351#p7 "Experts have argued that four pillars of freedom of thought are most relevant to neurotechnology: the freedom not to disclose thoughts; freedom from punishment for thoughts, real or inferred; freedom from impermissible alteration of thoughts; and an enabling environment for free thought") ✓. All four "may potentially" be affected, though the report denies mind-reading [A/81/351, para. 22](pin:A/81/351#p8 "Neurotechnology may potentially affect all four pillars of freedom of thought … While neurotechnology is not capable at present of “mind-reading”, it is reportedly capable of inferring emotions and internal reactions based on neural data") ✓.

**Neuromodulation of offenders and consent.** The report relays the Advisory Committee's view with its hedges intact [A/81/351, para. 29](pin:A/81/351#p10 "The Human Rights Council Advisory Committee is of the view that the use of neuromodulation techniques intended to alter the brain activity of offenders to reduce aggression or impulsivity may constitute treatment contrary to articles 7 or 10 of the Covenant when imposed without genuinely free and informed consent") ✓ (the cited report, [[a-hrc-57-61]], is in the inbox), then turns to custody and early release [A/81/351, para. 29](pin:A/81/351#p10 "In custodial settings, the pronounced power imbalance between the State and the individual may call into question the genuineness of consent … early release or favourable parole outcomes, there is a significant risk that consent may not be fully free or voluntary") ✓.

**Fair trial, self-incrimination, liberty.** Coercive lie detection "could call into question" article 14 (3) (g); Selvi v. State of Karnataka is cited (its footnote 63, on PDF p. 11, gives paras. 215–224 of the judgment); the exclusionary rule "could apply" [A/81/351, para. 32](pin:A/81/351#p10 "The coercive use of brain-based lie detection could call into question the privilege against self-incrimination, protected under article 14 (3) (g) of the Covenant … The Supreme Court of India, in Selvi v. State of Karnataka, held that the involuntary administration of brain electrical oscillation signature profiling tests, a form of brain-based lie detection, violates the constitutional protection against self-incrimination … This could apply to evidence obtained through the coercive use of neurotechnologies") ✓. Prediction "may also undermine the presumption of innocence" [A/81/351, para. 33](pin:A/81/351#p11 "the use of predictive neurotechnology purporting to assess future criminality may also undermine the presumption of innocence") ✓ and "may lead to arbitrary detention under article 9" [A/81/351, para. 34](pin:A/81/351#p11 "the use of brain-based deception technologies to determine whether a person should be detained, may lead to arbitrary detention under article 9") ✓.

**Regulation.** "Nascent and uneven", citing A/HRC/57/61 [A/81/351, para. 42](pin:A/81/351#p13 "the regulatory response to the human rights challenges posed by neurotechnology is still nascent and uneven") ✓. Chile [A/81/351, para. 43](pin:A/81/351#p13 "In Chile, in 2023, the Supreme Court applied the 2021 constitutional amendment, to protect brain activity and derived data, holding unlawful a company’s practices involving a portable brain-monitoring device") ✓ (its footnote 75, on the same PDF page, names Girardi v. Emotiv Inc., 9 August 2023); three US states [A/81/351, para. 45](pin:A/81/351#p14 "California, Colorado and Montana have extended sensitive data protections to neural data") ✓ (its footnote 79, on the same PDF page: Colorado HB 24-1058, California SB 1223, Montana SB 163); UNESCO and the UNODC–INTERPOL collaboration [A/81/351, para. 46](pin:A/81/351#p14 "the General Conference of UNESCO adopted its Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology in 2025 … In 2025, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime and the International Criminal Police Organization launched a collaboration") ✓.

**What the Secretary-General recommends.** The verb is "recommend", the addressee Member States [A/81/351, para. 50](pin:A/81/351#p15 "I recommend that Member States:") ✓: frameworks with impact assessments [A/81/351, para. 50 (a)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Establish regulatory frameworks, consistent with international human rights law") ✓; neural data as highly sensitive [A/81/351, para. 50 (b)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Recognize neural data as highly sensitive personal data subject to the highest level of legal protection") ✓; prohibition of coercive use [A/81/351, para. 50 (c)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Prohibit the compulsory or coercive use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice, including brain-based deception detection, predictive applications, decoding applications to “read” thoughts, intentions or memories, neuromodulation and arbitrary or unlawful cognitive surveillance and monitoring") ✓; exclusion of tainted neural data [A/81/351, para. 50 (d)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Prohibit the use of neural data obtained through torture or ill-treatment, or in violation of the rights to freedom of thought and opinion, as evidence in any proceedings") ✓; demanding consent [A/81/351, para. 50 (e)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Require free, prior, informed, explicit and revocable consent … any consent should be subject to the highest evidentiary standards and rigorous scrutiny") ✓; validated evidence [A/81/351, para. 50 (f)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Require rigorous independent scientific review and validation of any neurotechnology-derived evidence proposed for admission in court") ✓; safeguards for specific groups [A/81/351, para. 50 (g)](pin:A/81/351#p16 "Ensure enhanced safeguards for children, detainees, persons with disabilities, women, older persons") ✓ and Indigenous Peoples [A/81/351, para. 50 (h)](pin:A/81/351#p16 "the requirement of free, prior and informed consent") ✓; business due diligence [A/81/351, para. 50 (i)](pin:A/81/351#p16 "Urge all business enterprises involved in neurotechnology") ✓; training [A/81/351, para. 50 (j)](pin:A/81/351#p16 "specialized training for law enforcement officials, prosecutors, judges and defence counsel") ✓. No moratorium is recommended: para. 50 (c) prohibits coercion, paras. 50 (e)–(f) condition any other use.

## How NOT to read this

- A (c) report that synthesises submissions. Its verbs are "could", "may", "is of the view", "I recommend". Nothing here is a treaty-body finding; a recommendation to Member States is not an obligation.
- Para. 32 paraphrases General Comment No. 32 (its footnote 62, on the same PDF page) as "an absolute guarantee" against "any direct or indirect physical or psychological pressure". The Committee's words, pinned on [[ccpr-c-gc-32]] (para. 41), are "undue psychological pressure", and the Committee does not call article 14 (3) (g) absolute. Quote the Committee, not the paraphrase.
- Para. 5's "broad consensus" is a report citing three works (footnote 7), one of them scholarship in this library: a well-sourced claim, not a norm.
- Para. 29's view belongs to the Advisory Committee and to the "experts" of its footnote 56 (a UNODC submission and AHRC, Peace of Mind); the report adds no finding of its own.
- Footnote 42 (PDF p. 8) dates AHRC, Peace of Mind, to 2024; the library's copy is October 2025 ([[ahrc-2025]]).
- Paras. 42–46 report national positions from submissions; they are not findings of law.

## Where it feeds the wiki

[[neural-data]], [[mental-privacy]] (paras. 5, 24–26, 49, 50 (b)); [[freedom-of-thought]] (paras. 20–23); [[brain-based-lie-detection]], [[self-incrimination]] (paras. 8–9, 28, 32, 50 (c)–(d)); [[neuroprediction]] (paras. 10, 33–35); [[neuromodulation-of-offenders]], [[consent-in-custody]] (paras. 29–30, 50 (e)); [[reliability-and-admissibility]] (paras. 13, 33, 47, 50 (f)); [[discrimination]] (paras. 37–41, 50 (g)–(h)); [[regulatory-landscape]], [[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]] (paras. 16, 42–46, 48); [[moratorium]] (not recommended); [[what-should-states-do-now]] (para. 50). Entities: [[iccpr-art-7]], [[iccpr-art-9]], [[iccpr-art-14-3-g]], [[iccpr-art-17]], [[iccpr-art-18]], [[general-comment-22]], [[general-comment-32]], [[a-hrc-57-61]], [[unesco-recommendation-2025]], [[selvi-v-state-of-karnataka]], [[chile-supreme-court-2023]], [[colorado-neural-data-law]], [[california-neural-data-law]].

## Related

- [[unodc-interpol-2025]] (the collaboration para. 46 announces; the law-enforcement view)
- [[futures-lab-2026]] (a civil-society submission to the same call for input; asks for new standards)
- [[ahrc-2025]] (cited in footnotes 42, 45 and 56; reads the debate as settling for existing rights)
- [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (footnote 7's source for the neural data consensus)
- [[a-hrc-57-61]] (the Advisory Committee report cited at paras. 22, 29, 36, 37 and 42; inbox)
- [[ccpr-c-gc-32]] (the Committee's own wording on article 14 (3) (g))

pages.title: AHRC 2025: Peace of Mind

frontmatter.title: AHRC 2025: Peace of Mind

pages.body:
# AHRC 2025: Peace of Mind

**Full cite.** Australian Human Rights Commission, *Peace of Mind: Navigating the Ethical Frontiers of Neurotechnology and Human Rights* (Sydney: Australian Human Rights Commission, October 2025), CC BY 4.0, [publisher page](https://humanrights.gov.au/resource-hub/search-all-our-publications/reports-and-projects/reports/technology-and-human-rights/peace-of-mind-new-report-explores-neurotechnology-and-human-rights). The final report of a two-year project [AHRC 2025, p. 6](pin:AHRC-2025#p6 "this Final Report is the culmination of a multi-year project examining the human rights impacts of neurotechnology, it is not intended as the final word on this topic") ✓, with 18 recommendations [AHRC 2025, p. 9](pin:AHRC-2025#p9 "The final report makes 18 recommendations") ✓. Printed page = PDF page.

**Register.** (d): a national human rights institution addressing the Australian Government. Its Covenant readings are second-hand; chapters 5, 7 and 8 are largely Australian domestic law. Never cite it as (b): for any Covenant proposition go to the General Comment ([[general-comment-22]], [[ccpr-c-gc-32]], [[ccpr-c-gc-34]]) and use this report for what it adds.

**One-liner.** An NHRI records the neurorights debate as settling towards existing rights, asks the Human Rights Committee for a general comment on article 18, and takes the library's only institutional procedural position on criminal justice: an inquiry, a moratorium and interim inadmissibility.

## Key takeaways

**The debate (§6.3, p. 30).** [AHRC 2025, p. 30](pin:AHRC-2025#p30 "At the international and transnational level, these debates appear to be settling in favour of interpreting and adapting existing rights") ✓. An observation ("appear to be"), not a holding; the report then brackets the question [AHRC 2025, p. 30](pin:AHRC-2025#p30 "the broader discussion of neurorights is outside the scope of this report") ✓. None of its 18 recommendations proposes a new right.

**Freedom of thought (chapter 6, pp. 28–29).** Article 18 is the right most exposed, in the Committee's borrowed words [AHRC 2025, p. 28](pin:AHRC-2025#p28 "The right contained in art 18 ICCPR is ‘far reaching and profound’ and captures freedom of thought on all matters") ✓ (General Comment No. 22, para. 1: [[general-comment-22]]). The report then gives "four key pillars", attributed to the Special Rapporteur on freedom of religion or belief [AHRC 2025, p. 29](pin:AHRC-2025#p29 "freedom not to disclose thoughts … freedom from punishment for thoughts … freedom from impermissible alteration of thoughts … an enabling environment for freedom of thought") ✓. Its endnote 120 (PDF p. 77) cites A/76/380 (not in the library; [docs.un.org](https://docs.un.org/en/A/76/380)), where these are possible attributes; the AHRC hardens them into structure. The first pillar is read as mental privacy [AHRC 2025, p. 29](pin:AHRC-2025#p29 "mental privacy is a foundational element of free thought") ✓.

**Recommendation 4.** [AHRC 2025, p. 70](pin:AHRC-2025#p70 "The United Nations Human Rights Committee provide guidance on freedom of thought and neurotechnologies through the adoption of a general comment on article 18") ✓. First boxed on p. 28 (a box the passages do not carry; check by eye), repeated on p. 70.

**Chapter 7 is "initial observations" (p. 31).** [AHRC 2025, p. 31](pin:AHRC-2025#p31 "This chapter provides some initial observations of relevant risks and benefits and recommends that the Attorney-General request that the ALRC conduct an inquiry") ✓; meanwhile [AHRC 2025, p. 31](pin:AHRC-2025#p31 "it will be necessary to introduce a moratorium") ✓.

**Recommendation 6 and the preliminary view.** [AHRC 2025, p. 70](pin:AHRC-2025#p70 "examine in what circumstances (if any) it can be appropriately used. Until this work is completed there should be a moratorium on the use of neurotechnology in the criminal justice system") ✓ (boxed first on p. 31). The body text on p. 32 narrows the moratorium to investigations and adds interim inadmissibility [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "The Commission’s preliminary view is that a moratorium on the use of neurotechnology in criminal investigations should be imposed until the ALRC has published the findings of the recommended inquiry. Additionally, until that time, information gained via neurotechnology should be inadmissible at trial") ✓. Inadmissibility is body text, not part of the numbered recommendation.

**Lie detection and consent (7.1, pp. 31–32).** Brain-based lie detection is mapped onto article 14(3)(g) [AHRC 2025, p. 31](pin:AHRC-2025#p31 "there can be no direct or indirect physical or psychological pressure to secure a confession or testimony. The use of neurotechnology as a means of lie detection may threaten this human right") ✓ (the standard is General Comment No. 32, para. 41, whose "undue psychological pressure" the AHRC restates without "undue": [[ccpr-c-gc-32]]). The sharpest point is on inducements [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "if an accused was offered the opportunity for a reduced sentence or some level of immunity in exchange for consenting to the use of neurotechnology during questioning by police, it would be difficult to argue that any consent given was entirely voluntary") ✓, given [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "the imbalance of power in a criminal investigation") ✓. It adds a jury-role objection [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "neurotechnology’s ability to overtake a jury’s role in assessing witness credibility and determining truth") ✓.

**Memory recovery (7.2, p. 33).** TMS-assisted recall is placed under articles 17 and 18 [AHRC 2025, p. 33](pin:AHRC-2025#p33 "there is a real risk of breaching the right to privacy and freedom of thought as protected by arts 17 and 18 ICCPR") ✓, and forcible extraction under article 7, on the Advisory Committee's authority [AHRC 2025, p. 33](pin:AHRC-2025#p33 "The UN Human Rights Advisory Committee has observed that any misuse of the technology to this degree would represent a violation of art 7 ICCPR") ✓ (its endnote 170, PDF p. 79, cites A/HRC/57/61, paras. 34–35: [[a-hrc-57-61]]). Conclusion: [AHRC 2025, p. 33](pin:AHRC-2025#p33 "it should not be used in criminal investigations for memory recovery") ✓.

**Trial and mens rea (7.3, p. 34).** [AHRC 2025, p. 34](pin:AHRC-2025#p34 "Neurotechnology directly interferes with the offender’s mind, blurring the lines between sole responsibility and ‘third party’ involvement. This can have significant implications with respect to the application of current legal tests relating to criminal responsibility and establishing intention") ✓. Article 14 sets the limits [AHRC 2025, p. 34](pin:AHRC-2025#p34 "must not impede the right to be equal before the court and the presumption of innocence protected by art 14") ✓.

**Neuroprediction (7.4, pp. 34–35).** fMRI biomarkers as recidivism predictors [AHRC 2025, p. 34](pin:AHRC-2025#p34 "biological markers of human behaviours that correlate to behavioural traits … This is known as ‘neuroprediction’") ✓ are rejected [AHRC 2025, p. 35](pin:AHRC-2025#p35 "reminiscent of an outdated biological determinism that is an anathema to human rights") ✓, for discrimination [AHRC 2025, p. 35](pin:AHRC-2025#p35 "may breach human rights to be treated equally before the law and to non-discrimination") ✓ and self-fulfilling prophecy [AHRC 2025, p. 35](pin:AHRC-2025#p35 "may result in a self-fulfilling prophecy") ✓; the matter is routed to the inquiry [AHRC 2025, p. 35](pin:AHRC-2025#p35 "should only be used in criminal justice settings after specific research") ✓.

**Sentencing options (7.5, p. 35).** The custody problem in mirror image: [AHRC 2025, p. 35](pin:AHRC-2025#p35 "consent to the use of neurotechnology could be used transactionally for sentence reduction or an earlier parole – despite the offender’s preference not to be the subject of a neurointervention in the absence of such incentives") ✓; some offenders [AHRC 2025, p. 35](pin:AHRC-2025#p35 "may be unduly pressured into accepting it") ✓.

**Neural data and the regulatory map.** Neural data is [AHRC 2025, p. 21](pin:AHRC-2025#p21 "highly sensitive and valuable because it can provide unprecedented insights into human thought processes") ✓, yet [AHRC 2025, p. 22](pin:AHRC-2025#p22 "the Privacy Act does not provide any express protection for neural data") ✓. The report notes Colorado and California [AHRC 2025, p. 25](pin:AHRC-2025#p25 "Colorado signed House Bill 24-1058 to define and protect neural data and California has now amended the California Consumer Privacy Act 2018") ✓ and Chile [AHRC 2025, p. 25](pin:AHRC-2025#p25 "Chile has worked to introduce neural protections into its national legal system via constitutional amendment") ✓. It adopts UNESCO's definition [AHRC 2025, p. 8](pin:AHRC-2025#p8 "the Commission has adopted the definition set out by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)") ✓ and records the Council's commissioned report [AHRC 2025, p. 9](pin:AHRC-2025#p9 "The UN Human Rights Council adopted a resolution to commission a report on neurotechnology and human rights. The report was released in September 2024") ✓, which is A/HRC/57/61.

## How NOT to read this

1. **The "art 19.1" error (p. 33).** [AHRC 2025, p. 33](pin:AHRC-2025#p33 "the right to security of the person in art 19.1 ICCPR which provides that everyone has the right to ’hold opinions without interference’") ✓ conflates article 9(1) (security of person) with article 19(1) (opinion). The Committee's words it then quotes, [AHRC 2025, p. 33](pin:AHRC-2025#p33 "security of the person includes ‘freedom of injury to the body and the mind, or bodily or mental integrity’") ✓, come from its General Comment on article 9 (General Comment No. 35, not in the library; the AHRC's endnote 169, PDF p. 79, cites CCPR/C/GC/35, para. 3). Cite [[iccpr-art-9]] for security of person and [[ccpr-c-gc-34]] for article 19(1). Never repeat the AHRC's article number as correct.
2. **"UN Human Rights Advisory Committee" (p. 33)** is the Human Rights Council Advisory Committee, an expert body of the Council, not a treaty body: [[a-hrc-57-61]], register (c).
3. **The brain-fingerprinting case study (p. 32).** [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "with a statistical confidence of 99.9%") ✓ is secondary-sourced (the endnotes cite the technique's inventor) and scientifically contested. Never repeat the figure as fact: [[reliability-and-admissibility]].
4. **Australian law does not travel.** The Privacy Act analysis, the Evidence Act 1977 (Qld), R v Murray, the Lie Detector Act 1983 (NSW) [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "The use of polygraph testing is specifically regulated in New South Wales (NSW) through the Lie Detector Act 1983 (NSW)") ✓, VERA-2R, Static-99R and the ALRC machinery are domestic: comparative material, not international law.
5. **Status of chapter 7.** "Initial observations" (p. 31); the moratorium is a "preliminary view" (p. 32); Recommendation 6 is addressed to a government and is not an obligation. The report itself says the topic needs a standalone report.

## Where it feeds the wiki

[[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]] (§6.3, the (d) pole of the card) · [[freedom-of-thought]] (four pillars) · [[moratorium]] (Recommendation 6, preliminary view) · [[brain-based-lie-detection]] and [[self-incrimination]] (7.1) · [[consent-in-custody]] and [[can-a-suspect-consent-to-lie-detection]] (pp. 32, 35) · [[neuroprediction]] and [[discrimination]] (7.4) · [[neuromodulation-of-offenders]] (7.5) · [[reliability-and-admissibility]] (interim inadmissibility, jury role) · [[neural-data]] and [[mental-privacy]] (chapter 5, p. 29) · [[regulatory-landscape]] and [[what-should-states-do-now]] (Recommendations 4 and 6).

## Related

[[iccpr-art-18]] (Recommendation 4's article) · [[iccpr-art-14-3-g]] (7.1) · [[iccpr-art-7]] and [[iccpr-art-17]] (memory recovery) · [[iccpr-art-9]] (the correct home of "security of person") · [[general-comment-22]] (quoted at p. 28) · [[ccpr-c-gc-32]] (the no-pressure standard) · [[ccpr-c-gc-34]] (article 19(1), misnumbered at p. 33) · [[a-hrc-57-61]] (cited for article 7) · [[unesco-recommendation-2025]] (definition adopted) · [[chile-supreme-court-2023]] (the AHRC mentions only the constitutional amendment) · [[colorado-neural-data-law]] · [[california-neural-data-law]] (p. 25).

pages.title: General Comment No. 22: freedom of thought, conscience and religion (article 18)

frontmatter.title: General Comment No. 22: freedom of thought, conscience and religion (article 18)

pages.body:
# General Comment No. 22: freedom of thought, conscience and religion (article 18)

**Full cite.** Human Rights Committee, General Comment No. 22: The right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion (art. 18), UN Doc. CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4 (1993), 11 paragraphs, [docs.un.org](https://docs.un.org/en/CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4).

**Register.** (b) treaty-body interpretation: the Committee's reading of article 18 of the Covenant. It binds no one as such, but it is the highest authority in the library below the treaty text itself, and it outweighs any report that quotes it.

**One-liner.** Freedom of thought and conscience is absolute: no limitation, no derogation, no compulsion to reveal one's thoughts; only the manifestation of religion or belief may be restricted, and only under article 18(3).

## Key takeaways

**Far-reaching, equal, non-derogable.** The right "is far-reaching and profound"; thought and conscience "are protected equally with the freedom of religion and belief"; the provision "cannot be derogated from, even in time of public emergency" [General Comment No. 22, para. 1](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p1 "is far-reaching and profound; it encompasses freedom of thoughts on all matters, personal conviction … the freedom of thought and the freedom of conscience are protected equally with the freedom of religion and belief … this provision cannot be derogated from, even in time of public emergency") ✓.

**No limitation on thought; no compulsion to reveal it.** Article 18 separates the inner freedoms from their manifestation and "does not permit any limitations whatsoever on the freedom of thought and conscience"; these are "protected unconditionally, as is the right of everyone to hold opinions without interference in article 19 (1)"; and, "in accordance with articles 18 (2) and 17, no one can be compelled to reveal his thoughts" [General Comment No. 22, para. 3](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p2 "It does not permit any limitations whatsoever on the freedom of thought and conscience … These freedoms are protected unconditionally, as is the right of everyone to hold opinions without interference in article 19 (1). In accordance with articles 18 (2) and 17, no one can be compelled to reveal his thoughts or adherence to a religion or belief") ✓.

**Coercion.** Article 18(2) "bars coercions that would impair the right to have or adopt a religion or belief", including "the use of threat of physical force or penal sanctions"; policies "having the same intention or effect", such as restricting access to education, medical care or employment, are "similarly inconsistent"; and "the same protection is enjoyed by holders of all beliefs of a non-religious nature" [General Comment No. 22, para. 5](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p2 "Article 18 (2) bars coercions that would impair the right to have or adopt a religion or belief, including the use of threat of physical force or penal sanctions … Policies or practices having the same intention or effect, such as for example those restricting access to education, medical care, employment … The same protection is enjoyed by holders of all beliefs of a non-religious nature") ✓.

**Restrictions reach manifestation only, and strictly.** Article 18(3) permits restrictions "on the freedom to manifest religion or belief only"; freedom from coercion "cannot be restricted"; paragraph 3 "is to be strictly interpreted", with no restriction on grounds not listed, "such as national security"; and prisoners "continue to enjoy their rights to manifest their religion or belief to the fullest extent compatible with the specific nature of the constraint" [General Comment No. 22, para. 8](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p3 "The freedom from coercion to have or to adopt a religion or belief and the liberty of the parents and guardians to ensure religious and moral education cannot be restricted … paragraph 3 of article 18 is to be strictly interpreted: restrictions are not allowed on grounds not specified there, even if they would be allowed as restrictions to other rights protected in the Covenant, such as national security … Persons already subject to certain legitimate constraints, such as prisoners, continue to enjoy their rights to manifest their religion or belief to the fullest extent compatible with the specific nature of the constraint") ✓.

**Official ideology.** Treating a set of beliefs as official ideology "shall not result in any impairment of the freedoms under article 18" or in discrimination against those who do not accept it [General Comment No. 22, para. 10](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p4 "this shall not result in any impairment of the freedoms under article 18 or any other rights recognized under the Covenant nor in any discrimination against persons who do not accept the official ideology or who oppose it") ✓.

## How NOT to read this

- **It is from 1993 and never mentions neurotechnology**, brains, data or decoding. The step from "no one can be compelled to reveal his thoughts" to brain-based decoding is taken by the Secretary-General ([[a-81-351]], paras. 20–21) and the AHRC ([[ahrc-2025]], pp. 28–29, 39). Attribute the application to them, not to the Committee.
- **"Compelled to reveal" is about compulsion, and the Committee ties it to articles 18(2) and 17 and to "adherence to a religion or belief".** Whether inference from neural data without the person's participation is "compulsion to reveal" is a question the Committee has not addressed. Say so when the wiki uses paragraph 3 for [[brain-based-lie-detection]].
- **Paragraph 5's coercion standard is about having or adopting a belief**, with examples of force, penal sanctions and withheld benefits. Using it for inducements in custody ([[consent-in-custody]]) or for interventions that alter thought ([[neuromodulation-of-offenders]]) is the wiki's analogy; the Committee has said nothing about those settings.
- **Most of the document is about religion and belief** (paras. 2, 4, 6, 7, 9, 11: manifestation, education, state religion, conscientious objection). The forum internum points are paras. 1, 3, 5 and 8.
- **Wording.** The library text (and the PDF) reads "freedom of thoughts on all matters"; A/81/351 para. 20 quotes it as "freedom of thought on all matters". Pin the library text.
- **No General Comment on neurotechnology exists in the library.** The AHRC recommends that the Committee adopt one on article 18 and neurotechnologies ([[ahrc-2025]], p. 70), and [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] reports the Advisory Committee's similar recommendation. Those are calls for an instrument, not the instrument.

## Where it feeds the wiki

[[freedom-of-thought]] and [[iccpr-art-18]] (paras. 1, 3 and 8: absolute inner freedom, no derogation, restrictions only on manifestation); [[general-comment-22]] (the entity page: who in the library relies on which paragraph); [[mental-privacy]] (para. 3's "no one can be compelled to reveal his thoughts", read with article 17); [[brain-based-lie-detection]] (para. 3, applied by the reports); [[consent-in-custody]] and [[neuromodulation-of-offenders]] (para. 5 on coercion and withheld benefits, para. 8 on prisoners, both by analogy); [[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]] (the existing-rights pole rests on this document). Its cross-reference to article 19(1) connects it to [[ccpr-c-gc-34]].

## Related

- [[general-comment-22]] (how the library's reports use this General Comment)
- [[iccpr-art-18]] (the provision interpreted)
- [[freedom-of-thought]] (the concept page)
- [[ccpr-c-gc-34]] (article 19(1): opinion, named in para. 3 as equally unconditional)
- [[a-81-351]] (quotes paras. 1 and 3 and applies them to neurotechnology)
- [[ahrc-2025]] (quotes para. 1 and calls for a new general comment on article 18)
- [[mental-privacy]] (para. 3 read with article 17)
- [[brain-based-lie-detection]] (compulsion to reveal thoughts, as applied by the reports)

pages.title: General Comment No. 32: article 14, equality before courts and fair trial

frontmatter.title: General Comment No. 32: article 14, equality before courts and fair trial

pages.body:
# General Comment No. 32: article 14, equality before courts and fair trial

**Full cite.** Human Rights Committee, General Comment No. 32: Article 14: Right to equality before courts and tribunals and to a fair trial, UN Doc. CCPR/C/GC/32 (2007), 65 paragraphs, [docs.un.org](https://docs.un.org/en/CCPR/C/GC/32). It replaces General Comment No. 13 [General Comment No. 32, para. 1](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p1 "This general comment replaces general comment No. 13") ✓.

**Register.** (b) treaty-body interpretation of article 14: the highest authority in the library on self-incrimination, exclusion of evidence and the presumption of innocence. It outweighs every report that restates it.

**One-liner.** The privilege against self-incrimination means the absence of any direct or indirect physical or undue psychological pressure to obtain a confession; evidence obtained contrary to article 7 must be excluded; otherwise admissibility is primarily for domestic law.

## Key takeaways

**The self-incrimination standard (para. 41).** The guarantee "must be understood in terms of the absence of any direct or indirect physical or undue psychological pressure from the investigating authorities on the accused, with a view to obtaining a confession of guilt"; statements obtained in violation of article 7 must be excluded, and the State must then prove they were given freely [General Comment No. 32, para. 41](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p13 "This safeguard must be understood in terms of the absence of any direct or indirect physical or undue psychological pressure from the investigating authorities on the accused, with a view to obtaining a confession of guilt … Domestic law must ensure that statements or confessions obtained in violation of article 7 of the Covenant are excluded from the evidence … the burden is on the State to prove that statements made by the accused have been given of their own free will") ✓.

**Article 7 and article 14(3)(g) together (para. 60).** Forcing a confession under duress "violates both article 7 of the Covenant prohibiting torture and inhuman, cruel or degrading treatment and article 14, paragraph 3 (g)" [General Comment No. 32, para. 60](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p17 "To ill-treat persons against whom criminal charges are brought and to force them to make or sign, under duress, a confession admitting guilt violates both article 7 of the Covenant prohibiting torture and inhuman, cruel or degrading treatment and article 14, paragraph 3 (g) prohibiting compulsion to testify against oneself or confess guilt") ✓.

**Exclusion even in emergencies (para. 6).** Article 14 is not among the non-derogable rights, but because article 7 is, "no statements or confessions or, in principle, other evidence obtained in violation of this provision may be invoked as evidence in any proceedings covered by article 14, including during a state of emergency"; deviating from fundamental fair-trial principles "is prohibited at all times" [General Comment No. 32, para. 6](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p2 "no statements or confessions or, in principle, other evidence obtained in violation of this provision may be invoked as evidence in any proceedings covered by article 14, including during a state of emergency … Deviating from fundamental principles of fair trial, including the presumption of innocence, is prohibited at all times") ✓.

**Admissibility is otherwise domestic (paras. 39, 26).** Subject to those limits, "it is primarily for the domestic legislatures of States parties to determine the admissibility of evidence and how their courts assess it" [General Comment No. 32, para. 39](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p12 "subject to the limitations on the use of statements, confessions and other evidence obtained in violation of article 7 … it is primarily for the domestic legislatures of States parties to determine the admissibility of evidence and how their courts assess it") ✓; the Committee revisits a domestic evaluation of evidence only where it "was clearly arbitrary or amounted to a manifest error or denial of justice" [General Comment No. 32, para. 26](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p8 "unless it can be shown that such evaluation or application was clearly arbitrary or amounted to a manifest error or denial of justice") ✓.

**Disclosure about how evidence was obtained (para. 33).** Exculpatory material includes "indications that a confession was not voluntary"; where an article 7 violation is claimed, "information about the circumstances in which such evidence was obtained must be made available" [General Comment No. 32, para. 33](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p10 "other evidence that could assist the defence (e.g. indications that a confession was not voluntary). In cases of a claim that evidence was obtained in violation of article 7 of the Covenant, information about the circumstances in which such evidence was obtained must be made available") ✓.

**Presumption of innocence (para. 30).** It "imposes on the prosecution the burden of proving the charge", requires proof "beyond reasonable doubt", and bars presenting defendants "in a manner indicating that they may be dangerous criminals" [General Comment No. 32, para. 30](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p9 "imposes on the prosecution the burden of proving the charge, guarantees that no guilt can be presumed until the charge has been proved beyond reasonable doubt … presented to the court in a manner indicating that they may be dangerous criminals") ✓.

**Fairness and equality.** Fairness "entails the absence of any direct or indirect influence, pressure or intimidation or intrusion from whatever side and for whatever motive" [General Comment No. 32, para. 25](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p7 "Fairness of proceedings entails the absence of any direct or indirect influence, pressure or intimidation or intrusion from whatever side and for whatever motive") ✓. Procedural distinctions on the grounds listed in articles 2(1) or 26 "may also amount to discrimination" [General Comment No. 32, para. 65](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p18 "not only violate the requirement of paragraph 1 of this provision that “all persons shall be equal before the courts and tribunals,” but may also amount to discrimination") ✓.

## How NOT to read this

- **It is from 2007 and never mentions neurotechnology**, lie detection or brain imaging. Reading para. 41 to cover "the coercive use of brain-based lie detection" is the Secretary-General's step ([[a-81-351]], para. 32) and the AHRC's ([[ahrc-2025]], pp. 31–33). Attribute it to them.
- **"Undue" is part of the standard.** The Committee bars "direct or indirect physical or undue psychological pressure". A/81/351 (para. 32) and the AHRC (pp. 31, 33) restate it as "direct or indirect physical or psychological pressure", without "undue". Quote the Committee.
- **"Absolute" is the report's word.** A/81/351 para. 32 calls the privilege "an absolute guarantee". The Committee does not say so of article 14(3)(g); it uses "absolute" for the competence, independence and impartiality of a tribunal [General Comment No. 32, para. 19](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p5 "is an absolute right that is not subject to any exception") ✓, and para. 6 recalls that article 14 is not listed in article 4(2). The practical result is close; the label differs.
- **The standard is framed around confessions**, by "the investigating authorities". Whether a brain-based test that yields no statement is "testimony" is not decided here. Selvi v. State of Karnataka decided that under the Indian Constitution, not the Covenant ([[selvi-v-state-of-karnataka]]).
- **The exclusionary rule is keyed to article 7**, not to every involuntary or unreliable item. A/81/351 para. 32 says it "could apply" to coercively obtained neurotechnology evidence: keep "could". Reliability as such is left to domestic law (paras. 26, 39): see [[reliability-and-admissibility]].
- **The burden shift** ("the burden is on the State to prove … free will") arises where an article 7 violation is claimed, not in every consent dispute.

## Where it feeds the wiki

[[self-incrimination]] and [[iccpr-art-14-3-g]] (para. 41 is the operative standard; para. 60 the article 7 overlap); [[general-comment-32]] (the entity page); [[brain-based-lie-detection]] and [[can-a-suspect-consent-to-lie-detection]] (indirect and psychological pressure; the confession framing); [[consent-in-custody]] (the State's burden; disclosure of how evidence was obtained); [[reliability-and-admissibility]] (paras. 6, 26, 33, 39); [[iccpr-art-7]] (paras. 6, 41, 60); [[neuroprediction]] (para. 30, by analogy); [[discrimination]] (para. 65).

## Related

- [[general-comment-32]] (how the reports in the library use this General Comment)
- [[iccpr-art-14-3-g]] (the provision interpreted in para. 41)
- [[self-incrimination]] (the concept page)
- [[iccpr-art-7]] (the exclusionary rule's trigger)
- [[reliability-and-admissibility]] (what the Committee leaves to domestic law)
- [[a-81-351]] (applies para. 41 to brain-based lie detection; drops "undue")
- [[selvi-v-state-of-karnataka]] (the domestic case the Secretary-General pairs with para. 41)

pages.title: General Comment No. 34: article 19, freedoms of opinion and expression

frontmatter.title: General Comment No. 34: article 19, freedoms of opinion and expression

pages.body:
# General Comment No. 34: article 19, freedoms of opinion and expression

**Full cite.** Human Rights Committee, General Comment No. 34: Article 19: Freedoms of opinion and expression, UN Doc. CCPR/C/GC/34 (2011), 52 paragraphs, [docs.un.org](https://docs.un.org/en/CCPR/C/GC/34). It replaces General Comment No. 10 [General Comment No. 34, para. 1](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p1 "This general comment replaces general comment No. 10") ✓.

**Register.** (b) treaty-body interpretation of article 19. Most of it concerns expression and the media; the paragraphs that matter here are on holding opinions (paras. 5, 9, 10, 49) and, in passing, on personal data (para. 18).

**One-liner.** Holding an opinion is a right "to which the Covenant permits no exception or restriction"; any effort to coerce the holding or not holding of an opinion is prohibited; freedom to express includes freedom not to express.

## Key takeaways

**No exception, no restriction (para. 9).** Article 19(1) protects "the right to hold opinions without interference", a right "to which the Covenant permits no exception or restriction"; "no person may be subject to the impairment of any rights under the Covenant on the basis of his or her actual, perceived or supposed opinions"; and "arrest, detention, trial or imprisonment for reasons of the opinions they may hold" violates it [General Comment No. 34, para. 9](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p2 "This is a right to which the Covenant permits no exception or restriction … No person may be subject to the impairment of any rights under the Covenant on the basis of his or her actual, perceived or supposed opinions … The harassment, intimidation or stigmatization of a person, including arrest, detention, trial or imprisonment for reasons of the opinions they may hold, constitutes a violation of article 19, paragraph 1") ✓.

**No coercion; freedom not to express (para. 10).** "Any form of effort to coerce the holding or not holding of any opinion is prohibited", and freedom to express "necessarily includes freedom not to express one's opinion" [General Comment No. 34, para. 10](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p3 "Any form of effort to coerce the holding or not holding of any opinion is prohibited … Freedom to express one’s opinion necessarily includes freedom not to express one’s opinion") ✓.

**Opinion and thought; no reservation, no derogation (paras. 5, 49).** Given "the relationship of opinion and thought (article 18)", a reservation to article 19(1) would be incompatible with the Covenant's object and purpose; freedom of opinion cannot be derogated from, "since it can never become necessary to derogate from it during a state of emergency" [General Comment No. 34, para. 5](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p1 "as well as the relationship of opinion and thought (article 18), a reservation to paragraph 1 would be incompatible with the object and purpose of the Covenant … Freedom of opinion is one such element, since it can never become necessary to derogate from it during a state of emergency") ✓. Restrictions on freedom of opinion "should never be imposed" [General Comment No. 34, para. 49](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p12 "Restrictions on the right of freedom of opinion should never be imposed") ✓.

**Neighbouring articles; private actors (paras. 4, 7).** Articles 18, 17, 25 and 27 also "contain guarantees for freedom of opinion and/or expression" [General Comment No. 34, para. 4](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p1 "Among the other articles that contain guarantees for freedom of opinion and/or expression, are articles 18, 17, 25 and 27") ✓. The obligation binds the judiciary too, and States must protect persons "from any acts by private persons or entities that would impair the enjoyment of the freedoms of opinion and expression", so far as those rights apply between private parties [General Comment No. 34, para. 7](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p2 "All branches of the State (executive, legislative and judicial) … to ensure that persons are protected from any acts by private persons or entities that would impair the enjoyment of the freedoms of opinion and expression to the extent that these Covenant rights are amenable to application between private persons or entities") ✓.

**Personal data, restated from General Comment No. 16 (para. 18).** Everyone "should have the right to ascertain in an intelligible form, whether, and if so, what personal data is stored in automatic data files, and for what purposes", and to have incorrect or unlawfully collected data rectified [General Comment No. 34, para. 18](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p4 "every individual should have the right to ascertain in an intelligible form, whether, and if so, what personal data is stored in automatic data files, and for what purposes … If such files contain incorrect personal data or have been collected or processed contrary to the provisions of the law, every individual should have the right to have his or her records rectified") ✓.

**Restrictions apply to expression, not opinion (para. 21).** When a State restricts expression, "the relation between right and restriction and between norm and exception must not be reversed" [General Comment No. 34, para. 21](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p5 "these may not put in jeopardy the right itself. The Committee recalls that the relation between right and restriction and between norm and exception must not be reversed") ✓.

## How NOT to read this

- **It is from 2011 and never mentions neurotechnology.** The step from "no coercion to hold or not hold an opinion" to "forced neurological interventions … would violate this freedom" is the Secretary-General's ([[a-81-351]], para. 23, citing A/73/348), not the Committee's.
- **"Perceived or supposed opinions" (para. 9)** was written about ordinary attribution of opinions. Its use for decoded or predicted mental states is the wiki's application.
- **Opinion is not every mental state.** Para. 5 links opinion to thought (article 18) without drawing the boundary. Nothing here says that an emotion, a memory or a recognition signal is an "opinion". For thought, pin [[ccpr-c-21-rev-1-add-4]].
- **This is article 19, not article 9.** "Security of the person" is article 9 of the Covenant. The AHRC (p. 33) places "the right to security of the person" in "art 19.1 ICCPR" and pairs it with "hold opinions without interference"; the Committee's words it then quotes, on injury "to the body and the mind", concern security of person, not opinion. General Comment No. 34 contains no such passage, and the library holds no General Comment on article 9. See [[iccpr-art-9]] and [[ahrc-2025]].
- **Para. 18 is a restatement.** It repeats General Comment No. 16 on article 17, which is not in the library; pin para. 18 for the Committee's words. A/81/351 para. 26 relies on the same rules and adds that they "would also apply to neural data": that extension is the report's.
- **Do not run a proportionality test on opinion.** Paras. 21–36 govern restrictions on expression (article 19(2)–(3)); opinion (19(1)) admits none (paras. 9, 49). The AHRC quotes para. 21 at p. 20 in the context of expression, correctly.

## Where it feeds the wiki

[[freedom-of-thought]] (paras. 5, 9, 10: opinion as the second pillar of the forum internum, read with [[iccpr-art-18]]); [[general-comment-34]] (the entity page); [[neuromodulation-of-offenders]] (para. 10, as applied by the Secretary-General); [[discrimination]] (para. 9: no impairment of rights for actual, perceived or supposed opinions); [[neural-data]], [[iccpr-art-17]] and [[mental-privacy]] (para. 18's rules on stored personal data, which A/81/351 extends to neural data); [[iccpr-art-9]] (the AHRC's mislabelling of security of person, quarantined here).

## Related

- [[general-comment-34]] (how the reports in the library use this General Comment)
- [[ccpr-c-21-rev-1-add-4]] (article 18: the thought side of the forum internum)
- [[freedom-of-thought]] (the concept page for thought and opinion together)
- [[iccpr-art-17]] (para. 18's personal-data rules belong to article 17)
- [[iccpr-art-9]] (security of person: the article the AHRC confused with 19(1))
- [[a-81-351]] (applies paras. 9–10 to forced neurological interventions)
- [[ahrc-2025]] (quotes para. 21; mislabels security of person as art 19.1)

frontmatter.title: Futures Lab 2026: submission to the Secretary-General's report on neurotechnology and the administration of justice

pages.body:
# Futures Lab 2026: Neurotechnology and the Administration of Justice (submission to OHCHR)

**Full cite.** Futures Lab for Democracy, Tech & Human Rights, American University, *Neurotechnology and the Administration of Justice: Submission to the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights for Input to the Report of the UN Secretary-General Pursuant to UN General Assembly Resolution A/RES/79/172*, 9 March 2026, 8 printed pages (printed page = PDF page minus 1), submitted to OHCHR's call for input, https://www.ohchr.org/en/calls-for-input/2026/call-input-human-rights-administration-justice-neurotechnology-and-other. Contributors: Professor Jonathan Crock and twenty named co-contributors [Futures Lab 2026, p. 1](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p2 "Submitted by: Futures Lab for Democracy, Tech & Human Rights, American University Contributors: Professor Jonathan Crock, Joy Adjei") ✓.

**Register.** (e): civil society. An advocacy submission by a university lab, written as input to the Secretary-General's report ([[a-81-351]]); neither the text nor the footnotes of A/81/351 name it. Its weight is that of its argument and sources, which the library cannot check.

**One-liner.** A civil-society case for new UN standards on neurotechnology, framed in UDHR terms ("neurorights", "cognitive liberty", "sovereignty over one's brain"), with US state laws, Girardi v. Emotiv and discrimination risks as its evidence.

## Key takeaways

**New standards.** The central ask [Futures Lab 2026, p. 7](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p8 "the United Nations needs to develop new human rights standards that reflect the emerging and rapidly evolving nature of neurotechnology") ✓, stated also in the summary [Futures Lab 2026, p. 2](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p3 "the United Nations should establish global standards grounded in human dignity, cognitive liberty, and equality") ✓ and for data [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "specific international standards must be established to recognize the highly sensitive and personal nature of bio- and neurotechnologies") ✓. Until then, monitoring [Futures Lab 2026, p. 7](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p8 "Until such standards are established, the use of neurotechnology, particularly in legal responses to violations of neurorights, should be subject to careful monitoring") ✓. This is the library's clearest "new rights" pole: [[a-81-351]] records both views without choosing (para. 16) and [[ahrc-2025]] reads the debate as settling for existing rights (p. 30).

**UDHR framing.** [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "Neurorights safeguard fundamental aspects of human dignity, ensuring that mental processes and cognitive functions remain inviolable. They align with Articles 12 and 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR)") ✓. The submission never cites the Covenant, article 14, the Human Rights Committee or a General Comment; its other instrument is UNESCO's bioethics declaration [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "Although UNESCO’s Universal Declaration on Bioethics and Human Rights in Article 6 mandates") ✓. It asks for a right no UN document in the library names [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "stricter legal protections must be enacted to protect the human right to sovereignty over one’s brain") ✓.

**US state laws.** [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "California and Colorado are currently the only states to have passed legislation on neural data privacy, while a dozen others have legislation pending") ✓, with California's definition [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "information that is generated by measuring the activity of a consumer’s central or peripheral nervous system, and that is not inferred from nonneural information") ✓. "Only" is contradicted three times: [[a-81-351]] (para. 45) and [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (p. 3471) add Montana, and the submission itself later says [Futures Lab 2026, p. 8](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p9 "At least eight U.S. states have enacted legislation to protect neurorights") ✓. Treat its count as unreliable; keep its point that no federal standard exists [Futures Lab 2026, p. 2](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p3 "yet no federal standard exists") ✓.

**Girardi v. Emotiv.** The remedies [Futures Lab 2026, p. 6](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p7 "The Chilean Supreme Court ruled that Emotiv had sold the device without adequate oversight of health and human rights, ordering the deletion of collected neural data and the suspension of sales") ✓ and the lesson drawn [Futures Lab 2026, p. 6](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p7 "commercialization cannot be justified solely by click-through consent and emphasizes the need to institutionalize HRIAs as a pre-market requirement") ✓. [[a-81-351]] (para. 43) describes the same judgment as holding the company's practices unlawful under the 2021 constitutional amendment, without the remedies.

**Consent.** [Futures Lab 2026, p. 7](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p8 "Individuals should not be able to consent to overly broad uses of neurotechnology until clear and established neurorights are in place") ✓: a limit on consent itself, not only on its conditions.

**Participation.** Regulation is top-down and excludes those affected [Futures Lab 2026, p. 3](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p4 "Those directly impacted by neurotechnology, including defendants and prisoners … are regarded as secondary advisors or “objects” in the regulatory process") ✓; France is its example [Futures Lab 2026, p. 3](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p4 "France was the first country to allow brain imaging in judicial proceedings with consent, for medical or scientific research, or for forensic expertise, except for functional brain imaging") ✓. The same section sees promise in neuroprediction [Futures Lab 2026, p. 3](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p4 "While there is promise in neurotechnology’s assistance in assessing guilt, accountability, and the risk of recidivism in judicial proceedings") ✓: the only library document to say so; [[a-81-351]] (paras. 10, 33–35) and [[ahrc-2025]] treat recidivism prediction as a threat.

**Discrimination.** Biased datasets and people of African descent [Futures Lab 2026, p. 6](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p7 "The training data for these algorithms is often not diverse and draws on historical records, making outputs less accurate and potentially harmful to people of African descent") ✓; LGBTQI+ persons and "involuntary outing" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 7](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p8 "may infer sexual orientation or gender identity based on neural responses to stimuli, raising the possibility of involuntary outing in workplaces, medical contexts, or legal systems") ✓.

## How NOT to read this

- Advocacy, register (e): "needs", "must" and "should" are the authors' demands, not law, and "neurorights" or "cognitive liberty" are their vocabulary. The UN documents in the library use "neurorights" only as the name of domestic instruments ([[a-81-351]], para. 43).
- UDHR, not ICCPR: the rights map stops at the Declaration. For the Covenant, use [[iccpr-art-17]], [[iccpr-art-18]], [[iccpr-art-14-3-g]].
- Page 5 (PDF p. 6) calls UNESCO's standards a "draft" ("Draft global standards", "The UNESCO draft"); [[a-81-351]] (para. 46) records their adoption in 2025, before this March 2026 submission. See [[unesco-recommendation-2025]].
- The words it attributes to article 6 of the Universal Declaration on Bioethics and Human Rights cannot be checked in the library; quote that Declaration, not the submission.
- Section 10, "Judicial Decisions" (p. 8), is about AI in hiring (Amazon, Mobley v. Workday), not neurotechnology or the administration of justice.
- Its technical claims (79 per cent decoding accuracy, Neuralink's "21 clinical patients", NeuroXess, Kampto) are unverified in the library.

## Where it feeds the wiki

[[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]] (the "new standards" pole, pp. 2, 4, 7); [[neural-data]] and [[regulatory-landscape]] (California's definition, the state count, GDPR, pp. 2, 4, 8); [[consent-in-custody]] (consent limits, p. 7; click-through consent, pp. 2, 6); [[discrimination]] (pp. 2, 5–7); [[neuroprediction]] (the "promise" sentence, p. 3); [[moratorium]] (monitoring, not suspension, p. 7); [[mental-privacy]] and [[freedom-of-thought]] (UDHR arts. 12 and 18, p. 4). Entities: [[california-neural-data-law]], [[colorado-neural-data-law]] (p. 4), [[chile-supreme-court-2023]] (pp. 2, 6), [[unesco-recommendation-2025]] (p. 5, as "draft").

## Related

- [[a-81-351]] (the report this submission was written for; disagrees on Montana, on UNESCO's status and on neuroprediction)
- [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (names Colorado, California and Montana)
- [[ahrc-2025]] (the NHRI pole: existing rights, interpreted and adapted)
- [[unodc-interpol-2025]] (the law-enforcement pole; shares the consent and discrimination themes)
- [[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]] (the contested card this submission anchors)

pages.title: Prainsack et al. 2022: Data solidarity

frontmatter.title: Prainsack et al. 2022: Data solidarity

pages.body:
# Prainsack et al. 2022: Data solidarity

**Full cite.** Barbara Prainsack, Seliem El-Sayed, Nikolaus Forgó, Łukasz Szoszkiewicz and Philipp Baumer, "Data solidarity: a blueprint for governing health futures", *The Lancet Digital Health*, vol. 4 (November 2022), pp. e773–e774, [doi:10.1016/S2589-7500(22)00189-3](https://doi.org/10.1016/S2589-7500(22)00189-3), CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. A two-page Comment; the authors are at the University of Vienna and, for Szoszkiewicz, Adam Mickiewicz University in Poznań (author block on PDF p. 2, not in the passages).

**Register.** (f) scholarship. Łukasz Szoszkiewicz, the trainer of this workshop, is a co-author. It is a position piece in a medical journal, not a legal analysis: no treaty provision is cited. Weight ½ on the ladder.

**One-liner.** Giving individuals more control over their data is not enough; "data solidarity" would govern data by the public value and risk of each use, through three pillars: facilitate good uses, prevent and mitigate harm, return profits to the public.

## Key takeaways

**The problem.** Digital technologies increase inequalities, and people harmed by data use often have no remedy, "either because they cannot prove who and what caused the harm, or because no law was broken" [Prainsack et al. 2022, p. e773](pin:Prainsack-et-al-2022#p1 "Individuals harmed by data use often have no access to remedies, either because they cannot prove who and what caused the harm, or because no law was broken") ✓.

**Control is not enough.** Frameworks built on individual control "are not enough": control "cannot address the vast power asymmetries between data processors and data subjects", and harm "can affect wider groups of people than only the primary data subjects" [Prainsack et al. 2022, p. e773](pin:Prainsack-et-al-2022#p1 "regulatory frameworks that seek to prevent harm mostly by strengthening the control that individuals have over their data are not enough. Although individual control is important, it cannot address the vast power asymmetries between data processors and data subjects … harm—just as benefits— can affect wider groups of people than only the primary data subjects") ✓.

**The public-value test.** Data use "creates public value when it benefits people and communities without posing grave risks"; use with little public value but substantial risk "should be prohibited, with fines severe enough to deter even powerful corporations"; low-risk, high-benefit use "should receive more public support" [Prainsack et al. 2022, p. e773](pin:Prainsack-et-al-2022#p1 "Data use creates public value when it benefits people and communities without posing grave risks … Data use that creates little or no public value but poses substantial risks should be prohibited, with fines severe enough to deter even powerful corporations from breaking the law … should receive more public support") ✓.

**Three pillars.** Data solidarity "complements and helps to realise justice" and "consists of three main pillars" [Prainsack et al. 2022, p. e773](pin:Prainsack-et-al-2022#p1 "It consists of three main pillars: facilitating good data use (pillar 1); preventing and mitigating harm (pillar 2); and returning profits to the public domain (pillar 3)") ✓.

- *Pillar 1.* High-value uses, "often in non-profit health research", are blocked by onerous regulation or practical barriers and should get support "by removing red tape or by providing financial and practical assistance" [Prainsack et al. 2022, p. e773](pin:Prainsack-et-al-2022#p1 "Data solidarity requires that such data uses receive more public support by removing red tape or by providing financial and practical assistance") ✓.
- *Pillar 2.* Grave-risk uses call for "the full force of the law"; for large corporations, multiplied fines for repeat offenders and cross-border enforcement; and, since some risks remain even in beneficial uses, "harm mitigation bodies" to complement legal remedies [Prainsack et al. 2022, p. e773](pin:Prainsack-et-al-2022#p1 "data solidarity requires making use of the full force of the law to prohibit such harmful practices … One way to reach this goal is the creation of harm mitigation bodies at regional, national, or supranational level that would complement existing legal remedies") ✓.
- *Pillar 3.* Where profits accrue, "some of these profits need to come back to the people and communities that enabled them", through digital corporate taxation or data commons governed "by the values of fairness, equality, justice, and sustainability" [Prainsack et al. 2022, p. e774](pin:Prainsack-et-al-2022#p2 "some of these profits need to come back to the people and communities that enabled them in the first place … data commons, in which data and other digital resources are governed collaboratively, guided by the values of fairness, equality, justice, and sustainability") ✓.

**Closing claim.** "Societies have a collective responsibility" to ensure digital practices improve all lives and that harms are prevented; data solidarity "provides a blueprint" [Prainsack et al. 2022, p. e774](pin:Prainsack-et-al-2022#p2 "Societies have a collective responsibility to ensure that digital practices help to improve the lives of all people, and that harms are prevented more effectively. Data solidarity provides a blueprint of how to make this happen") ✓.

## How NOT to read this

- **Not about neurotechnology.** The words neurotechnology, neural data and brain do not appear. The article is about health and digital data in general. Its application to neural data is made by [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (p. 3471, "echoing the concept of data solidarity") and by this wiki's [[data-solidarity]] page: an analogy drawn by others, not a claim of this article.
- **Not anti-consent.** "Individual control is important"; the claim is that it is insufficient. Do not cite it as rejecting consent-based protection.
- **Power asymmetry means processors versus data subjects**, mostly companies and citizens. Transferring the point to the State and a detainee ([[consent-in-custody]]) is a further analogy; the documents that make the custodial point are the Secretary-General and UNODC–INTERPOL, not this article.
- **Proposals, not law.** Harm mitigation bodies, multiplied fines, digital taxes and data commons are "one way", "could", "proposed". No instrument in the library adopts them.
- **The figure.** The public-value/risk matrix refers to a figure on PDF p. 1 that the passages do not reproduce; open the PDF to see it.
