- **Register.** A Comment in a medical journal; no human rights instrument is cited. It cannot support a claim about what the Covenant requires.

## Where it feeds the wiki

[[data-solidarity]] (the source of the concept: the three pillars and the public-value test); [[neural-data]] and [[is-neural-data-special]] (as the governance alternative to control-only protection that Szoszkiewicz & Yuste apply to neural data); [[regulatory-landscape]] and [[what-should-states-do-now]] (facilitate, prevent, return profits, as a template States could adapt); [[consent-in-custody]] (the "control is not enough" argument, by analogy only).

## Related

- [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (applies this article's model to neural data)
- [[data-solidarity]] (the concept page built on this source)
- [[neural-data]] (where control-based protection is weighed against solidarity)
- [[is-neural-data-special]] (whether neural data need a category of their own, or a governance model)
- [[consent-in-custody]] (power asymmetry and the limits of consent, as an analogy)
- [[what-should-states-do-now]] (facilitate, prevent, return profits)

pages.title: Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025: Mental privacy

frontmatter.title: Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025: Mental privacy

pages.body:
# Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025: Mental privacy

**Full cite.** Łukasz Szoszkiewicz and Rafael Yuste, "Mental privacy: navigating risks, rights and regulation", *EMBO Reports*, vol. 26 (July 2025), pp. 3469–3473, published online 25 June 2025, [doi:10.1038/s44319-025-00505-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44319-025-00505-6), CC BY 4.0. A five-page "Science & Society" piece. Its disclosure statement (PDF p. 5, not in the passages) says both authors are affiliated with the Neurorights Foundation.

**Register.** (f) scholarship. Łukasz Szoszkiewicz, the first author, is the trainer of this workshop. Read the page as his published position, pinned like any other source, not as authority: it weighs ½ on the ladder, and one General Comment outweighs it.

**One-liner.** Neural data are uniquely sensitive and largely unprotected outside medicine; the article maps the rules as of 2025 (Chile, three US states, the EU, soft law) and proposes three additions: user agency, restricted circulation (data solidarity or a medical-device model) and precaution.

## Key takeaways

**Definitions.** Mental privacy is "defined here as the protection of the mental activity of an individual"; neural data "are uniquely sensitive because they reveal our most intimate processes" and "reflect subconscious and involuntary activity" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "Mental privacy, defined here as the protection of the mental activity of an individual … Neural data are uniquely sensitive because they reveal our most intimate processes—thoughts, memories, mental states, emotions, behavior, personality and health conditions—and can even forecast future behavior … these signals also reflect subconscious and involuntary activity") ✓. Neural data are "information generated by measuring activity in the nervous systems, sometimes extending to inferences drawn from that data", "not limited to electrical brainwaves", and include peripheral signals such as EMG [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "information generated by measuring activity in the nervous systems, sometimes extending to inferences drawn from that data … neural data is not limited to electrical brainwaves … Some peripheral biosignals should also fall under the category of neural data: for example, muscle nerve signals (EMG)") ✓. The regulatory section uses a second, wider formulation [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "Neural data, defined here as any data collected by neurotechnological devices, are not classified as sensitive information when collected outside medical contexts by consumer products") ✓.

**Capabilities and risks.** Implanted sensors decoded attempted speech in ALS patients at "accuracy levels as high as 97.5%" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3469](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p1 "successfully decoded attempted speech in individuals with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), reaching accuracy levels as high as 97.5%") ✓; consumer EEG headsets decode attention and basic emotions "although with considerable variability between individuals" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "These devices can achieve satisfactory accuracy, although with considerable variability between individuals") ✓. The courtroom is named directly: the admission of wearable data in criminal proceedings "is already provoking intense debate", a reason, for the authors, to strengthen the right against self-incrimination [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "The question of if and how data extracted from wearables should be admitted in criminal proceedings is already provoking intense debate among legal experts … underlining the urgent need to strengthen protections for the right against self-incrimination in the era of neurotechnology") ✓.

**Human rights framing.** Intrusions on mental privacy "may, in some instances, amount to a violation of the freedom of thought and conscience", and neural data "must be treated as fundamentally distinct" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "intrusions on mental privacy may, in some instances, amount to a violation of the freedom of thought and conscience, an absolute right protected under international human rights law. If thought is inviolable, so too should be the data that can be used to infer it … neural data must be treated as fundamentally distinct, with enhanced safeguards") ✓.

**Regulatory approaches compared.** Chile's 2021 constitutional amendment protects "cerebral activity and the information drawn from it", applied in a 2023 Supreme Court ruling ordering a company to delete a consumer's neural data [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "Chile’s pioneering 2021 constitutional amendment, which protects “cerebral activity and the information drawn from it” … a 2023 unanimous ruling by Chile’s Supreme Court ordering a company to delete a consumer’s neural data") ✓. Three US states fold neural data into existing consumer privacy law [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "Colorado, California and Montana now explicitly include neurotechnology and neural data in their statutory definitions, and apply to these data existing consumer legislation for personal sensitive data") ✓. The GDPR offers "stronger safeguards for neural data than those in many other jurisdictions", yet "neurotechnology is not explicitly mentioned in the GDPR" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "already offer stronger safeguards for neural data than those in many other jurisdictions. Nevertheless, neurotechnology is not explicitly mentioned in the GDPR") ✓. Among soft-law steps, the Advisory Committee's call for General Comments is singled out [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "the UN Human Rights Council Advisory Committee recommended developing General Comments on the freedom of thought and mental integrity for persons with disabilities. General Comments offer authoritative interpretations of treaty obligations") ✓. The authors see a converging definition [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "“Neural data” is generally defined as information generated by measuring activity in the central or peripheral nervous systems, sometimes extending to inferences drawn from that data") ✓.

**What it proposes.** These steps "may be insufficient, as three critical vulnerabilities persist" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "we think that they may be insufficient, as three critical vulnerabilities persist that should be addressed") ✓. First, agency [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "users need to exert meaningful control over their own neural data … the consumer has no practical way to inspect, amend or delete the data that have been captured") ✓. Second, circulation: a total ban is the "hard-line solution"; the "more balanced alternative" is data solidarity [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "the circulation of neural data needs to be restricted, instead of driven by market forces … One hard-line solution would be to ban all sharing or trade of neural data. A more balanced alternative—echoing the concept of data solidarity—would treat neural data as a shared resource that serves the public good (Prainsack et al, 2022)") ✓, or else the medical model [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3472](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p4 "Another practical alternative is to follow the medical model and consider all neurotechnology, including consumer-grade, as medical devices") ✓. Third, precaution, including "temporary moratoria" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3472](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p4 "lawmakers should be guided by the precautionary principle … temporary moratoria on the most controversial neurotechnologies until longitudinal data accrue … guard against both premature bans and unchecked deployment") ✓. The conclusion warns against "alarmist narratives" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3472](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p4 "it is equally important to avoid alarmist narratives or overhyping potential harms or regulatory overreach") ✓.

## How NOT to read this

- **Not treaty law.** "May, in some instances, amount to a violation of the freedom of thought" is the authors' view. The Committee has not addressed neurotechnology ([[ccpr-c-21-rev-1-add-4]]); the Secretary-General records both sides of the new-rights debate ([[a-81-351]], para. 16; [[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]]).
- **Two definitions of neural data.** Page 3470 defines it by measurement of nervous-system activity (plus inferences); page 3471 by the device ("any data collected by neurotechnological devices"). The second is wider. Quote the one you mean.
- **Laboratory accuracy is not courtroom reliability.** The 97.5% figure is from implanted sensors in a research setting; the article itself reports "considerable variability between individuals" for consumer devices. See [[reliability-and-admissibility]].
- **Options, not one recommendation.** Data solidarity and the medical-device model are alternatives ("would", "could"); moratoria are "temporary" and on "the most controversial" technologies; the article warns against "premature bans".
- **The precautionary principle** is attributed to international human rights law via a cited source (Donders and Plozza, 2023), not via any treaty text or General Comment in the library.
- **Chile 2023.** The article does not name the parties; Futures Lab does (Girardi v. Emotiv): see [[chile-supreme-court-2023]].
- **Cited by the Secretary-General.** A/81/351 cites this article in footnote 7 (to para. 5, PDF p. 3, among the sources for the "broad consensus" that neural data are highly sensitive) and in footnote 25 (to para. 14, PDF p. 5, on consumer neural data reaching State authorities and courts), both read in the PDF. The pins to those paragraphs live on [[a-81-351]].

## Where it feeds the wiki

[[mental-privacy]] and [[neural-data]] (the definitions and their extensions to inferences and peripheral signals); [[is-neural-data-special]] (the "fundamentally distinct" claim); [[data-solidarity]] (the bridge to [[prainsack-et-al-2022]]); [[regulatory-landscape]], [[colorado-neural-data-law]], [[california-neural-data-law]] and [[chile-supreme-court-2023]] (the comparison; Montana is named only here and in A/81/351); [[moratorium]] (temporary moratoria as a precautionary step); [[self-incrimination]] (wearables in court).

## Related

- [[prainsack-et-al-2022]] (the data-solidarity source this article applies to neural data)
- [[a-81-351]] (cites this article in footnotes 7 and 25)
- [[neural-data]] (definition and scope)
- [[mental-privacy]] (the concept this article defines)
- [[data-solidarity]] (the governance model proposed here)
- [[regulatory-landscape]] (Chile, US states, EU, soft law)
- [[moratorium]] (precaution and temporary moratoria)

pages.title: UNODC–INTERPOL 2025: Neurotechnology, Law Enforcement and Criminal Justice (background paper)

frontmatter.title: UNODC–INTERPOL 2025: Neurotechnology, Law Enforcement and Criminal Justice (background paper)

pages.body:
# UNODC–INTERPOL 2025: Neurotechnology, Law Enforcement and Criminal Justice

**Full cite.** United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) and International Criminal Police Organization (INTERPOL), *Neurotechnology, Law Enforcement and Criminal Justice: background paper* (United Nations, October 2025; "© United Nations, October 2025. All rights reserved."), 8 printed pages, https://www.interpol.int/How-we-work/Innovation/INTERPOL-UNODC-Neurotechnology-assessment. The PDF has 11 pages; a printed page is the PDF page minus 3, and pin labels carry the printed page. The paper calls itself "preliminary thoughts" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 3](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p6 "This background paper shares some preliminary thoughts on the field of neurotechnology and its significance for law enforcement and the criminal justice system, focusing on opportunities, risks, and human rights safeguards") ✓, opens a consultation towards a Technology Assessment [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 6](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p9 "Building on this background paper, a Technology Assessment will be developed to provide more comprehensive guidance") ✓ and dates that document's presentation [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 8](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p11 "The final version of the Technology Assessment will be presented during the Fifteenth United Nations Congress on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice which will be held from 25 to 30 April 2026 in Abu Dhabi") ✓. Only this public paper is in the library.

**Register.** (c): a UN agency paper, written with a police organisation for a consultation. It is the only library document written from the law-enforcement side: it claims a "pivotal role" in guiding police [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 3](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p6 "UNODC and INTERPOL have a pivotal role to play in facilitating global dialogue, and in guiding law enforcement agencies and criminal justice institutions toward a responsible stance") ✓. It cites the Advisory Committee and the Special Rapporteur on the right to privacy; it makes no treaty analysis of its own.

**One-liner.** A consultation paper that lists what police and courts might do with neurotechnology, the rights at stake and the safeguards that must come first, then asks the field for evidence.

## Key takeaways

**Definition.** Neural data is [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 1](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p4 "information obtained by measuring the activity of a person's central or peripheral nervous system") ✓. Compare the UNESCO definition adopted in [[a-81-351]] (para. 5) and California's statutory one reported in [[futures-lab-2026]] (p. 4): the library holds three definitions, not one.

**Uses in view.** Lie detection and risk assessment first [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 1](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p4 "they are increasingly considered for use in criminal investigations for lie detection and risk assessments") ✓; then a wider list, including officer monitoring, with a readiness caveat [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 3](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p6 "Potential uses include memory detection, risk assessment, the decoding of thoughts in the form of words, or neuroenhancement … these use cases vary significantly in their level of scientific validity and technical readiness") ✓. Reintegration uses (neurofeedback, brain stimulation for violent offenders) rest on studies the paper itself calls preliminary [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 2](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p5 "many of these studies are preliminary") ✓.

**The test it proposes.** Benefit, then necessity and proportionality [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 3](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p6 "A demonstrable and significant benefit for law enforcement functions must also be shown, and the necessity and proportionality of their use assessed against the potential human rights impacts") ✓.

**Rights at stake.** Brain activity is "among the most intimate forms of personal information" and monitoring it "without genuine consent would represent a profound intrusion" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "Brain activity is among the most intimate forms of personal information … without genuine consent would represent a profound intrusion into human dignity, autonomy, and privacy") ✓. Due process is listed by name [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "Due process rights are also at stake, including the right to appear before a competent judicial authority, the presumption of innocence, the privilege against self-incrimination, and the right to appeal") ✓, and so is the "offered" use that is coercive in effect [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "under conditions in which individuals are “offered” the use of these technologies in ways that are coercive, or under the guise of moral-enhancement") ✓. Discrimination is "a key concern", relayed from the Advisory Committee [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "the potential for the discriminatory use of neurotechnologies … is a key concern") ✓. Governance must track the treaties "as interpreted by treaty monitoring bodies" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "clear governance frameworks that align innovation with human rights protection as established in human rights treaties and as interpreted by treaty monitoring bodies") ✓.

**Evidence.** Accuracy is open and admissibility case by case [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "questions remain about the accuracy of technologies that seek to detect memory or deception. While there is no standardized approach to this globally, courts in some jurisdictions have assessed the admissibility of neuroimaging evidence on a case-by-case basis") ✓. The paper asks, without answering [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 5](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p8 "Can courts legally order a criminal defendant, even in narrow circumstances, to cooperate with law enforcement in the use of neurotechnologies?") ✓.

**Safeguards.** A precondition of deployment [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 5](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p8 "Technologies should therefore not be deployed until their accuracy, safety, and feasibility have been rigorously demonstrated through independent testing and peer-reviewed research") ✓; control over neural data and judicial oversight [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 6](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p9 "Individuals must retain control over their neural data, and any interference with mental integrity or cognitive processes must be strictly limited, lawful, and subject to judicial oversight") ✓; consent in custody [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 6](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p9 "Consent must be voluntary and informed, free of coercion or undue influence, particularly in custodial or correctional settings where power imbalances are acute") ✓; rules on admissibility and oversight [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 6](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p9 "developing clear rules on admissibility of evidence, establishing independent mechanisms for oversight and accountability") ✓; harmonisation across borders [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 6](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p9 "international cooperation and harmonization of standards will be essential") ✓.

**Criminal misuse.** The paper's distinctive angle: attacks on BCIs and neural data as new crimes [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 5](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p8 "Unauthorized access to BCIs, manipulation of neural data, or the use of neurotechnologies for covert communication could present new and unprecedented threats") ✓, with "few legal frameworks in place to criminalize" them [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 3](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p6 "there are currently few legal frameworks in place to criminalize the malicious or irresponsible use of neurotechnologies") ✓.

## How NOT to read this

- Not the Technology Assessment. The paper announces that document; nothing in the library says what it contains, and this page says nothing about it.
- A law-enforcement perspective. It starts from "opportunities" and a "demonstrable and significant benefit" test; the Secretary-General starts from rights and recommends prohibiting coercive use ([[a-81-351]], para. 50 (c)); AHRC proposes a moratorium ([[ahrc-2025]]). Its "not be deployed until" is a validation condition, not a moratorium.
- "They have also been used to decode human thought in the form of words into text on a screen" (p. 1, PDF p. 4) describes research with consenting participants. [[a-81-351]] says neurotechnology "is not capable at present of mind-reading" (para. 22) and that decoding's reliability for justice is unknown (para. 11).
- Pages 7–8 are a call for submissions (questions, areas of focus, a deadline of 10 November 2025): a questionnaire, not findings.
- Printed page = PDF page minus 3. The pin labels are right; a reader paging the PDF by hand must subtract.

## Where it feeds the wiki

[[neural-data]] (the definition, p. 1); [[brain-based-lie-detection]] and [[reliability-and-admissibility]] (pp. 1, 4, 6); [[neuroprediction]] (risk assessment, pp. 1, 3); [[consent-in-custody]] and [[self-incrimination]] (pp. 4–6: the "offered" use, the court-order question, custodial consent); [[discrimination]] (pp. 2, 4, 6); [[moratorium]] (the validation precondition, p. 5); [[regulatory-landscape]] (pp. 3–4, 6: few frameworks, cross-border gaps, the forthcoming Assessment); [[what-should-states-do-now]] (section IV). Entities: [[a-hrc-57-61]] (cited at p. 4), [[iccpr-art-14-3-g]] (named at p. 4).

## Related

- [[a-81-351]] (para. 46 records the 2025 UNODC–INTERPOL collaboration; the rights-first counterpart)
- [[ahrc-2025]] (the NHRI that would pause criminal-justice use outright)
- [[futures-lab-2026]] (civil society; the same consent and discrimination themes, different vocabulary)
- [[a-hrc-57-61]] (the Advisory Committee report it relays on discrimination; inbox)

pages.title: Brain-based lie detection

frontmatter.title: Brain-based lie detection

pages.body:
# Brain-based lie detection

**One-liner.** An umbrella term for techniques that measure brain activity to infer deception, or recognition of crime-related information, in interrogation. The library describes fMRI "lie detection" and the "guilty knowledge" tests sold as "brain fingerprinting" and brain electrical oscillation signature profiling; reports that no method has general acceptance in court; and treats coercive use as a threat to article 14(3)(g), article 7 and freedom of thought. The Secretary-General recommends prohibiting compulsory or coercive use; the AHRC would suspend all use in criminal investigations pending an inquiry.

Terms this page covers: lie detection, deception detection and "brain-based deception technologies" (the Secretary-General's terms), "guilty knowledge" or concealed information testing, brain fingerprinting, brain electrical oscillation signature (BEOS) profiling, fMRI lie detection, polygraph (the predecessor), truthfulness, P300. A search for "lie detection" alone misses A/81/351 paras. 8, 9, 20 and 50 (c), which say "deception detection".

## What the library says

### (b) The General Comments say nothing about lie detection

No General Comment in the library mentions lie detection, deception or neurotechnology. Two Committee standards are applied to it by the reports: the article 14(3)(g) standard, "the absence of any direct or indirect physical or undue psychological pressure from the investigating authorities on the accused" [General Comment No. 32, para. 41](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p13 "the absence of any direct or indirect physical or undue psychological pressure from the investigating authorities on the accused") ✓ (see [[self-incrimination]]), and the forum internum rule that "no one can be compelled to reveal his thoughts" [General Comment No. 22, para. 3](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p2 "no one can be compelled to reveal his thoughts or adherence to a religion or belief") ✓ (see [[freedom-of-thought]]). Both are the Committee's words on other questions; their application to brain-based tests is the reports' work.

### (c) The Secretary-General (A/81/351) and UNODC–INTERPOL 2025

**What it is.** The Secretary-General defines brain-based deception detection as "an umbrella term for technologies that measure central nervous system activity with the goal of “detecting deception”", from which "probabilistic inferences are drawn about certain mental states and about cognitive processes, like memory or recognition of a place" [A/81/351, para. 8](pin:A/81/351#p4 "an umbrella term for technologies that measure central nervous system activity with the goal of “detecting deception”. From the neural data retrieved, probabilistic inferences are drawn about certain mental states and about cognitive processes, like memory or recognition of a place") ✓. He distinguishes fMRI "lie detection" from "“guilty knowledge” or “concealed information” testing, which are commercialized under labels such as “brain fingerprinting” and brain electrical oscillation signature profiling" [A/81/351, para. 8](pin:A/81/351#p4 "“guilty knowledge” or “concealed information” testing, which are commercialized under labels such as “brain fingerprinting” and brain electrical oscillation signature profiling") ✓; the latter "measure physiological or brain responses to determine whether a person recognizes concealed or crime-related information" [A/81/351, para. 8](pin:A/81/351#p4 "measure physiological or brain responses to determine whether a person recognizes concealed or crime-related information") ✓. Such use is rarer than neuroimaging as expert evidence: "Less commonly, neurotechnology has been used in interrogation contexts, especially for brain-based deception detection" [A/81/351, para. 8](pin:A/81/351#p4 "Less commonly, neurotechnology has been used in interrogation contexts, especially for brain-based deception detection") ✓.

**Reliability and courts.** "No brain-based deception detection method has achieved general acceptance for courtroom use" [A/81/351, para. 9](pin:A/81/351#p4 "No brain-based deception detection method has achieved general acceptance for courtroom use") ✓. The report gives two cases. "A United States federal appeals court excluded lie detection evidence based on functional magnetic resonance imaging, finding it insufficiently reliable and not generally accepted under evidentiary standards" [A/81/351, para. 9](pin:A/81/351#p4 "A United States federal appeals court excluded lie detection evidence based on functional magnetic resonance imaging, finding it insufficiently reliable and not generally accepted under evidentiary standards") ✓ (its footnote 16, on the same PDF page, names United States v. Semrau, Sixth Circuit, 12 April 2012). The Supreme Court of India "held that the involuntary administration of brain electrical oscillation signature profiling tests violates the constitutional protection against self-incrimination and renders the resulting evidence inadmissible" [A/81/351, para. 9](pin:A/81/351#p4 "held that the involuntary administration of brain electrical oscillation signature profiling tests violates the constitutional protection against self-incrimination and renders the resulting evidence inadmissible") ✓; para. 32 names the case, and its footnote 63 (PDF p. 11) cites paras. 215–224 of the judgment; see [[selvi-v-state-of-karnataka]]. Yet "voluntary use appears to have continued in practice" [A/81/351, para. 9](pin:A/81/351#p4 "However, voluntary use appears to have continued in practice") ✓ (footnote 18, same PDF page, cites a 2025 news article in Science, not a court record).

**Rights engaged.** Dignity: "If these signals are treated as direct indicators of thoughts, intentions or truthfulness, the use of neural data points could undermine how we understand and value each of us as human beings" [A/81/351, para. 18](pin:A/81/351#p6 "If these signals are treated as direct indicators of thoughts, intentions or truthfulness, the use of neural data points could undermine how we understand and value each of us as human beings") ✓. Freedom of thought: deception detection "could reveal information that the person has not chosen to disclose" [A/81/351, para. 20](pin:A/81/351#p7 "Neurotechnologies used to infer mental states, memory or recognition, through brain-based deception detection technology or decoding, could reveal information that the person has not chosen to disclose") ✓. Articles 7 and 10(1): brain-based lie detection "applied in detention or investigative contexts, may result in mental or physical suffering" [A/81/351, para. 28](pin:A/81/351#p9 "The use of brain-based lie detection, decoding of readable information about thoughts, intentions or memories, coercive interrogation techniques, and neuromodulation, applied in detention or investigative contexts, may result in mental or physical suffering contravening the protection provided under articles 7 and 10 (1)") ✓. Article 14(3)(g): "The coercive use of brain-based lie detection could call into question the privilege against self-incrimination" [A/81/351, para. 32](pin:A/81/351#p10 "The coercive use of brain-based lie detection could call into question the privilege against self-incrimination, protected under article 14 (3) (g) of the Covenant") ✓. Article 9: using "brain-based deception technologies to determine whether a person should be detained, may lead to arbitrary detention" [A/81/351, para. 34](pin:A/81/351#p11 "the use of brain-based deception technologies to determine whether a person should be detained, may lead to arbitrary detention under article 9") ✓. Discrimination: tools rely on "non-representative, male-centric data sets that can distort assessments of veracity" [A/81/351, para. 37](pin:A/81/351#p12 "non-representative, male-centric data sets that can distort assessments of veracity or recidivism risk") ✓. Every verb here is "could" or "may".

**The recommendation.** "Prohibit the compulsory or coercive use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice, including brain-based deception detection" [A/81/351, para. 50 (c)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Prohibit the compulsory or coercive use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice, including brain-based deception detection") ✓. It targets compulsory or coercive use; it does not ask for a ban on voluntary use (see [[consent-in-custody]]).

UNODC and INTERPOL record that neurotechnologies "are increasingly considered for use in criminal investigations for lie detection and risk assessments" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 1](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p4 "they are increasingly considered for use in criminal investigations for lie detection and risk assessments") ✓, list "memory detection" among potential uses that "vary significantly in their level of scientific validity and technical readiness" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 3](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p6 "Potential uses include memory detection, risk assessment, the decoding of thoughts in the form of words, or neuroenhancement … these use cases vary significantly in their level of scientific validity and technical readiness") ✓, and state that "questions remain about the accuracy of technologies that seek to detect memory or deception" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "questions remain about the accuracy of technologies that seek to detect memory or deception") ✓.

### (d) The Australian Human Rights Commission (2025)

The AHRC places the techniques in a lineage: "Lie detector mechanisms (such as polygraph testing) have been used by authorities since the 1940s. However, there is well established scepticism surrounding their use" [AHRC 2025, p. 31](pin:AHRC-2025#p31 "Lie detector mechanisms (such as polygraph testing) have been used by authorities since the 1940s. However, there is well established scepticism surrounding their use due to their reliance on physiological responses to determine guilt") ✓. It describes the claim as a claim: "operators of neurotechnology claim to be able to detect the presence of concealed information through the monitoring of brain waves", via EEG, fMRI, PET and SPECT, "a method otherwise known as ‘brain fingerprinting’" [AHRC 2025, p. 31](pin:AHRC-2025#p31 "operators of neurotechnology claim to be able to detect the presence of concealed information through the monitoring of brain waves … a method otherwise known as ‘brain fingerprinting’") ✓. It reports, as an allegation, that "police in Dubai are alleged to have already acquired neural devices which have been used in their investigations to determine if a suspect has a guilty mind" [AHRC 2025, p. 31](pin:AHRC-2025#p31 "police in Dubai are alleged to have already acquired neural devices which have been used in their investigations to determine if a suspect has a guilty mind") ✓. When it writes that "The UN has stated that the use of neurotechnology as a form of lie detection is particularly concerning" [AHRC 2025, p. 31](pin:AHRC-2025#p31 "The UN has stated that the use of neurotechnology as a form of lie detection is particularly concerning, and claimed that neurotechnology is already being used for this purpose") ✓, its endnote 143 (PDF p. 78) cites A/HRC/57/61, para. 47: "the UN" here is the Human Rights Council Advisory Committee, whose report waits in the inbox ([[a-hrc-57-61]]), not a treaty body.

**A case study to handle with care.** The AHRC reports that in 1999 Lawrence Farwell administered brain fingerprinting to J. B. Grinder and that the test detected details of the crime "with a statistical confidence of 99.9%" [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "After agreeing to do the test, it detected that specific details of the crime were recorded in Grinder’s brain, with a statistical confidence of 99.9%") ✓. The figure is one the AHRC reports from a secondary source: its endnotes 152 and 153 (PDF p. 78) cite a 2012 review by Farwell himself, the developer of the technique. Nothing in the library validates the figure, and the Secretary-General's finding that no method has general acceptance stands against it. Do not repeat it as fact.

The AHRC also notes a different use, stimulation "to reduce the ability of people to lie" [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "neurotechnology could be used to reduce the ability of people to lie. For example, transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) or transcranial direct stimulation (TDS) can cause changes in brain activity") ✓, which belongs with [[neuromodulation-of-offenders]].

Its conclusion is procedural. Given "neurotechnology’s ability to overtake a jury’s role in assessing witness credibility and determining truth – in conjunction with grave risks to the right to silence, it is preferable to err on the side of caution" [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "given neurotechnology’s ability to overtake a jury’s role in assessing witness credibility and determining truth – in conjunction with grave risks to the right to silence, it is preferable to err on the side of caution") ✓, and so "The Commission’s preliminary view is that a moratorium on the use of neurotechnology in criminal investigations should be imposed until the ALRC has published the findings of the recommended inquiry. Additionally, until that time, information gained via neurotechnology should be inadmissible at trial" [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "The Commission’s preliminary view is that a moratorium on the use of neurotechnology in criminal investigations should be imposed until the ALRC has published the findings of the recommended inquiry. Additionally, until that time, information gained via neurotechnology should be inadmissible at trial") ✓. See [[moratorium]]. This is an NHRI's "preliminary view", addressed to one government.

### (e) Civil society

The Futures Lab submission is the one document that calls the prospect promising: "While there is promise in neurotechnology’s assistance in assessing guilt, accountability, and the risk of recidivism in judicial proceedings, it also carries risks regarding access to the regulatory process" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 3](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p4 "While there is promise in neurotechnology’s assistance in assessing guilt, accountability, and the risk of recidivism in judicial proceedings, it also carries risks regarding access to the regulatory process") ✓. It warns that policing use "could expand into brain-reading of suspects or witnesses" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 6](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p7 "its use in policing could expand into brain-reading of suspects or witnesses") ✓, and reports that France "was the first country to allow brain imaging in judicial proceedings with consent … except for functional brain imaging" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 3](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p4 "France was the first country to allow brain imaging in judicial proceedings with consent, for medical or scientific research, or for forensic expertise, except for functional brain imaging") ✓: domestic law, reported by a submission that criticises how it was adopted.

### (f) Scholarship

Neither journal article discusses lie detection. The library's only mention of the P300 is in Szoszkiewicz and Yuste, where consumer EEG headsets "detect brainwaves and “P300” responses to control smartphone applications" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "These detect brainwaves and “P300” responses to control smartphone applications, decode states such as attention, relaxation and basic emotions") ✓. The library does not connect the P300 to deception detection, so this wiki does not either.

## Open questions

- Validation: the Secretary-General calls the inferences "probabilistic" and no method generally accepted; the AHRC repeats a 99.9% figure that traces to the technique's developer. The library contains no independent validation study. See [[reliability-and-admissibility]].
- Voluntary use "appears to have continued": the Secretary-General's prohibition targets compulsory or coercive use, and the Indian holding concerns "involuntary administration". Whether consent in custody can be free is the question on [[consent-in-custody]] and [[can-a-suspect-consent-to-lie-detection]].
- Exculpatory use: the AHRC's R v Murray example is a test tendered by the accused; the Secretary-General's framework is written against the State. The library does not say whether an accused may insist on a test.
- Is the output "testimony"? See [[self-incrimination]].

## Related

- [[self-incrimination]] (the guarantee the reports apply)
- [[consent-in-custody]] (whether "voluntary" use is voluntary)
- [[reliability-and-admissibility]] (no general acceptance; Semrau; validation)
- [[freedom-of-thought]] (information "the person has not chosen to disclose")
- [[iccpr-art-14-3-g]], [[iccpr-art-7]], [[iccpr-art-9]] (the articles engaged)
- [[moratorium]] (the AHRC's preliminary view)
- [[neuromodulation-of-offenders]] (stimulation to reduce the ability to lie)
- [[selvi-v-state-of-karnataka]] (the BEOS case)
- [[a-hrc-57-61]] (the Advisory Committee report behind the AHRC's "the UN has stated")
- [[a-81-351]], [[unodc-interpol-2025]], [[ahrc-2025]], [[futures-lab-2026]], [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (source pages)
- [[can-a-suspect-consent-to-lie-detection]] (the question page)

pages.title: Consent in custody

frontmatter.title: Consent in custody

pages.body:
# Consent in custody

**One-liner.** Every document that addresses consent to neurotechnology in detention, interrogation or sentencing treats it as fragile. The Secretary-General would require free, prior, informed, explicit and revocable consent and subject it to "the highest evidentiary standards"; UNODC and INTERPOL want consent "free of coercion or undue influence, particularly in custodial or correctional settings"; the AHRC doubts that consent given against a reduced sentence is voluntary. No document says consent alone makes brain-based lie detection lawful.

Terms this page covers: consent, voluntary and voluntariness, free and informed consent, genuine consent, inducement (a reduced sentence, immunity, early release, parole), coercion, undue influence, power imbalance, custody, detention, correctional settings, "offered".

## What the library says

### (a) Treaty text

Article 7 of the Covenant adds, after the prohibition of torture, that no one shall be subjected without his free consent to medical or scientific experimentation ([ICCPR art. 7](https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-mechanisms/instruments/international-covenant-civil-and-political-rights), not in the library); see [[iccpr-art-7]]. The Secretary-General and the AHRC both quote that sentence (below).

### (b) The Human Rights Committee, General Comment No. 32

The Committee's words concern confessions, not consent to a test. The article 14(3)(g) standard already reaches indirect and psychological pressure: "the absence of any direct or indirect physical or undue psychological pressure from the investigating authorities on the accused" [General Comment No. 32, para. 41](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p13 "the absence of any direct or indirect physical or undue psychological pressure from the investigating authorities on the accused, with a view to obtaining a confession of guilt") ✓. Where article 7 is in issue, "the burden is on the State to prove that statements made by the accused have been given of their own free will" [General Comment No. 32, para. 41](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p13 "the burden is on the State to prove that statements made by the accused have been given of their own free will") ✓. Exculpatory material the defence must see includes "indications that a confession was not voluntary" [General Comment No. 32, para. 33](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p10 "indications that a confession was not voluntary") ✓. The General Comment does not say what makes consent to a procedure free; the reports supply that. See [[general-comment-32]].

### (c) The Secretary-General (A/81/351) and UNODC–INTERPOL 2025

Consent is the first of four concerns the Secretary-General attaches to deception detection, "consent, coercion, reliability, and the privilege against self-incrimination" [A/81/351, para. 9](pin:A/81/351#p4 "raise serious concerns regarding consent, coercion, reliability, and the privilege against self-incrimination") ✓, and he records that "voluntary use appears to have continued in practice" [A/81/351, para. 9](pin:A/81/351#p4 "voluntary use appears to have continued in practice") ✓ after the Indian court struck down involuntary administration (see [[brain-based-lie-detection]]).

The fullest treatment is in the article 7 section, on neuromodulation of offenders. The report attributes to the Human Rights Council Advisory Committee the view that such techniques "may constitute treatment contrary to articles 7 or 10 of the Covenant when imposed without genuinely free and informed consent" [A/81/351, para. 29](pin:A/81/351#p10 "may constitute treatment contrary to articles 7 or 10 of the Covenant when imposed without genuinely free and informed consent") ✓ (the Advisory Committee's own report, [[a-hrc-57-61]], is in the inbox and is not pinned here). It then states in its own voice that "In custodial settings, the pronounced power imbalance between the State and the individual may call into question the genuineness of consent", and attributes to experts the view that where techniques "are presented in connection with prospects such as early release or favourable parole outcomes, there is a significant risk that consent may not be fully free or voluntary" [A/81/351, para. 29](pin:A/81/351#p10 "In custodial settings, the pronounced power imbalance between the State and the individual may call into question the genuineness of consent. Experts affirm that where such techniques are presented in connection with prospects such as early release or favourable parole outcomes, there is a significant risk that consent may not be fully free or voluntary") ✓ (its footnote 56, on the same PDF page, cites a UNODC submission and the AHRC report). It quotes article 7's free-consent sentence and adds that "The difficulty of establishing that consent is genuinely free given the particularly vulnerable status of those who are detained has been acknowledged by the Human Rights Committee" [A/81/351, para. 29](pin:A/81/351#p10 "The difficulty of establishing that consent is genuinely free given the particularly vulnerable status of those who are detained has been acknowledged by the Human Rights Committee") ✓. That acknowledgement is reported, not pinned: footnotes 57 and 58 on the same PDF page cite General Comment No. 20 (1992), para. 7, which is not in the library. See [[neuromodulation-of-offenders]].

The recommendations set consent as a gate, never as a licence. States should "Prohibit the compulsory or coercive use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice" [A/81/351, para. 50 (c)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Prohibit the compulsory or coercive use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice, including brain-based deception detection") ✓; "Require free, prior, informed, explicit and revocable consent for any potential use of neurotechnology in the administration of justice, accompanied by full transparency regarding risks, access to independent legal counsel of one’s own choice and effective avenues for redress", and, "Given the constrained and coercive nature of justice settings, any consent should be subject to the highest evidentiary standards and rigorous scrutiny" [A/81/351, para. 50 (e)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Require free, prior, informed, explicit and revocable consent for any potential use of neurotechnology in the administration of justice, accompanied by full transparency regarding risks, access to independent legal counsel of one’s own choice and effective avenues for redress. Given the constrained and coercive nature of justice settings, any consent should be subject to the highest evidentiary standards and rigorous scrutiny") ✓; and "Ensure enhanced safeguards for children, detainees" and others "with particular attention to the conditions of consent" [A/81/351, para. 50 (g)](pin:A/81/351#p16 "Ensure enhanced safeguards for children, detainees … with particular attention to the conditions of consent") ✓. Read together, 50 (c) and 50 (e) leave room for a consented use that passes "the highest evidentiary standards"; the report never says which use would.

UNODC and INTERPOL make the same two moves. Without consent the intrusion is grave: "any attempt to monitor, decode or manipulate it for identification, investigative, preventive or therapeutic purposes without genuine consent would represent a profound intrusion into human dignity, autonomy, and privacy" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "any attempt to monitor, decode or manipulate it for identification, investigative, preventive or therapeutic purposes without genuine consent would represent a profound intrusion into human dignity, autonomy, and privacy") ✓. And consent can itself be a form of coercion: "there is concern about the potential for neurotechnology to be used coercively, or under conditions in which individuals are “offered” the use of these technologies in ways that are coercive, or under the guise of moral-enhancement, or similar" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "there is concern about the potential for neurotechnology to be used coercively, or under conditions in which individuals are “offered” the use of these technologies in ways that are coercive, or under the guise of moral-enhancement, or similar") ✓. Among its safeguards: "ensuring voluntary and informed consent from individuals" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 6](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p9 "key precautionary measures must be implemented, including, but not limited to, establishing clear legal and ethical frameworks to protect human rights, ensuring voluntary and informed consent from individuals") ✓, and "Consent must be voluntary and informed, free of coercion or undue influence, particularly in custodial or correctional settings where power imbalances are acute" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 6](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p9 "Consent must be voluntary and informed, free of coercion or undue influence, particularly in custodial or correctional settings where power imbalances are acute") ✓. The paper also asks, without answering, whether "courts [can] legally order a criminal defendant, even in narrow circumstances, to cooperate" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 5](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p8 "Can courts legally order a criminal defendant, even in narrow circumstances, to cooperate with law enforcement in the use of neurotechnologies?") ✓.

### (d) The Australian Human Rights Commission (2025)

The AHRC supplies the concrete scenario. "The right to remain silent not only protects against direct pressure but also indirect pressure, which may arise in informing an accused of the consequences of refusing to undergo questioning via neurotechnology" [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "The right to remain silent not only protects against direct pressure but also indirect pressure, which may arise in informing an accused of the consequences of refusing to undergo questioning via neurotechnology") ✓. "if an accused was offered the opportunity for a reduced sentence or some level of immunity in exchange for consenting to the use of neurotechnology during questioning by police, it would be difficult to argue that any consent given was entirely voluntary" [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "if an accused was offered the opportunity for a reduced sentence or some level of immunity in exchange for consenting to the use of neurotechnology during questioning by police, it would be difficult to argue that any consent given was entirely voluntary") ✓. The reason is structural: "the imbalance of power in a criminal investigation and the indirect pressure that might attach by virtue of the consequences of refusing to consent" [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "Considering the imbalance of power in a criminal investigation and the indirect pressure that might attach by virtue of the consequences of refusing to consent to the use of neurotechnology during questioning, this could foreseeably have serious implications for the right to remain silent and not self-incriminate") ✓. At sentencing the same worry returns: consent "could be used transactionally for sentence reduction or an earlier parole – despite the offender’s preference not to be the subject of a neurointervention in the absence of such incentives" [AHRC 2025, p. 35](pin:AHRC-2025#p35 "consent to the use of neurotechnology could be used transactionally for sentence reduction or an earlier parole – despite the offender’s preference not to be the subject of a neurointervention in the absence of such incentives") ✓; some offenders "may be unduly pressured into accepting it" [AHRC 2025, p. 35](pin:AHRC-2025#p35 "others may be unduly pressured into accepting it") ✓. Its general point, written about medical users rather than detainees, travels in structure if not in finding: "Consent may be illusory when people must make a choice that is starkly binary: either consent to the conditions set, or do not receive the technology" [AHRC 2025, p. 62](pin:AHRC-2025#p62 "Consent may be illusory when people must make a choice that is starkly binary: either consent to the conditions set, or do not receive the technology") ✓. Its remedy for investigations is not a consent test but a moratorium and interim inadmissibility (see [[moratorium]]).

### (e) Civil society

The Futures Lab submission anchors consent in bioethics: UNESCO's Universal Declaration on Bioethics and Human Rights, article 6, requires that "all scientific and medical interventions must be carried out with the individual’s prior, free, and informed consent" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "all scientific and medical interventions must be carried out with the individual’s prior, free, and informed consent") ✓, and it asks States to "ensure free, prior, and informed consent" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "ensure free, prior, and informed consent") ✓. It would also cap what consent can do: "Individuals should not be able to consent to overly broad uses of neurotechnology until clear and established neurorights are in place" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 7](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p8 "Individuals should not be able to consent to overly broad uses of neurotechnology until clear and established neurorights are in place") ✓. Its Chilean example is a consumer case, not a custodial one: commercialisation "cannot rely solely on click-through consent" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 2](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p3 "demonstrates that commercialization cannot rely solely on click-through consent") ✓.

### (f) Scholarship

Szoszkiewicz and Yuste write about consumers, not detainees: headsets stream data "under wafer-thin consent" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "Consumer-grade headsets often stream raw brain signals or algorithmic inferences under wafer-thin consent") ✓, and "True agency requires that individuals retain ongoing, transparent control over their neural data" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "True agency requires that individuals retain ongoing, transparent control over their neural data") ✓. Nothing in the two journal articles addresses consent in custody.

## Contested claims

```contested
claim: A suspect's genuinely free and informed consent can make brain-based lie detection lawful.
verdict: leans-contest
note: No document says consent alone suffices. The (c) reports make consent a necessary gate under "the highest evidentiary standards"; the NHRI and the civil-society submission would not rely on consent in custody at all; no General Comment addresses consent to a brain-based test.
~ c | [A/81/351, para. 50 (e)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Require free, prior, informed, explicit and revocable consent for any potential use of neurotechnology in the administration of justice … any consent should be subject to the highest evidentiary standards and rigorous scrutiny") ✓ | consent required for any use, under the highest scrutiny: a gate, not a licence | [[a-81-351]]
~ c | [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 6](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p9 "Consent must be voluntary and informed, free of coercion or undue influence, particularly in custodial or correctional settings where power imbalances are acute") ✓ | consent as a safeguard, with custody flagged as the hard case | [[unodc-interpol-2025]]
- d | [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "it would be difficult to argue that any consent given was entirely voluntary") ✓ | consent against a reduced sentence or immunity is not voluntary; moratorium and inadmissibility instead | [[ahrc-2025]]
- e | [Futures Lab 2026, p. 7](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p8 "Individuals should not be able to consent to overly broad uses of neurotechnology until clear and established neurorights are in place") ✓ | consent should be limited in scope until standards exist | [[futures-lab-2026]]
```

## Open questions

- The library names the pressures (power imbalance, inducements, the consequences of refusal) but gives no test for when consent in custody is free. The Secretary-General's "highest evidentiary standards" is a burden of proof, not a test.
- "Revocable" consent (50 (e)) in a test that runs in minutes: the library does not say what revocation would mean for data already recorded. See [[neural-data]].
- Consent by the accused to an exculpatory test (the AHRC's R v Murray) is a different case from consent sought by the State; no document treats it separately.
- Consent and admissibility are separate questions: a freely consented test can still fail on reliability. See [[reliability-and-admissibility]].

## Related

- [[can-a-suspect-consent-to-lie-detection]] (the question page that answers this card)
- [[self-incrimination]] (the standard: direct or indirect, physical or undue psychological pressure)
- [[brain-based-lie-detection]] (the use consent is asked for; "voluntary use appears to have continued")
- [[neuromodulation-of-offenders]] (consent against early release or parole)
- [[reliability-and-admissibility]] (consent does not settle reliability)
- [[moratorium]] (the AHRC's alternative to a consent test)
- [[iccpr-art-7]] (free consent to experimentation) and [[iccpr-art-14-3-g]] (compulsion)
- [[general-comment-32]] (the burden on the State to prove free will)
- [[neural-data]] (what revocation would have to cover)
- [[a-hrc-57-61]] (the Advisory Committee view the Secretary-General reports)
- [[a-81-351]], [[unodc-interpol-2025]], [[ahrc-2025]], [[futures-lab-2026]], [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (source pages)
- [[what-should-states-do-now]] (recommendation 50 (e) among the asks)

pages.title: Data solidarity

frontmatter.title: Data solidarity

pages.body:
# Data solidarity

**One-liner.** A way of governing data collectively rather than only through each person's consent: support uses with public value, prohibit harmful ones, return profits to the public. Proposed for health data in 2022; applied to neural data by one article in the library; no UN document, NHRI or civil-society submission in the library uses the term.

## What the library says

Only two documents use the term, both scholarship (f), and both co-authored by the trainer of this workshop. No General Comment (b), UN report (c), NHRI report (d) or civil-society submission (e) in the library mentions data solidarity.

**The idea (health data).** Prainsack et al. start from a diagnosis: frameworks that rely on individual control "are not enough" [Prainsack et al. 2022, p. e773](pin:Prainsack-et-al-2022#p1 "regulatory frameworks that seek to prevent harm mostly by strengthening the control that individuals have over their data are not enough") ✓, because control "cannot address the vast power asymmetries between data processors and data subjects" [Prainsack et al. 2022, p. e773](pin:Prainsack-et-al-2022#p1 "Although individual control is important, it cannot address the vast power asymmetries between data processors and data subjects") ✓. Their answer has three parts [Prainsack et al. 2022, p. e773](pin:Prainsack-et-al-2022#p1 "It consists of three main pillars: facilitating good data use (pillar 1); preventing and mitigating harm (pillar 2); and returning profits to the public domain (pillar 3).") ✓:

- **Public value decides.** Data use with little public value and substantial risk "should be prohibited", while low-risk, beneficial use "should receive more public support" [Prainsack et al. 2022, p. e773](pin:Prainsack-et-al-2022#p1 "Data use that creates little or no public value but poses substantial risks should be prohibited, with fines severe enough to deter even powerful corporations from breaking the law, and effective enforcement") ✓.
- **Remedies for harm** that remains, e.g. "harm mitigation bodies" next to existing legal remedies [Prainsack et al. 2022, p. e773](pin:Prainsack-et-al-2022#p1 "One way to reach this goal is the creation of harm mitigation bodies at regional, national, or supranational level that would complement existing legal remedies.") ✓.
- **Profits back** to the people and communities that made them possible, by taxation or data commons [Prainsack et al. 2022, p. e774](pin:Prainsack-et-al-2022#p2 "Where commercial profits accrue from data use, some of these profits need to come back to the people and communities that enabled them in the first place.") ✓.

**The application to neural data.** Szoszkiewicz & Yuste offer data solidarity as the middle course between a market in neural data and a ban on sharing it: neural data as "a shared resource that serves the public good" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "A more balanced alternative—echoing the concept of data solidarity—would treat neural data as a shared resource that serves the public good (Prainsack et al, 2022).") ✓. They set it beside the medical-device model as a path that "both protects individual rights and unlocks neural data for socially beneficial purposes" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3472](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p4 "data solidarity governance offers a path that both protects individual rights and unlocks neural data for socially beneficial purposes") ✓, and close by naming "user agency, solidarity and precaution" as the principles a legal framework should implement [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3472](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p4 "implement the principles of user agency, solidarity and precaution") ✓. Precaution may include "temporary moratoria on the most controversial neurotechnologies" (see [[moratorium]]) [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3472](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p4 "temporary moratoria on the most controversial neurotechnologies until longitudinal data accrue") ✓.

Read together: data solidarity answers a governance question (who decides which uses of data go ahead, and who gains), not the category question that [[is-neural-data-special]] asks (whether neural data need a legal class of their own).

## How NOT to read this

- Prainsack et al. 2022 is about health and digital data in general. It never mentions neurotechnology or criminal justice. The step to neural data is Szoszkiewicz & Yuste's, three years later.
- Both are (f) scholarship, written partly by the workshop's trainer. Neither is a statement of what international law requires.
- In custody, "power asymmetries" take a sharper form than between a company and its users. The library does not apply data solidarity there; [[consent-in-custody]] collects what it does say about that setting.

## Open questions

- Could data solidarity's public-value test work in the administration of justice, where the "public" interest is often the State's own interest in conviction?
- Who would sit on a "harm mitigation body" for neural data, and would it reach police and prison uses?
- The Secretary-General's recommendations (see [[what-should-states-do-now]]) speak of safeguards and prohibitions, not of collective governance: an ingest of A/HRC/57/61 may show whether the Advisory Committee goes further.

## Related

- [[prainsack-et-al-2022]] (where the idea comes from)
- [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (its application to neural data)
- [[neural-data]] (the data to be governed)
- [[mental-privacy]] (what individual protection covers)
- [[regulatory-landscape]] (the laws that exist now)
- [[is-neural-data-special]] (the category question, a different one)
- [[moratorium]] (precaution, the third principle)

pages.title: Discrimination and neurotechnology

frontmatter.title: Discrimination and neurotechnology

pages.body:
# Discrimination and neurotechnology

**One-liner.** Every document in the library that touches criminal justice says the same thing in its own register: neurotechnology in the administration of justice will fall hardest on people already over-represented in it and under-represented in the data it is built on. General Comment No. 32 gives the (b) baseline (equality before courts; no procedural distinctions on article 2 (1) or 26 grounds); the Secretary-General names the groups and recommends enhanced safeguards; UNODC–INTERPOL, the AHRC and Futures Lab agree on the mechanism: biased data, tools validated on narrow populations, structural inequality.

## What the library says

### (b) The Human Rights Committee

General Comment No. 32 predates neurotechnology; its rules apply to any evidence or tool. Equality before courts "ensures that the parties to the proceedings in question are treated without any discrimination" [General Comment No. 32, para. 8](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p2 "ensures that the parties to the proceedings in question are treated without any discrimination") ✓. Racial bias in the tribunal is a fairness defect: "Expressions of racist attitudes by a jury … or a racially biased jury selection are other instances which adversely affect the fairness of the procedure" [General Comment No. 32, para. 25](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p7 "Expressions of racist attitudes by a jury … or a racially biased jury selection are other instances which adversely affect the fairness of the procedure") ✓. Procedural rules that distinguish on the grounds in articles 2 (1) or 26 "may also amount to discrimination" [General Comment No. 32, para. 65](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p18 "Procedural laws or their application that make distinctions based on any of the criteria listed in article 2, paragraph 1 or article 26 … may also amount to discrimination") ✓.

### (c) The Secretary-General, A/81/351

Non-discrimination is among the rights the report says neurotechnology "may engage", alongside CERD, CEDAW, the CRC and the CRPD [A/81/351, para. 15](pin:A/81/351#p5 "freedom of thought, expression and opinion, non-discrimination and an effective remedy. Other relevant treaties include … the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination") ✓. The groups are the Advisory Committee's, "groups experiencing structural discrimination and marginalized people or those in positions of socioeconomic disadvantage", and the mechanism is the report's: "Discrimination stems from biased training data, tools validated on limited populations and structural inequalities in criminal justice systems" [A/81/351, para. 37](pin:A/81/351#p12 "groups experiencing structural discrimination and marginalized people or those in positions of socioeconomic disadvantage … Discrimination stems from biased training data, tools validated on limited populations and structural inequalities in criminal justice systems") ✓ (the citation is to A/HRC/57/61, para. 37, the Advisory Committee's report [[a-hrc-57-61]], in the inbox). Women are exposed to "non-representative, male-centric data sets that can distort assessments of veracity or recidivism risk" [A/81/351, para. 37](pin:A/81/351#p12 "non-representative, male-centric data sets that can distort assessments of veracity or recidivism risk") ✓.

"Technology is never neutral": people of African descent and racialized minorities "are disproportionately affected by algorithmic bias in data sets that underrepresent them and by predictive tools that mirror and amplify historical discrimination", Indigenous Peoples and minorities are more exposed "given their disproportionate representation in criminal justice systems", and "Inclusive validation, cultural competence, community-based governance, accountability and the meaningful participation of affected groups are essential preconditions for the lawful deployment of neurotechnology" [A/81/351, para. 39](pin:A/81/351#p12 "disproportionately affected by algorithmic bias in data sets that underrepresent them and by predictive tools that mirror and amplify historical discrimination … given their disproportionate representation in criminal justice systems … Inclusive validation, cultural competence, community-based governance, accountability and the meaningful participation of affected groups are essential preconditions for the lawful deployment of neurotechnology") ✓. Persons with disabilities and neurodivergent people "may experience misinterpretation of atypical neural patterns, pressure towards forced “normalization” and discrimination on the basis of neurological difference" [A/81/351, para. 41](pin:A/81/351#p13 "persons with disabilities and neurodivergent individuals may experience misinterpretation of atypical neural patterns, pressure towards forced “normalization” and discrimination on the basis of neurological difference") ✓. Children's exposure to predictive labelling is on [[neuroprediction]]. The recommendation: "enhanced safeguards for children, detainees, persons with disabilities, women, older persons, persons belonging to particular racial or ethnic groups, including people of African descent, Indigenous Peoples and persons in situations of vulnerability", with consultation of affected groups [A/81/351, para. 50 (g)](pin:A/81/351#p16 "Ensure enhanced safeguards for children, detainees, persons with disabilities, women, older persons, persons belonging to particular racial or ethnic groups, including people of African descent, Indigenous Peoples and persons in situations of vulnerability") ✓, and regulation with "data-testing protocols and thresholds to identify and mitigate risks of algorithmic bias" [A/81/351, para. 50 (a)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "including data-testing protocols and thresholds to identify and mitigate risks of algorithmic bias") ✓.

### (c) UNODC–INTERPOL 2025

The paper relays the same Advisory Committee concern: "the potential for the discriminatory use of neurotechnologies – particularly in relation to groups that have been marginalized, subjected to structural discrimination, or are socioeconomically disadvantaged – is a key concern" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "the potential for the discriminatory use of neurotechnologies – particularly in relation to groups that have been marginalized, subjected to structural discrimination, or are socioeconomically disadvantaged – is a key concern") ✓. In prisons, where people with mental health conditions are over-represented, "the neurotechnologies used in this context must not be used to further discriminate against these individuals" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 2](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p5 "given the vulnerability of this population, the neurotechnologies used in this context must not be used to further discriminate against these individuals") ✓. The safeguard: "Safeguards must also ensure that neurotechnologies are not deployed in ways that reinforce existing inequalities or result in discriminatory impacts on marginalized groups" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 6](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p9 "Safeguards must also ensure that neurotechnologies are not deployed in ways that reinforce existing inequalities or result in discriminatory impacts on marginalized groups") ✓.

### (d) AHRC 2025

The Commission's principle: "Anti-discrimination law principles should be applied to the development and use of neurotechnology, considering especially the needs of people who are in vulnerable situations" [AHRC 2025, p. 11](pin:AHRC-2025#p11 "Anti-discrimination law principles should be applied to the development and use of neurotechnology, considering especially the needs of people who are in vulnerable situations") ✓. In criminal justice its worry is categorisation by biomarker: "the risk of discrimination and stigmatisation of groups of people because neurotechnology identifies that they have biological markers that indicate a higher risk of criminal activity", which "may breach human rights to be treated equally before the law and to non-discrimination" [AHRC 2025, p. 35](pin:AHRC-2025#p35 "the risk of discrimination and stigmatisation of groups of people because neurotechnology identifies that they have biological markers that indicate a higher risk of criminal activity") ✓. The report coins "neurodiscrimination" for the workplace (Australian law, outside justice): "neurodivergent people may be at heightened risk of neurodiscrimination" and older workers of "age discrimination on the basis of neural data" [AHRC 2025, p. 42](pin:AHRC-2025#p42 "neurodivergent people may be at heightened risk of neurodiscrimination. Equally older workers may be disproportionately impacted as a result of age discrimination on the basis of neural data") ✓.

### (e) Futures Lab 2026

The submission names "people of African descent, queer individuals, and other marginalized groups, particularly in policing, employment, and judicial contexts" as those "Biased datasets and predictive systems may disproportionately harm" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 2](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p3 "Biased datasets and predictive systems may disproportionately harm people of African descent, queer individuals, and other marginalized groups, particularly in policing, employment, and judicial contexts") ✓. Two points are its own. Participation: those most affected, "including defendants and prisoners", are "regarded as secondary advisors or “objects” in the regulatory process", and "perspectives from low- and middleincome countries and the Global South are underrepresented" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 3](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p4 "including defendants and prisoners, patients and users, vulnerable groups, and marginalized communities, are regarded as secondary advisors or “objects” in the regulatory process … perspectives from low- and middleincome countries and the Global South are underrepresented") ✓. Inference of identity: "mind-reading" tools "may infer sexual orientation or gender identity based on neural responses to stimuli, raising the possibility of involuntary outing in workplaces, medical contexts, or legal systems" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 7](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p8 "may infer sexual orientation or gender identity based on neural responses to stimuli, raising the possibility of involuntary outing in workplaces, medical contexts, or legal systems") ✓.

### (f) Scholarship

Prainsack and colleagues supply the structural frame, about data generally rather than neurotechnology: "We live in an era of inequalities, many of which are being increased by digital technologies" [Prainsack et al. 2022, p. e773](pin:Prainsack-et-al-2022#p1 "We live in an era of inequalities, many of which are being increased by digital technologies") ✓. Their answer, collective governance, is on [[data-solidarity]].

## Open questions

- Evidence. No document reports a case of neurotechnology-based discrimination in a justice setting; the AHRC's COMPAS precedent (on [[neuroprediction]]) is an algorithm, not a brain measurement. The claims are anticipatory, by analogy with algorithmic bias.
- Proof. Indirect discrimination through "non-representative data sets" needs a burden of proof and access to the data; the library does not say who carries it.
- Grounds. Only Futures Lab names sexual orientation and gender identity; only A/81/351 names "neurological difference". Whether that is a protected ground under article 26 is not addressed. The Advisory Committee's list of groups (A/HRC/57/61, para. 37) is cited by two documents but not yet in the library: ingest [[a-hrc-57-61]].

## Related

- [[a-81-351]] (the mechanism, the groups, Recommendations 50 (a) and (g))
- [[unodc-interpol-2025]] (structural discrimination; prisons)
- [[ahrc-2025]] (anti-discrimination principles; biomarker stigmatisation; "neurodiscrimination")
- [[futures-lab-2026]] (participation; inference of sexual orientation and gender identity)
- [[prainsack-et-al-2022]] (inequality increased by digital technologies)
- [[ccpr-c-gc-32]] and [[general-comment-32]] (equality before courts; article 2 (1) and 26 grounds)
- [[neuroprediction]] (where biased data does the most damage)
- [[neural-data]] (what the data can reveal)
- [[data-solidarity]] (collective governance as a response)
- [[consent-in-custody]] (vulnerability and power imbalance in detention)

pages.title: Freedom of thought and the forum internum

frontmatter.title: Freedom of thought and the forum internum

pages.body:
# Freedom of thought and the forum internum

**One-liner.** Article 18 of the ICCPR protects thought itself, the forum internum, without any limitation. The library applies that protection to brain decoding and coercive neuromodulation, and adds a four-"pillar" scheme that comes from a Special Rapporteur's report outside the library. The two must be kept apart.

## What the library says

### (b) The Human Rights Committee

The Committee reads article 18(1) as [General Comment No. 22, para. 1](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p1 "far-reaching and profound; it encompasses freedom of thoughts on all matters") ✓, and the provision [General Comment No. 22, para. 1](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p1 "cannot be derogated from, even in time of public emergency, as stated in article 4 (2) of the Covenant") ✓.

The forum internum is absolute. Article 18 [General Comment No. 22, para. 3](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p2 "does not permit any limitations whatsoever on the freedom of thought and conscience … These freedoms are protected unconditionally") ✓, and [General Comment No. 22, para. 3](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p2 "In accordance with articles 18 (2) and 17, no one can be compelled to reveal his thoughts or adherence to a religion or belief") ✓. Limitations attach only to manifestation ([General Comment No. 22, para. 8](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p3 "Article 18 (3) permits restrictions on the freedom to manifest religion or belief only if limitations are prescribed by law") ✓). Coercion is read broadly: article 18(2) bars [General Comment No. 22, para. 5](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p2 "the use of threat of physical force or penal sanctions to compel believers or non-believers … Policies or practices having the same intention or effect") ✓.

Opinion, the neighbour of thought, has the same unconditional cover: article 19(1) is [General Comment No. 34, para. 9](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p2 "a right to which the Covenant permits no exception or restriction … No person may be subject to the impairment of any rights under the Covenant on the basis of his or her actual, perceived or supposed opinions") ✓, and [General Comment No. 34, para. 10](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p3 "Any form of effort to coerce the holding or not holding of any opinion is prohibited") ✓. None of the General Comments mentions neurotechnology, neural data or "pillars".

### (c) The Secretary-General and UNODC–INTERPOL

The Secretary-General applies the Committee's words to decoding and deception detection, which [A/81/351, para. 20](pin:A/81/351#p7 "could reveal information that the person has not chosen to disclose … Such technologies could thus have a profound impact on the freedom of thought") ✓. He notes the Special Rapporteur on freedom of religion or belief's finding that the right's scope and content [A/81/351, para. 21](pin:A/81/351#p7 "“remain largely underdeveloped and poorly understood” (A/76/380, para. 4)") ✓, and reports that [A/81/351, para. 21](pin:A/81/351#p7 "Experts have argued that four pillars of freedom of thought are most relevant to neurotechnology: the freedom not to disclose thoughts; freedom from punishment for thoughts, real or inferred; freedom from impermissible alteration of thoughts; and an enabling environment for free thought") ✓. In his view [A/81/351, para. 22](pin:A/81/351#p8 "Neurotechnology may potentially affect all four pillars of freedom of thought") ✓, although [A/81/351, para. 22](pin:A/81/351#p8 "neurotechnology is not capable at present of “mind-reading”, it is reportedly capable of inferring emotions and internal reactions based on neural data") ✓. On opinion, [A/81/351, para. 23](pin:A/81/351#p8 "Forced neurological interventions, indoctrination programmes or threats of violence designed to compel individuals to form particular opinions or change their opinion would violate this freedom") ✓.

His recommendations follow: States should [A/81/351, para. 50 (c)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Prohibit the compulsory or coercive use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice, including brain-based deception detection, predictive applications, decoding applications to “read” thoughts, intentions or memories, neuromodulation") ✓ and [A/81/351, para. 50 (d)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Prohibit the use of neural data obtained through torture or ill-treatment, or in violation of the rights to freedom of thought and opinion, as evidence in any proceedings") ✓.
