UNODC and INTERPOL list freedom of thought among the rights that justice institutions [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "will need to ensure individuals’ rights to privacy, freedom of thought, bodily integrity, non-discrimination") ✓.

### (d) The Australian Human Rights Commission

The AHRC repeats the Committee's "far reaching and profound" and adds that [AHRC 2025, p. 28](pin:AHRC-2025#p28 "Freedom of thought is considered part of an individual’s forum internum (internal realm) and is non-derogable") ✓, while calling it [AHRC 2025, p. 28](pin:AHRC-2025#p28 "Often described as a ‘forgotten freedom’") ✓. It attributes the pillars to [AHRC 2025, p. 29](pin:AHRC-2025#p29 "The Special Rapporteur on freedom of religion or belief (whose mandate also extends to freedom of thought)") ✓ and reads article 18(2) so that it [AHRC 2025, p. 29](pin:AHRC-2025#p29 "would protect people from being subject to the nonconsensual use of neurotechnology devices that may alter thought or neural patterns or behaviours") ✓. Its remedy is institutional: the Committee should [AHRC 2025, p. 70](pin:AHRC-2025#p70 "provide guidance on freedom of thought and neurotechnologies through the adoption of a general comment on article 18") ✓.

### (e) and (f)

The Futures Lab frames the matter as "neurorights" that [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "align with Articles 12 and 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights") ✓ and asks for standards grounded in [Futures Lab 2026, p. 2](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p3 "human dignity, cognitive liberty, and equality") ✓: the Declaration rather than the Covenant, and a term ("cognitive liberty") that no General Comment uses. Szoszkiewicz and Yuste tie the data to the right, [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "If thought is inviolable, so too should be the data that can be used to infer it") ✓, and report that the Advisory Committee [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "recommended developing General Comments on the freedom of thought and mental integrity for persons with disabilities") ✓ (see [[a-hrc-57-61]]).

## Two things to keep apart

1. **The absolute protection** is the Committee's (register b): no limitation on thought, no compelled revelation (General Comment No. 22, para. 3). It predates neurotechnology. Its application to decoding is the Secretary-General's and the AHRC's, not the Committee's.
2. **The four pillars** come from the Special Rapporteur's report [A/76/380](https://docs.un.org/en/A/76/380) (not in the library; its symbol is named by A/81/351, para. 21). The Secretary-General attributes them to "Experts", the AHRC to the Special Rapporteur. They are an analytic scheme in registers (c) and (d), not treaty-body interpretation. The second pillar, "punishment for thoughts, real or inferred", goes beyond the words of General Comment No. 22; the nearest Committee text is General Comment No. 34, para. 9, on "actual, perceived or supposed opinions".

Where the registers agree: thought is absolute and non-derogable, and non-disclosure is part of it. Where they part: (b) is silent on neurotechnology; (c) and (d) apply it with "could" and "may"; (d), and the Advisory Committee as reported, ask for a new General Comment; (e) argues from the Declaration and "cognitive liberty".

## Open questions

- Is an inferred emotion a "thought" within General Comment No. 22, para. 3? The Secretary-General separates "mind-reading" from inference without saying where article 18 begins.
- Does "freedom from punishment for inferred thoughts" follow from the Committee's "perceived or supposed opinions" (article 19), or does it need new text under article 18? The library does not say.
- Would the general comment the AHRC asks for adopt the pillars, or the Committee's own two-sentence rule?

## Related

- [[iccpr-art-18]] (the treaty text), [[general-comment-22]] and [[general-comment-34]] (the authorities, and who in the library relies on them)
- [[ccpr-c-21-rev-1-add-4]], [[ccpr-c-gc-34]], [[a-81-351]], [[unodc-interpol-2025]], [[ahrc-2025]], [[futures-lab-2026]], [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (the source pages pinned here)
- [[a-hrc-57-61]] (the Advisory Committee report that A/81/351 and Szoszkiewicz and Yuste cite; in the inbox)
- [[mental-privacy]] (the non-disclosure limb, read with article 17), [[self-incrimination]] and [[brain-based-lie-detection]] (where compelled revelation meets article 14(3)(g)), [[neuromodulation-of-offenders]] (the alteration limb), [[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]] (whether article 18 needs new text)

frontmatter.title: Mental privacy

pages.body:
# Mental privacy

**One-liner.** "Mental privacy" is the protection of a person's mental activity and of the data that can reveal it. In the library it sits where article 17 (privacy) meets article 18 (thought): the Human Rights Committee links the two articles without using the term; the Secretary-General, the AHRC and the scholarship use it; Chile, as reported, has enacted it.

## What the library says

### (b) The Human Rights Committee

The Committee never says "mental privacy", but it joins the two articles in one sentence: [General Comment No. 22, para. 3](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p2 "In accordance with articles 18 (2) and 17, no one can be compelled to reveal his thoughts or adherence to a religion or belief") ✓. On data it recalls, under article 17, that [General Comment No. 34, para. 18](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p4 "every individual should have the right to ascertain in an intelligible form, whether, and if so, what personal data is stored in automatic data files, and for what purposes") ✓ and, where data are incorrect or unlawfully processed, [General Comment No. 34, para. 18](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p4 "the right to have his or her records rectified") ✓. Neither General Comment mentions neurotechnology.

### (c) The Secretary-General and UNODC–INTERPOL

The Secretary-General uses the term descriptively. Neurotechnologies [A/81/351, para. 24](pin:A/81/351#p8 "affect physical and mental privacy by exposing the individual’s private space and integrity") ✓; article 17 applies, and [A/81/351, para. 24](pin:A/81/351#p8 "Neurotechnology introduces new threats to privacy by significantly increasing the level of possible interference") ✓. He extends the Committee's reading of article 17 to neural data: the right [A/81/351, para. 25](pin:A/81/351#p9 "protects personal data, communications and the integrity of private life. This protection would include neural data") ✓, and the Committee's requirements on regulation by law, security, access and rectification [A/81/351, para. 26](pin:A/81/351#p9 "would also apply to neural data and other information retrieved through the use of neurotechnologies") ✓. The verb is "would": the application is his, not the Committee's. He points to the Special Rapporteur on the right to privacy's [A/81/351, para. 27](pin:A/81/351#p9 "foundations and principles for the regulation of neurotechnology and the processing of neural data, including the protection of human dignity and mental privacy") ✓ and to a model law ([A/80/283](https://docs.un.org/en/A/80/283), not in the library).

In justice settings he warns that consumer neural data [A/81/351, para. 14](pin:A/81/351#p5 "may reportedly be accessed by State authorities or introduced as evidence in legal proceedings without recognition of its uniquely sensitive character") ✓, and that [A/81/351, para. 30](pin:A/81/351#p10 "Constant monitoring of the brains of those detained as a form of surveillance could cause mental distress") ✓ under article 10(1). Chile's 2023 ruling was [A/81/351, para. 43](pin:A/81/351#p13 "among the first globally to address neural data under the rights to mental privacy and physical and mental integrity") ✓ (see [[chile-supreme-court-2023]]).

UNODC and INTERPOL: [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "Brain activity is among the most intimate forms of personal information, and any attempt to monitor, decode or manipulate it … without genuine consent would represent a profound intrusion into human dignity, autonomy, and privacy") ✓; and [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 6](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p9 "Individuals must retain control over their neural data") ✓.

### (d) The Australian Human Rights Commission

The AHRC makes mental privacy the first pillar of free thought: the protection against compelled revelation [AHRC 2025, p. 29](pin:AHRC-2025#p29 "confirms that mental privacy is a foundational element of free thought") ✓, and decoding without safeguards [AHRC 2025, p. 29](pin:AHRC-2025#p29 "threatens both freedom of thought and the right to privacy") ✓. On memory recovery it sees [AHRC 2025, p. 33](pin:AHRC-2025#p33 "a real risk of breaching the right to privacy and freedom of thought as protected by arts 17 and 18 ICCPR") ✓. It lists a "right to mental privacy" among the new rights some propose, and treats that debate as settling the other way ([[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]]). One caution: it writes [AHRC 2025, p. 39](pin:AHRC-2025#p39 "As provided for under arts 18.2 and 17 ICCPR, ‘no one shall be compelled to reveal … thoughts’") ✓; those words are the Committee's (General Comment No. 22, para. 3), not the Covenant's.

### (e) and (f)

The Futures Lab speaks of [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "protections for neural privacy") ✓ in US state law and of tools [Futures Lab 2026, p. 7](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p8 "threatening cognitive privacy") ✓. Szoszkiewicz and Yuste define the term: [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "Mental privacy, defined here as the protection of the mental activity of an individual, presents distinct challenges beyond those of traditional data protection") ✓, because neural signals [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "also reflect subconscious and involuntary activity, exposing information that individuals may not consciously recognize") ✓. They tie it to article 18: intrusions [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "may, in some instances, amount to a violation of the freedom of thought and conscience, an absolute right") ✓, and [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3472](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p4 "mental privacy should enjoy enhanced protection as it is intimately tied to freedom of thought") ✓.

## Where the registers agree and part

All registers place mental privacy on both article 17 and article 18, and the Committee's one sentence (General Comment No. 22, para. 3) is the anchor every later document quotes or paraphrases. They part on status. The Committee has no such right by name. The Secretary-General uses the phrase and extends article 17 to neural data with "would". The AHRC treats it as a pillar of article 18, not a separate right. Szoszkiewicz and Yuste call for "a tailored regulatory framework"; the Futures Lab for new standards. Chile, as the Secretary-General and the scholarship report it, has made it a constitutional right.

## Open questions

- Is an interference with mental privacy to be tested under article 17's "arbitrary or unlawful" standard (limitable) or under article 18's unconditional protection? The Secretary-General sets out both (paras. 20 and 24) without saying which governs decoding in an interrogation.
- Does "mental privacy" cover inferences (emotions, reactions) as well as the raw signal? The scholarship says yes; the Committee's texts speak of "thoughts" and "personal data".
- Whether neural data need a category of their own is argued on [[neural-data]] and [[is-neural-data-special]].

## Related

- [[iccpr-art-17]] and [[iccpr-art-18]] (the two treaty texts), [[general-comment-22]] (the sentence that joins them)
- [[ccpr-c-21-rev-1-add-4]], [[ccpr-c-gc-34]], [[a-81-351]], [[unodc-interpol-2025]], [[ahrc-2025]], [[futures-lab-2026]], [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (the source pages pinned here)
- [[freedom-of-thought]] (the forum internum and the four pillars), [[neural-data]] (the data that reveal mental activity), [[chile-supreme-court-2023]] (mental privacy enforced in domestic law), [[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]] (whether a right to mental privacy is needed), [[is-neural-data-special]] (the question page)

pages.title: A moratorium on neurotechnology in criminal justice

frontmatter.title: A moratorium on neurotechnology in criminal justice

pages.body:
# A moratorium on neurotechnology in criminal justice

**One-liner.** Only one document in the library asks for a moratorium: the Australian Human Rights Commission, an NHRI, which would suspend the use of neurotechnology in the criminal justice system until a law reform inquiry has reported. The UN documents take another route: prohibit compulsory or coercive uses outright, and surround any lawful use with validation, consent rules and oversight. The real disagreement is not "moratorium or nothing" but "moratorium or regulated use with safeguards".

## What the library says

### (b) The Human Rights Committee

Neither General Comment mentions a moratorium or neurotechnology. General Comment No. 32 does settle who decides admissibility: within the limits of article 7, "it is primarily for the domestic legislatures of States parties to determine the admissibility of evidence and how their courts assess it" [General Comment No. 32, para. 39](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p12 "subject to the limitations on the use of statements, confessions and other evidence obtained in violation of article 7 … it is primarily for the domestic legislatures of States parties to determine the admissibility of evidence and how their courts assess it") ✓. An interim rule of inadmissibility, such as the AHRC proposes, is a domestic choice the Covenant leaves open: neither required nor forbidden.

### (c) The Secretary-General, A/81/351

The word "moratorium" does not appear. The Secretary-General recommends a standing prohibition of a class of uses: Member States should "Prohibit the compulsory or coercive use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice, including brain-based deception detection, predictive applications, decoding applications" and "neuromodulation" [A/81/351, para. 50 (c)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Prohibit the compulsory or coercive use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice, including brain-based deception detection, predictive applications, decoding applications to “read” thoughts, intentions or memories, neuromodulation") ✓. What remains is regulated, not suspended: States should "Accompany any lawful deployment of neurotechnology in the administration of justice with effective oversight, accountability and governance mechanisms" [A/81/351, para. 50 (f)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Accompany any lawful deployment of neurotechnology in the administration of justice with effective oversight, accountability and governance mechanisms and incorporate continuous monitoring and evaluation") ✓. For the applications still in research (wearable monitoring of offenders, neurostimulation for aggression) there is a timing rule: their human rights issues "should be addressed before the technologies are deployed" [A/81/351, para. 12](pin:A/81/351#p5 "Both of these technologies, if ever considered for use in the administration of justice, would likely raise complex human rights issues that should be addressed before the technologies are deployed") ✓.

### (c) UNODC–INTERPOL 2025

The background paper comes closest to a moratorium in substance, without the word: "Technologies should therefore not be deployed until their accuracy, safety, and feasibility have been rigorously demonstrated through independent testing and peer-reviewed research" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 5](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p8 "Technologies should therefore not be deployed until their accuracy, safety, and feasibility have been rigorously demonstrated through independent testing and peer-reviewed research") ✓. The trigger for lifting the pause is scientific, paired with a necessity test: "A demonstrable and significant benefit for law enforcement functions must also be shown, and the necessity and proportionality of their use assessed against the potential human rights impacts" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 3](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p6 "A demonstrable and significant benefit for law enforcement functions must also be shown, and the necessity and proportionality of their use assessed against the potential human rights impacts") ✓.

### (d) AHRC 2025

The criminal justice chapter opens with the moratorium: "Until expertise and time can be put towards examining the opportunities and risks of neurotechnology in the criminal justice system, it will be necessary to introduce a moratorium" [AHRC 2025, p. 31](pin:AHRC-2025#p31 "Until expertise and time can be put towards examining the opportunities and risks of neurotechnology in the criminal justice system, it will be necessary to introduce a moratorium") ✓. Recommendation 6 (so numbered in the box on p. 31 and the list on p. 70) asks the Attorney-General to refer an inquiry to the Australian Law Reform Commission: "Until this work is completed there should be a moratorium on the use of neurotechnology in the criminal justice system" [AHRC 2025, p. 70](pin:AHRC-2025#p70 "Until this work is completed there should be a moratorium on the use of neurotechnology in the criminal justice system") ✓. For investigations, the Commission's "preliminary view is that a moratorium on the use of neurotechnology in criminal investigations should be imposed until the ALRC has published the findings of the recommended inquiry", with information so gained "inadmissible at trial" meanwhile [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "The Commission’s preliminary view is that a moratorium on the use of neurotechnology in criminal investigations should be imposed until the ALRC has published the findings of the recommended inquiry. Additionally, until that time, information gained via neurotechnology should be inadmissible at trial") ✓. The reasoning is precautionary: "it is preferable to err on the side of caution" [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "it is preferable to err on the side of caution") ✓. The recommendation is addressed to an Australian minister, and the same report warns that "decision-makers must also be conscious where they seek to prohibit or reduce access to the technology of the impact this may have in limiting human rights benefits" [AHRC 2025, p. 20](pin:AHRC-2025#p20 "decision-makers must also be conscious where they seek to prohibit or reduce access to the technology of the impact this may have in limiting human rights benefits") ✓.

### (e) Futures Lab 2026

The submission wants new UN standards and, meanwhile, monitoring rather than suspension: "Until such standards are established, the use of neurotechnology, particularly in legal responses to violations of neurorights, should be subject to careful monitoring" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 7](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p8 "Until such standards are established, the use of neurotechnology, particularly in legal responses to violations of neurorights, should be subject to careful monitoring") ✓. It also asks for the "establishment of redlines" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 3](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p4 "The demand for independent audits and evaluations, establishment of redlines, and binding recommendations to enforcement agencies is critical to prevent regulatory capture") ✓.

### (f) Scholarship

Szoszkiewicz and Yuste derive a precautionary approach from human rights law and list "temporary moratoria on the most controversial neurotechnologies until longitudinal data accrue" among possible steps that "guard against both premature bans and unchecked deployment" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3472](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p4 "Practical steps might include post-market surveillance of consumer EEG devices, mandatory human rights risk assessments, or temporary moratoria on the most controversial neurotechnologies until longitudinal data accrue … guard against both premature bans and unchecked deployment") ✓. A targeted, time-limited moratorium in a consumer and research context, not a general one on criminal justice.

## Contested claims

```contested
claim: The use of neurotechnology in criminal justice should be suspended until it has been assessed.
verdict: contested
note: Only the AHRC (d) asks for a general moratorium; the UN documents (c) prohibit coercive uses outright and regulate the rest; Futures Lab (e) wants monitoring, not suspension. The real split is moratorium versus regulated use with safeguards, and the (c) register sits on the second side.
+ d | [AHRC 2025, p. 70](pin:AHRC-2025#p70 "Until this work is completed there should be a moratorium on the use of neurotechnology in the criminal justice system") ✓ | Recommendation 6: moratorium until a law reform inquiry reports | [[ahrc-2025]]
+ d | [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "a moratorium on the use of neurotechnology in criminal investigations should be imposed until the ALRC has published the findings of the recommended inquiry") ✓ | preliminary view: moratorium on investigations plus interim inadmissibility | [[ahrc-2025]]
~ c | [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 5](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p8 "Technologies should therefore not be deployed until their accuracy, safety, and feasibility have been rigorously demonstrated") ✓ | no deployment until scientifically validated: a pause by validation, not a legal moratorium | [[unodc-interpol-2025]]
~ c | [A/81/351, para. 50 (c)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Prohibit the compulsory or coercive use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice") ✓ | permanent prohibition of coercive uses, not a suspension of all uses | [[a-81-351]]
- c | [A/81/351, para. 50 (f)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Accompany any lawful deployment of neurotechnology in the administration of justice with effective oversight, accountability and governance mechanisms") ✓ | contemplates lawful deployment now, under oversight | [[a-81-351]]
- e | [Futures Lab 2026, p. 7](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p8 "Until such standards are established, the use of neurotechnology, particularly in legal responses to violations of neurorights, should be subject to careful monitoring") ✓ | careful monitoring, not suspension, until new UN standards exist | [[futures-lab-2026]]
~ f | [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3472](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p4 "temporary moratoria on the most controversial neurotechnologies until longitudinal data accrue") ✓ | targeted, temporary moratoria as one precautionary tool among several | [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]]
```

## Open questions

- Scope. The AHRC's moratorium covers "the use of neurotechnology in the criminal justice system" without exception. Would it reach neuroimaging offered by a defendant in mitigation (see [[reliability-and-admissibility]]), or an assistive brain-computer interface a defendant needs to communicate (the AHRC's own caution on p. 20)? The report does not say.
- The trigger. Four documents name four different events that would end the pause: a domestic inquiry (AHRC), scientific validation (UNODC–INTERPOL), new UN standards (Futures Lab), longitudinal data (Szoszkiewicz & Yuste). They are not the same clock.
- Equivalence. If consent in custody is as doubtful as A/81/351 para. 29 says, a prohibition of "compulsory or coercive" use may suspend most uses in practice: see [[consent-in-custody]]. The Advisory Committee's report [[a-hrc-57-61]] is in the inbox; read its recommendations against this card once ingested.

## Related

- [[ahrc-2025]] (the only general moratorium; Recommendation 6)
- [[a-81-351]] (prohibition of coercive uses plus safeguards)
- [[unodc-interpol-2025]] (no deployment until validated)
- [[futures-lab-2026]] (monitoring until new standards)
- [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (temporary, targeted moratoria)
- [[ccpr-c-gc-32]] (admissibility is for domestic legislatures)
- [[regulatory-landscape]] and [[what-should-states-do-now]] (the recommendations side by side)
- [[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]] (whether new standards are needed)
- [[reliability-and-admissibility]] (the validation gate)
- [[neuroprediction]] and [[brain-based-lie-detection]] (the uses a moratorium would cover first)
- [[consent-in-custody]] (why prohibiting coercion may do a moratorium's work)

pages.title: Neural data

frontmatter.title: Neural data

pages.body:
# Neural data

**One-liner.** Data about the structure, activity and function of the nervous system, gathered through neurotechnology. Every register in the library calls them highly sensitive. The documents part on the vehicle of protection: the top tier of existing data-protection law (the Secretary-General, the AHRC, the US statutes as reported) or a category and standards of their own (the Futures Lab and, with qualifications, the scholarship).

## What the library says

### Definitions

The Secretary-General adopts UNESCO's definition: [A/81/351, para. 5](pin:A/81/351#p3 "“qualitative and quantitative data about the structure, activity and function of the nervous system gathered through neurotechnology”") ✓ (its footnote 6, on the same PDF page, cites the UNESCO Recommendation; see [[unesco-recommendation-2025]]). UNODC and INTERPOL: [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 1](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p4 "information obtained by measuring the activity of a person's central or peripheral nervous system") ✓. The scholarship widens it: [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "neural data is not limited to electrical brainwaves. It encompasses any measurable signal that reflects neural activity, whether obtained electrically, chemically or via other means") ✓, including muscle nerve signals. The Futures Lab reports California's narrower statutory wording: [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "information that is generated by measuring the activity of a consumer’s central or peripheral nervous system, and that is not inferred from nonneural information") ✓. Whether inferences count is therefore unsettled across the library.

### Why they are treated as sensitive

(c) [A/81/351, para. 5](pin:A/81/351#p3 "There is broad consensus that neural data are highly sensitive, providing unprecedented access to internal mental states, and that they require heightened ethical and legal protection") ✓ (its footnote 7, on the same PDF page, cites A/HRC/58/58, Szoszkiewicz and Yuste 2025, and Genser, Damianos and Yuste 2024). Neural data are [A/81/351, para. 25](pin:A/81/351#p9 "uniquely revealing since they are capable of disclosing certain aspects of identity and personality") ✓ and [A/81/351, para. 25](pin:A/81/351#p9 "biometric in character and may reportedly be re-identified across data sets and yield insights that were not foreseeable at the time of collection") ✓. The same report is the library's counterweight on reliability: [A/81/351, para. 13](pin:A/81/351#p5 "Brain data are complex and uncertain, and links between brain activity and behaviour can be misunderstood") ✓. Sensitive is not the same as probative (see [[reliability-and-admissibility]]).

(d) The AHRC: neural data [AHRC 2025, p. 21](pin:AHRC-2025#p21 "is highly sensitive and valuable because it can provide unprecedented insights into human thought processes and functions") ✓; brain scans [AHRC 2025, p. 44](pin:AHRC-2025#p44 "can be as unique as an individual’s fingerprint") ✓. (f) Szoszkiewicz and Yuste: they [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "reveal our most intimate processes—thoughts, memories, mental states, emotions, behavior, personality and health conditions—and can even forecast future behavior") ✓.

### How the law reaches them

(b) The Committee's article 17 data rights predate neurotechnology: [General Comment No. 34, para. 18](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p4 "every individual should have the right to ascertain in an intelligible form, whether, and if so, what personal data is stored in automatic data files, and for what purposes") ✓.

(c) The Secretary-General applies them: article 17's protection of personal data [A/81/351, para. 25](pin:A/81/351#p9 "would include neural data") ✓, and the Committee's requirements [A/81/351, para. 26](pin:A/81/351#p9 "would also apply to neural data and other information retrieved through the use of neurotechnologies") ✓. He concludes that [A/81/351, para. 49](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Neural data, as uniquely sensitive personal data, demand heightened protection, especially considering their increasing collection by private actors and potential reuse in legal proceedings") ✓ and recommends that States [A/81/351, para. 50 (b)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Recognize neural data as highly sensitive personal data subject to the highest level of legal protection; impose clear limitations on its collection, processing, sale, storage, retention, reuse and sharing") ✓. He reports the same route in domestic law: [A/81/351, para. 45](pin:A/81/351#p14 "California, Colorado and Montana have extended sensitive data protections to neural data") ✓, and in Brazil [A/81/351, para. 43](pin:A/81/351#p13 "neural data is classified as sensitive personal data") ✓. The split he does draw is between devices: invasive ones are licensed medical devices whose data fall under health-data law, while consumer devices [A/81/351, para. 4](pin:A/81/351#p2 "are generally subject to little or no regulation, even though wearable devices are also medicalgrade, and the data that they collect are extremely sensitive") ✓.

(d) The AHRC finds that Australia's Privacy Act [AHRC 2025, p. 22](pin:AHRC-2025#p22 "does not provide any express protection for neural data") ✓ but, being technology-neutral, [AHRC 2025, p. 22](pin:AHRC-2025#p22 "should be adaptable to changing technologies and environments, including neurotechnology") ✓; whether neural data are "personal" or "sensitive" information [AHRC 2025, p. 25](pin:AHRC-2025#p25 "needs to be clarified") ✓.

(e) The Futures Lab accepts that the GDPR [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "ensures that personal and sensitive neurobiometric data about health and mental status are legally classified and protected") ✓, yet asks for more: [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "specific international standards must be established to recognize the highly sensitive and personal nature of bio- and neurotechnologies") ✓.

(f) Szoszkiewicz and Yuste name the gap: neural data [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "are not classified as sensitive information when collected outside medical contexts by consumer products") ✓. Their answer is [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3469](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p1 "strengthening existing data protection regulations with a broad approach to safeguard neural data") ✓, while also holding that [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "neural data must be treated as fundamentally distinct, with enhanced safeguards") ✓. A second route they float is the medical model, which [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3472](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p4 "would render all neural data medical and thus, protected by appropriate regulation already implemented in most countries") ✓.

Where the registers agree: sensitivity, and the need for heightened protection. Where they part: the Secretary-General and the AHRC work inside existing categories; the Futures Lab wants specific international standards; Szoszkiewicz and Yuste want both ("fundamentally distinct", by strengthening existing law).

## Contested claims

```contested
claim: Neural data need a legal category of their own, rather than protection as sensitive personal data under existing privacy and data-protection law.
verdict: leans-contest
note: The library agrees that neural data are highly sensitive; the weight of it, led by the Secretary-General, folds them into the highest tier of existing sensitive-data law, and the call for a category of their own comes from civil society and, with qualifications, scholarship.
- c | [A/81/351, para. 50 (b)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Recognize neural data as highly sensitive personal data subject to the highest level of legal protection") ✓ | the top tier of the existing category, not a new one | [[a-81-351]]
- c | [A/81/351, para. 25](pin:A/81/351#p9 "This protection would include neural data") ✓ | article 17 already reaches neural data | [[a-81-351]]
~ c | [A/81/351, para. 5](pin:A/81/351#p3 "they require heightened ethical and legal protection") ✓ | heightened protection; the vehicle is not specified | [[a-81-351]]
- d | [AHRC 2025, p. 22](pin:AHRC-2025#p22 "it should be adaptable to changing technologies and environments, including neurotechnology") ✓ | technology-neutral privacy law, once clarified | [[ahrc-2025]]
+ e | [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "specific international standards must be established to recognize the highly sensitive and personal nature of bio- and neurotechnologies") ✓ | specific standards for neural data | [[futures-lab-2026]]
+ f | [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "neural data must be treated as fundamentally distinct, with enhanced safeguards") ✓ | distinct, though by strengthening existing data-protection law | [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]]
```

## Open questions

- Do inferences drawn from neural data count as neural data? California's statute, as reported, says no; the scholarship and the Secretary-General's definition leave it open.
- In justice settings, who controls neural data gathered by a consumer device and later sought by a prosecutor? The Secretary-General flags the risk (para. 14) without a rule; [[data-solidarity]] holds the one collective model in the library.
- Does "highest level of legal protection" (para. 50 (b)) mean a consent-only regime, or something stricter in custody? The library does not say.

## Related

- [[iccpr-art-17]] (the treaty text) and [[ccpr-c-gc-34]] (the Committee's data rights)
- [[a-81-351]], [[unodc-interpol-2025]], [[ahrc-2025]], [[futures-lab-2026]], [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (the source pages pinned here)
- [[colorado-neural-data-law]], [[california-neural-data-law]], [[unesco-recommendation-2025]] (the instruments that define or classify neural data)
- [[mental-privacy]] (what the data reveal), [[data-solidarity]] (governing the data collectively), [[regulatory-landscape]] (where neural data are regulated), [[reliability-and-admissibility]] (sensitive is not probative), [[is-neural-data-special]] (the question page), [[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]] (the wider debate)

pages.title: Neuromodulation of offenders

frontmatter.title: Neuromodulation of offenders

pages.body:
# Neuromodulation of offenders

**One-liner.** Neuromodulation "writes" to the brain: deep brain stimulation, transcranial magnetic or direct current stimulation, neurofeedback. Applied to offenders it is discussed as treatment to reduce aggression or impulsivity, as a sentencing option, or as a route to earlier release. The library's common ground is narrow and firm: it can be lawful only with genuinely free and informed consent, and in custody that consent is doubtful. The Human Rights Council Advisory Committee, as the Secretary-General reports it, is of the view that such techniques "may constitute" treatment contrary to articles 7 or 10 of the Covenant when imposed without such consent; the Secretary-General recommends prohibiting coercive neuromodulation outright.

## What the library says

### (b) The Human Rights Committee

Neither General Comment mentions neuromodulation; the application is the Secretary-General's. The rules: article 18 "does not permit any limitations whatsoever on the freedom of thought and conscience" [General Comment No. 22, para. 3](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p2 "It does not permit any limitations whatsoever on the freedom of thought and conscience or on the freedom to have or adopt a religion or belief of one’s choice") ✓, and "Any form of effort to coerce the holding or not holding of any opinion is prohibited" [General Comment No. 34, para. 10](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p3 "Any form of effort to coerce the holding or not holding of any opinion is prohibited") ✓.

### (c) The Secretary-General, A/81/351

The report places the offender application in research: "There is also research on the use of neurostimulation to modulate neural processes associated with aggression or impulse control", whose issues "should be addressed before the technologies are deployed" [A/81/351, para. 12](pin:A/81/351#p5 "There is also research on the use of neurostimulation to modulate neural processes associated with aggression or impulse control … should be addressed before the technologies are deployed") ✓.

The central paragraph relays the Advisory Committee's position with its hedges intact. The Committee "is of the view that the use of neuromodulation techniques intended to alter the brain activity of offenders to reduce aggression or impulsivity may constitute treatment contrary to articles 7 or 10 of the Covenant when imposed without genuinely free and informed consent"; where techniques are tied to "early release or favourable parole outcomes, there is a significant risk that consent may not be fully free or voluntary" [A/81/351, para. 29](pin:A/81/351#p10 "is of the view that the use of neuromodulation techniques intended to alter the brain activity of offenders to reduce aggression or impulsivity may constitute treatment contrary to articles 7 or 10 of the Covenant when imposed without genuinely free and informed consent … early release or favourable parole outcomes, there is a significant risk that consent may not be fully free or voluntary") ✓. The same paragraph recalls that article 7 "expressly prohibits medical or scientific experimentation without the free consent of the person concerned", and that the Human Rights Committee has acknowledged the difficulty of free consent for detainees [A/81/351, para. 29](pin:A/81/351#p10 "Article 7 of the Covenant “expressly prohibits medical or scientific experimentation without the free consent of the person concerned”. The difficulty of establishing that consent is genuinely free given the particularly vulnerable status of those who are detained has been acknowledged by the Human Rights Committee") ✓ (its footnotes 57 and 58, on the same PDF page, cite General Comment No. 20 (1992), para. 7, not in the library). The Advisory Committee's own report is [[a-hrc-57-61]], in the inbox.

Article 10 (1) ICCPR (not in the library; text on the [OHCHR ICCPR page](https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-mechanisms/instruments/international-covenant-civil-and-political-rights)) entitles detainees to be treated with humanity and dignity. The report reads neuromodulation "applied in detention or investigative contexts" as something that "may result in mental or physical suffering contravening the protection provided under articles 7 and 10 (1)" [A/81/351, para. 28](pin:A/81/351#p9 "coercive interrogation techniques, and neuromodulation, applied in detention or investigative contexts, may result in mental or physical suffering contravening the protection provided under articles 7 and 10 (1)") ✓, and glosses "humanity" as meaning that detainees "should not be subjected to any hardship or constraint other than that resulting from the deprivation of liberty itself" [A/81/351, para. 30](pin:A/81/351#p10 "“Humanity” means that detainees should not be subjected to any hardship or constraint other than that resulting from the deprivation of liberty itself") ✓ (its footnote 59, on the same PDF page, cites article 10 and General Comment No. 21). On thought and opinion: "Forced neurological interventions, indoctrination programmes or threats of violence designed to compel individuals to form particular opinions or change their opinion would violate this freedom" [A/81/351, para. 23](pin:A/81/351#p8 "Forced neurological interventions, indoctrination programmes or threats of violence designed to compel individuals to form particular opinions or change their opinion would violate this freedom") ✓. On legal personality: coercive neuromodulation "that alters personality, affective responses or cognitive recall could also constitute a direct threat to the right to recognition as a person before the law" [A/81/351, para. 35](pin:A/81/351#p11 "Use of coercive neuromodulation that alters personality, affective responses or cognitive recall could also constitute a direct threat to the right to recognition as a person before the law") ✓.

The recommendations: prohibit compulsory or coercive use, naming "neuromodulation" [A/81/351, para. 50 (c)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Prohibit the compulsory or coercive use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice, including … neuromodulation") ✓, and, given "the constrained and coercive nature of justice settings", subject any consent "to the highest evidentiary standards and rigorous scrutiny" [A/81/351, para. 50 (e)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Given the constrained and coercive nature of justice settings, any consent should be subject to the highest evidentiary standards and rigorous scrutiny") ✓.

### (c) UNODC–INTERPOL 2025

The paper is the library's most favourable voice, and it hedges too. It sees "promising potential uses of emerging neurotechnologies for the reintegration of incarcerated persons": EEG neurofeedback for self-regulation, and non-invasive brain stimulation "for its potential use in improving decisionmaking behaviours among violent offenders" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 2](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p5 "there are promising potential uses of emerging neurotechnologies for the reintegration of incarcerated persons back into society … non-invasive brain stimulation has been examined for its potential use in improving decisionmaking behaviours among violent offenders") ✓. But "many of these studies are preliminary", and the technologies "must not be used to further discriminate against these individuals" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 2](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p5 "many of these studies are preliminary. Additionally, given the vulnerability of this population, the neurotechnologies used in this context must not be used to further discriminate against these individuals") ✓. It flags technologies "offered" in coercive conditions "or under the guise of moral-enhancement" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "“offered” the use of these technologies in ways that are coercive, or under the guise of moral-enhancement, or similar") ✓ and requires consent "free of coercion or undue influence, particularly in custodial or correctional settings where power imbalances are acute" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 6](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p9 "Consent must be voluntary and informed, free of coercion or undue influence, particularly in custodial or correctional settings where power imbalances are acute") ✓.

### (d) AHRC 2025

The Commission frames neuromodulation as a sentencing option: "Neurotechnology could offer sentencing options that are more rehabilitative than punitive. Nonconsensual medical treatment could, however, violate medical ethics and human rights" [AHRC 2025, p. 35](pin:AHRC-2025#p35 "Neurotechnology could offer sentencing options that are more rehabilitative than punitive. Nonconsensual medical treatment could, however, violate medical ethics and human rights") ✓. Its example is court-mandated post-prison treatment in the Netherlands, where neurointerventions "are not acting as a ’biological fix’" but "identify neural precursors that trigger feelings of aggression and then stimulate the brain to calm the person down" [AHRC 2025, p. 35](pin:AHRC-2025#p35 "Such neurointerventions are not acting as a ’biological fix’. Instead, they are used (for example) to identify neural precursors that trigger feelings of aggression and then stimulate the brain to calm the person down") ✓. The consent problem is stated as a transaction: consent "could be used transactionally for sentence reduction or an earlier parole – despite the offender’s preference not to be the subject of a neurointervention in the absence of such incentives" [AHRC 2025, p. 35](pin:AHRC-2025#p35 "consent to the use of neurotechnology could be used transactionally for sentence reduction or an earlier parole – despite the offender’s preference not to be the subject of a neurointervention in the absence of such incentives") ✓.

### (f) Scholarship

Szoszkiewicz and Yuste draw the read/write line that organises this page: today's devices are "capable of both decoding and modulating neural activity" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3469](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p1 "The current neurotechnology landscape encompasses a range of invasive and noninvasive devices capable of both decoding and modulating neural activity") ✓. The article does not discuss offenders.

## Open questions

- Is there a disagreement? UNODC–INTERPOL and the AHRC see a rehabilitative use; the Secretary-General prohibits coercive use. All make consent the hinge, and all doubt consent in custody. The split, if any, is whether "voluntary" neuromodulation tied to release is possible: see the card on [[consent-in-custody]].
- Is court-mandated treatment (the AHRC's Dutch example) "compulsory" within A/81/351 para. 50 (c)? The library does not say.
- Everything here is prospective: no document reports a State modulating offenders' brains as a sentence. General Comments No. 20 and 21, cited by A/81/351, are not in the library.

## Related

- [[a-81-351]] (the Advisory Committee's "may constitute"; articles 7 and 10; prohibition of coercive neuromodulation)
- [[unodc-interpol-2025]] (reintegration uses; "preliminary" studies; moral enhancement by coercion)
- [[ahrc-2025]] (sentencing options; transactional consent)
- [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (decoding versus modulating)
- [[ccpr-c-21-rev-1-add-4]] and [[ccpr-c-gc-34]] (no limitation on thought; no coercion of opinion)
- [[iccpr-art-7]] (experimentation without free consent; ill-treatment)
- [[iccpr-art-18]] and [[freedom-of-thought]] (alteration of thought)
- [[consent-in-custody]] (whether consent tied to release can be free)
- [[neuroprediction]] (the "read" counterpart)
- [[a-hrc-57-61]] (the Advisory Committee's report, in the inbox)

frontmatter.title: Neuroprediction

pages.body:
# Neuroprediction

**One-liner.** "Neuroprediction" is the use of brain measurements to estimate what a person will do: the risk of reoffending for sentencing, parole or continued detention, or the risk of offending before any offence. The library treats it as largely experimental, scientifically fragile and legally the most exposed use of neurotechnology in justice: it engages the presumption of innocence, article 9 (liberty), equality before the law and non-discrimination, and the Secretary-General recommends prohibiting its compulsory or coercive use.

## What the library says

### (b) The Human Rights Committee

General Comment No. 32 (2007) is about courtroom practice, not neurotechnology; the application to prediction is the reports' own. The presumption of innocence "guarantees that no guilt can be presumed until the charge has been proved beyond reasonable doubt", and defendants should not be presented "in a manner indicating that they may be dangerous criminals" [General Comment No. 32, para. 30](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p9 "guarantees that no guilt can be presumed until the charge has been proved beyond reasonable doubt … Defendants should normally not be shackled or kept in cages during trials or otherwise presented to the court in a manner indicating that they may be dangerous criminals") ✓. Equality of arms demands that each side have "the opportunity to contest all the arguments and evidence adduced by the other party" [General Comment No. 32, para. 13](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p3 "demands, inter alia, that each side be given the opportunity to contest all the arguments and evidence adduced by the other party") ✓.

### (c) The Secretary-General, A/81/351

Claim and concern sit in one paragraph: "Some research claims that certain neurotechnologies can assess the risk of recidivism", and "The prospect of identifying individuals as future offenders before an offence has been committed raises particularly serious human rights concerns, including related to the presumption of innocence" [A/81/351, para. 10](pin:A/81/351#p4 "Some research claims that certain neurotechnologies can assess the risk of recidivism … The prospect of identifying individuals as future offenders before an offence has been committed raises particularly serious human rights concerns, including related to the presumption of innocence") ✓. The scientific caveat: "Particular caution is warranted when translating findings established at the group or population level into conclusions about individual persons" [A/81/351, para. 13](pin:A/81/351#p5 "Particular caution is warranted when translating findings established at the group or population level into conclusions about individual persons, given intra- and inter-individual variability and the probabilistic nature of many neuroscientific findings") ✓.

Three rights follow. Fair trial: "predictive neurotechnology purporting to assess future criminality may also undermine the presumption of innocence", and the defence needs "access to the scientific expertise and proprietary data" to challenge it [A/81/351, para. 33](pin:A/81/351#p11 "the use of predictive neurotechnology purporting to assess future criminality may also undermine the presumption of innocence … access to the scientific expertise and proprietary data needed to interpret and challenge neurotechnology-derived evidence") ✓. Liberty: recidivism tools "may lead to arbitrary detention under article 9"; detention "must be based on reasons specific to that individual"; such tools "often rely on statistical correlations from non-representative data sets, potentially leading to prolonged or preventive detention based on what a person might do rather than what the person has done" [A/81/351, para. 34](pin:A/81/351#p11 "may lead to arbitrary detention under article 9 … must be based on reasons specific to that individual … often rely on statistical correlations from non-representative data sets, potentially leading to prolonged or preventive detention based on what a person might do rather than what the person has done") ✓. Legal personality: such use "risks prioritizing biological determinism over recognition of the individual as a legal subject" [A/81/351, para. 35](pin:A/81/351#p11 "Neurotechnology claiming to assess the potential for recidivism risks prioritizing biological determinism over recognition of the individual as a legal subject") ✓. The groups most exposed (women, children, people of African descent) are on [[discrimination]]. The recommendation: prohibit compulsory or coercive use, "including … predictive applications" [A/81/351, para. 50 (c)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Prohibit the compulsory or coercive use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice, including brain-based deception detection, predictive applications") ✓.

### (c) UNODC–INTERPOL 2025

The paper lists "risk assessment" among potential uses, which "vary significantly in their level of scientific validity and technical readiness, with many still in experimental or early deployment stages" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 3](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p6 "Potential uses include memory detection, risk assessment, the decoding of thoughts in the form of words, or neuroenhancement … vary significantly in their level of scientific validity and technical readiness, with many still in experimental or early deployment stages") ✓.

### (d) AHRC 2025

The Commission supplies the definition: an offender's fMRI scan "could be used to determine whether they have biological markers of human behaviours that correlate to behavioural traits – including those that may indicate a heightened risk of reoffending. This is known as ‘neuroprediction’" [AHRC 2025, p. 34](pin:AHRC-2025#p34 "An offender’s brain scan (via fMRI) could be used to determine whether they have biological markers of human behaviours that correlate to behavioural traits – including those that may indicate a heightened risk of reoffending. This is known as ‘neuroprediction’") ✓. Its precedent is algorithmic, not neural: COMPAS is "still used in the US to predict the risk of recidivism, despite recognised findings of racial bias within its algorithm" [AHRC 2025, p. 34](pin:AHRC-2025#p34 "Tools such as the Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions (COMPAS) are still used in the US to predict the risk of recidivism, despite recognised findings of racial bias within its algorithm") ✓. Its verdict is double-edged: neuroprediction "is reminiscent of an outdated biological determinism that is an anathema to human rights", yet "it may also provide important insights when making decisions about parole or sentences", so it "should only be used in criminal justice settings after specific research" [AHRC 2025, p. 35](pin:AHRC-2025#p35 "reminiscent of an outdated biological determinism that is an anathema to human rights. However, it may also provide important insights when making decisions about parole or sentences … should only be used in criminal justice settings after specific research") ✓.

### (e) Futures Lab 2026

The submission is the most open to the use: "While there is promise in neurotechnology’s assistance in assessing guilt, accountability, and the risk of recidivism in judicial proceedings, it also carries risks regarding access to the regulatory process" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 3](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p4 "While there is promise in neurotechnology’s assistance in assessing guilt, accountability, and the risk of recidivism in judicial proceedings, it also carries risks regarding access to the regulatory process") ✓.

## Contested claims

```contested
claim: Neuroprediction can have a legitimate role in sentencing and parole decisions.
verdict: leans-contest
note: The only support is conditional (Futures Lab's "promise", the AHRC's "important insights" after research); the Secretary-General calls the premise biological determinism, ties detention to reasons specific to the individual, and recommends prohibiting coercive predictive applications. No document endorses neuroprediction as it stands.
+ e | [Futures Lab 2026, p. 3](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p4 "there is promise in neurotechnology’s assistance in assessing guilt, accountability, and the risk of recidivism in judicial proceedings") ✓ | sees promise, subject to participation in regulation | [[futures-lab-2026]]
~ d | [AHRC 2025, p. 35](pin:AHRC-2025#p35 "it may also provide important insights when making decisions about parole or sentences. Neurotechnologyinformed risk assessment poses serious risks and should only be used in criminal justice settings after specific research") ✓ | possible insights, but only after specific research and an inquiry | [[ahrc-2025]]
- c | [A/81/351, para. 34](pin:A/81/351#p11 "the decision to detain, or continue to detain, a person must be based on reasons specific to that individual") ✓ | statistical risk is not a reason specific to the individual | [[a-81-351]]
- c | [A/81/351, para. 50 (c)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Prohibit the compulsory or coercive use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice, including brain-based deception detection, predictive applications") ✓ | recommends prohibiting coercive predictive applications | [[a-81-351]]
```

## Open questions

- Voluntary neuroprediction. A/81/351 para. 50 (c) prohibits "compulsory or coercive" use. The library does not say whether a defendant may offer a predictive scan in their own favour, or whether a parole board may invite one.
- Can research cure the inference problem? The AHRC wants "specific research"; the Secretary-General's warning on group-to-individual inference suggests the gap may be structural, not a matter of more data.
- No document reports an actual sentencing or parole decision based on neuroprediction; the claims are anticipatory. The Advisory Committee's report [[a-hrc-57-61]] is in the inbox.

## Related

- [[a-81-351]] (presumption of innocence, article 9, biological determinism, prohibition)
- [[unodc-interpol-2025]] (risk assessment as a use of uncertain validity)
- [[ahrc-2025]] (the definition, COMPAS, the conditional door)
- [[futures-lab-2026]] (the most open position)
- [[ccpr-c-gc-32]] and [[general-comment-32]] (presumption of innocence; equality of arms)
- [[iccpr-art-9]] (detention must rest on reasons specific to the individual)
- [[discrimination]] (non-representative data; the groups exposed)
- [[moratorium]] (the AHRC would suspend this use first)
- [[reliability-and-admissibility]] (group-to-individual inference; validation)
- [[neuromodulation-of-offenders]] (the "write" counterpart)

pages.title: New rights or existing rights?

frontmatter.title: New rights or existing rights?

pages.body:
# New rights or existing rights?

**One-liner.** Should neurotechnology be met with new rights ("neurorights", cognitive liberty, a right to mental privacy) or with the rights already in the treaties, interpreted for it? The UN reports and the NHRI in the library lean to existing rights, clarified; the civil-society submission asks for new UN standards; the article sits in between.

## What the library says

**The question, as the documents put it.** The AHRC states it plainly: create new rights "focused directly on protecting the human mind", or "interpret and adapt existing rights" [AHRC 2025, p. 30](pin:AHRC-2025#p30 "whether new human rights focused directly on protecting the human mind (e.g. right to mental privacy, cognitive liberty etc) should be created, or if it is better to interpret and adapt existing rights in response to new technology") ✓. The case for new rights rests on the claim "that existing rights are insufficient" [AHRC 2025, p. 30](pin:AHRC-2025#p30 "The call for new rights – often called neurorights – is predicated on the basis that existing rights are insufficient to protect against the misuse of neurotechnology.") ✓.

**(b) What existing law already holds.** No General Comment in the library speaks of neurotechnology. What the Human Rights Committee did say, in 1993, is that article 18 "does not permit any limitations whatsoever on the freedom of thought" [General Comment No. 22, para. 3](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p2 "It does not permit any limitations whatsoever on the freedom of thought and conscience or on the freedom to have or adopt a religion or belief of one’s choice.") ✓. Whether that protection reaches a brain scan is a question of interpretation, which is the whole debate (see [[freedom-of-thought]]).

**(c) The Secretary-General.** The report records both views without choosing between them [A/81/351, para. 16](pin:A/81/351#p6 "While some contend that the challenges of neurotechnology may require development of new legal frameworks, others affirm that the risks of misuse or abuse of neurotechnology may be addressed within the existing international human rights law framework") ✓, then concludes that international human rights law "provides an applicable framework" which needs "further clarification and consistent application" [A/81/351, para. 48](pin:A/81/351#p15 "International human rights law provides an applicable framework to address the risks of neurotechnology, but further clarification and consistent application are needed.") ✓. The Human Rights Council has chosen the same route: guidelines from its Advisory Committee "on applying existing human rights standards" [A/81/351, para. 46](pin:A/81/351#p14 "The Human Rights Council has tasked its Advisory Committee with drafting guidelines on applying existing human rights standards throughout the neurotechnology life cycle") ✓. UNODC and INTERPOL quote the Secretary-General's *Our Common Agenda* on "updating or clarifying" the application of existing frameworks [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 2](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p5 "consideration should, for instance, be given to updating or clarifying our application of human rights frameworks and standards to address frontier issues") ✓.

**(d) The AHRC.** It reads the international debate as "settling in favour of interpreting and adapting existing rights", and leaves neurorights outside its scope [AHRC 2025, p. 30](pin:AHRC-2025#p30 "At the international and transnational level, these debates appear to be settling in favour of interpreting and adapting existing rights.") ✓. Its own answer is a new interpretation, not a new right: a Human Rights Committee general comment on article 18 and neurotechnologies [AHRC 2025, p. 70](pin:AHRC-2025#p70 "The United Nations Human Rights Committee provide guidance on freedom of thought and neurotechnologies through the adoption of a general comment on article 18") ✓.

**(e) Futures Lab.** The submission asks the United Nations to "develop new human rights standards" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 7](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p8 "the United Nations needs to develop new human rights standards that reflect the emerging and rapidly evolving nature of neurotechnology") ✓, while also presenting neurorights as aligned with articles 12 and 18 of the Universal Declaration [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "They align with Articles 12 and 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) which protect privacy and freedom of thought, conscience, and religion.") ✓.

**(f) Szoszkiewicz & Yuste.** They propose "strengthening existing data protection regulations" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3469](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p1 "We propose strengthening existing data protection regulations with a broad approach to safeguard neural data") ✓, yet also see "growing consensus that additional rules are needed" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3472](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p4 "national and international regulations signal growing consensus that additional rules are needed") ✓: existing rights, with new, specific rules on top.

## Contested claims

```contested
claim: Existing human rights law, interpreted and clarified, is enough to address neurotechnology in the administration of justice; no new rights are needed.
verdict: leans-support
note: No treaty text or General Comment decides it. The UN reports and the NHRI treat existing law as applicable but in need of clarification; only civil society asks for new standards. "Clarification" can itself mean new instruments (guidelines, a general comment), so the two camps are closer than the labels suggest.
~ c | [A/81/351, para. 16](pin:A/81/351#p6 "While some contend that the challenges of neurotechnology may require development of new legal frameworks, others affirm that the risks of misuse or abuse of neurotechnology may be addressed within the existing international human rights law framework") ✓ | records both views without choosing | [[a-81-351]]
+ c | [A/81/351, para. 48](pin:A/81/351#p15 "International human rights law provides an applicable framework to address the risks of neurotechnology, but further clarification and consistent application are needed.") ✓ | the report's own conclusion: applicable, needs clarification | [[a-81-351]]
+ c | [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 2](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p5 "updating or clarifying our application of human rights frameworks and standards") ✓ | clarify existing frameworks | [[unodc-interpol-2025]]
+ d | [AHRC 2025, p. 30](pin:AHRC-2025#p30 "these debates appear to be settling in favour of interpreting and adapting existing rights") ✓ | an NHRI reads the debate as settling; neurorights left out of scope | [[ahrc-2025]]
- e | [Futures Lab 2026, p. 7](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p8 "the United Nations needs to develop new human rights standards that reflect the emerging and rapidly evolving nature of neurotechnology") ✓ | calls for new UN standards | [[futures-lab-2026]]
~ f | [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3472](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p4 "national and international regulations signal growing consensus that additional rules are needed") ✓ | strengthen existing law, add specific rules | [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]]
```

**Reading.** The weight lies with "existing rights, clarified", but it is the weight of (c) and (d) documents, not of a treaty body. The decisive voice would be the Human Rights Committee itself, which the AHRC asks to adopt a general comment. Until then, this is a policy choice, and an ingest of A/HRC/57/61 ([[a-hrc-57-61]]) adds the Advisory Committee's own view.

## How NOT to read this

- "Appear to be settling" is the AHRC's observation of a debate, not a holding that existing rights suffice.
- Futures Lab's "new standards" need not mean new treaty rights: it frames neurorights through the Universal Declaration.
- Chile's constitutional "neurorights" are domestic law ([[regulatory-landscape]]); they show one country's choice, not the state of international law.

## Open questions

- Is a general comment that reads article 18 to cover neural decoding "interpretation" or a new right in all but name?
- What would a new right protect that article 17 privacy and the absolute forum internum do not?

## Related

- [[freedom-of-thought]] (the existing right most often said to suffice)
- [[mental-privacy]] (the right most often proposed as new)
- [[neural-data]] (the parallel card on a legal category for the data)
- [[regulatory-landscape]] (national neurorights and data-protection laws)
- [[iccpr-art-18]], [[ccpr-c-21-rev-1-add-4]] (the treaty text and the Committee's reading)
- [[what-should-states-do-now]] (the recommendations that follow from each view)
- [[a-81-351]], [[ahrc-2025]], [[futures-lab-2026]], [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]], [[unodc-interpol-2025]] (the documents on the card)

frontmatter.title: Regulatory landscape

pages.body:
# Regulatory landscape

**One-liner.** What law and guidance already exist on neurotechnology, as the library reports them: a few national laws, most of them about neural data in consumer markets; soft-law instruments at the international level; almost nothing written for police, courts and prisons.

## What the library says

No treaty (a) or General Comment (b) in the library deals with neurotechnology. Everything below is reported by (c)–(f) documents, and domestic law is known only second-hand: check the law itself before relying on it.

**The overall picture.** The Secretary-General finds the national response "still nascent and uneven" [A/81/351, para. 42](pin:A/81/351#p13 "At the national level, the regulatory response to the human rights challenges posed by neurotechnology is still nascent and uneven") ✓, and concludes that international human rights law "provides an applicable framework" that needs "further clarification and consistent application" [A/81/351, para. 48](pin:A/81/351#p15 "International human rights law provides an applicable framework to address the risks of neurotechnology, but further clarification and consistent application are needed.") ✓. For criminal justice in particular, UNODC and INTERPOL note "few legal frameworks in place to criminalize the malicious or irresponsible use of neurotechnologies" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 3](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p6 "An important consideration is that there are currently few legal frameworks in place to criminalize the malicious or irresponsible use of neurotechnologies.") ✓ and that courts assess neuroimaging evidence "on a case-by-case basis" (see [[reliability-and-admissibility]]) [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "While there is no standardized approach to this globally, courts in some jurisdictions have assessed the admissibility of neuroimaging evidence on a case-by-case basis") ✓.

**International and regional soft law (c).** The Secretary-General lists the Inter-American Declaration of 2023, the UNESCO Recommendation adopted in 2025 ([[unesco-recommendation-2025]]), the OECD recommendation of 2019, a Council mandate for Advisory Committee guidelines, and the UNODC–INTERPOL collaboration [A/81/351, para. 46](pin:A/81/351#p14 "At the international level, the General Conference of UNESCO adopted its Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology in 2025, which calls for national coordinating bodies for neurotechnology, among other measures.") ✓. The Human Rights Council "has tasked its Advisory Committee with drafting guidelines" for its sixty-fourth session [A/81/351, para. 46](pin:A/81/351#p14 "The Human Rights Council has tasked its Advisory Committee with drafting guidelines on applying existing human rights standards throughout the neurotechnology life cycle") ✓: a follow-up to the Committee's report A/HRC/57/61 ([[a-hrc-57-61]], in the inbox).

**Latin America.** Chile's 2021 constitutional amendment and the Supreme Court's 2023 ruling ([[chile-supreme-court-2023]]); a proposed general law in Mexico; neural data as sensitive data in Brazil and "neurorights" in the constitution of Rio Grande do Sul [A/81/351, para. 43](pin:A/81/351#p13 "In Brazil, neural data is classified as sensitive personal data, and Rio Grande do Sul has enshrined “neurorights” protections in its state constitution.") ✓. The AHRC adds draft amendments to Argentina's Criminal Procedure Code, the one justice-specific national measure in the library [AHRC 2025, p. 25](pin:AHRC-2025#p25 "In Argentina draft amendments to the Criminal Procedure Code addressed neurorights – expressly guaranteeing mental privacy and ensuring the protection of neural data.") ✓.

**Europe.** Under the EU AI Act, neurotechnologies "may be classified as high-risk"; France and Spain have their own texts [A/81/351, para. 44](pin:A/81/351#p13 "under the Artificial Intelligence Act of 2024, artificial intelligence-driven neurotechnologies and emotion-recognition systems may be classified as high-risk where they involve profiling or affect fundamental rights") ✓. Szoszkiewicz & Yuste read the GDPR as already offering "stronger safeguards for neural data than those in many other jurisdictions", while its application is "a subject to debate" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "GDPR’s definitions of personal and sensitive data—and its enforcement mechanisms —already offer stronger safeguards for neural data than those in many other jurisdictions.") ✓. Futures Lab holds the EU up as the model for a US federal framework [Futures Lab 2026, p. 8](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p9 "To leverage this, the United States must implement a federal framework grounded in human rights law using the EU model.") ✓.

**United States and China.** No federal law; state laws extend sensitive-data rules to neural data ([[colorado-neural-data-law]], [[california-neural-data-law]]). The documents do not agree on how many states:

- California, Colorado and Montana, says the Secretary-General [A/81/351, para. 45](pin:A/81/351#p14 "While the United States has no federal neurotechnology-specific laws, California, Colorado and Montana have extended sensitive data protections to neural data") ✓, as do Szoszkiewicz & Yuste, who add six states "considering similar legislation" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "Colorado, California and Montana now explicitly include neurotechnology and neural data in their statutory definitions") ✓;
- Colorado and California, says the AHRC, without saying "only" [AHRC 2025, p. 25](pin:AHRC-2025#p25 "For example in the US, Colorado signed House Bill 24-1058 to define and protect neural data and California has now amended the California Consumer Privacy Act 2018") ✓;
- Futures Lab says both "currently the only states" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "California and Colorado are currently the only states to have passed legislation on neural data privacy, while a dozen others have legislation pending.") ✓ and, four pages later, "at least eight" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 8](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p9 "At least eight U.S. states have enacted legislation to protect neurorights") ✓.

China adopted ethical guidelines for brain-computer interface research in 2024 [A/81/351, para. 45](pin:A/81/351#p14 "In 2024, China adopted ethical guidelines for brain-computer interface research covering research integrity, scientific validity and informed consent.") ✓.

## How NOT to read this

- **A snapshot, taken at different times.** Szoszkiewicz & Yuste (mid-2025) still describe UNESCO's text as "a draft instrument … currently under intergovernmental negotiation" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "UNESCO published a draft instrument in 2024, currently under intergovernmental negotiation.") ✓; the Secretary-General (August 2026) reports it adopted. Date every regulatory claim.
- **Mostly consumer and data law.** Almost every measure listed governs neural data in markets or research, not the use of neurotechnology by the State against a suspect or prisoner. Do not read a consumer privacy law as a rule of criminal procedure.
- **Second-hand.** The library holds none of these laws. Where documents disagree (the US count above), the wiki records the disagreement rather than choosing.

## Open questions

- Will the Advisory Committee's guidelines (sixty-fourth session) address criminal justice specifically? Ingesting [[a-hrc-57-61]] shows what its first report said.
- Does "neurorights" legislation (Chile, Rio Grande do Sul) protect more in practice than data-protection law (GDPR, the US states)? That is the question of [[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]].

## Related

- [[neural-data]] (what most of these laws regulate)
- [[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]] (constitutional neurorights or adapted existing law)
- [[unesco-recommendation-2025]], [[a-hrc-57-61]] (the international instruments)
- [[chile-supreme-court-2023]], [[colorado-neural-data-law]], [[california-neural-data-law]] (the national cases and laws)
- [[reliability-and-admissibility]] (how courts handle neuroscientific evidence without rules)
- [[what-should-states-do-now]] (what the library asks of States)
- [[data-solidarity]] (a governance model none of these laws adopts)
- [[a-81-351]], [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]], [[ahrc-2025]], [[futures-lab-2026]], [[unodc-interpol-2025]] (the documents pinned here)
