frontmatter.title: Reliability and admissibility of neuroscientific evidence

pages.body:
# Reliability and admissibility of neuroscientific evidence

**One-liner.** Two questions the library keeps apart: whether neurotechnology-derived evidence is reliable enough to say anything about an individual, and whether a court may admit it. The Human Rights Committee leaves admissibility to domestic law, subject to the exclusion of evidence obtained contrary to article 7. The Secretary-General records courts admitting clinical neuroimaging as corroborative material, finds no deception-detection method generally accepted, and recommends independent validation before admission; UNODC and INTERPOL would deploy nothing until accuracy is demonstrated; the AHRC would make all such information inadmissible in Australia pending an inquiry.

Terms this page covers: reliability, accuracy, validity and scientific validation, admissibility, evidentiary weight, probative value, expert evidence, corroborative versus determinative, the exclusionary rule, equality of arms, contestability, "black box", automation bias. Not in the library by name: Daubert, Frye. United States v. Semrau appears only in a footnote of A/81/351 (footnote 16, PDF p. 4).

## What the library says

### (b) The Human Rights Committee, General Comment No. 32

Admissibility is for domestic law: "subject to the limitations on the use of statements, confessions and other evidence obtained in violation of article 7", "it is primarily for the domestic legislatures of States parties to determine the admissibility of evidence and how their courts assess it" [General Comment No. 32, para. 39](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p12 "subject to the limitations on the use of statements, confessions and other evidence obtained in violation of article 7 … it is primarily for the domestic legislatures of States parties to determine the admissibility of evidence and how their courts assess it") ✓. The article 7 limit is absolute: "no statements or confessions or, in principle, other evidence obtained in violation of this provision may be invoked as evidence in any proceedings covered by article 14" [General Comment No. 32, para. 6](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p2 "no statements or confessions or, in principle, other evidence obtained in violation of this provision may be invoked as evidence in any proceedings covered by article 14") ✓, and "Domestic law must ensure that statements or confessions obtained in violation of article 7 of the Covenant are excluded from the evidence" [General Comment No. 32, para. 41](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p13 "Domestic law must ensure that statements or confessions obtained in violation of article 7 of the Covenant are excluded from the evidence") ✓. Equality of arms "demands, inter alia, that each side be given the opportunity to contest all the arguments and evidence adduced by the other party" [General Comment No. 32, para. 13](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p3 "demands, inter alia, that each side be given the opportunity to contest all the arguments and evidence adduced by the other party") ✓, and adequate facilities for the defence "must include access to documents and other evidence" [General Comment No. 32, para. 33](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p10 "must include access to documents and other evidence") ✓. The presumption of innocence "imposes on the prosecution the burden of proving the charge, guarantees that no guilt can be presumed until the charge has been proved beyond reasonable doubt" [General Comment No. 32, para. 30](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p9 "imposes on the prosecution the burden of proving the charge, guarantees that no guilt can be presumed until the charge has been proved beyond reasonable doubt") ✓. The Committee says nothing about scientific reliability or neurotechnology; the applications below are the reports'. See [[general-comment-32]] and [[ccpr-c-gc-32]].

### (c) The Secretary-General (A/81/351) and UNODC–INTERPOL 2025

**Where evidence is admitted today.** "the most common use of neurotechnology in judicial contexts is the introduction of neuroimaging as medical or expert evidence", and "Where accepted, such material is generally treated as corroborative rather than determinative" [A/81/351, para. 6](pin:A/81/351#p3 "the most common use of neurotechnology in judicial contexts is the introduction of neuroimaging as medical or expert evidence … Where accepted, such material is generally treated as corroborative rather than determinative") ✓. "While the admissibility and evidentiary weight of neuroimaging remain contested, several jurisdictions permit its limited and carefully circumscribed use" [A/81/351, para. 7](pin:A/81/351#p3 "While the admissibility and evidentiary weight of neuroimaging remain contested, several jurisdictions permit its limited and carefully circumscribed use") ✓: courts of appeal in the Netherlands "have accepted neuroimaging and neuropsychological evidence as corroborative material", the Court of Appeal of England and Wales "has accepted neuroscientific evidence as corroborative – using it to support rather than determine assessments of culpability and sentencing", and in Canada it "is not treated as determinative" [A/81/351, para. 7](pin:A/81/351#p3 "have accepted neuroimaging and neuropsychological evidence as corroborative material … has accepted neuroscientific evidence as corroborative – using it to support rather than determine assessments of culpability and sentencing … is not treated as determinative") ✓. These are reports of domestic practice, not a UN endorsement of it.

**Where it is not.** "No brain-based deception detection method has achieved general acceptance for courtroom use" [A/81/351, para. 9](pin:A/81/351#p4 "No brain-based deception detection method has achieved general acceptance for courtroom use") ✓; a United States federal appeals court excluded fMRI lie detection "finding it insufficiently reliable and not generally accepted under evidentiary standards" [A/81/351, para. 9](pin:A/81/351#p4 "finding it insufficiently reliable and not generally accepted under evidentiary standards") ✓ (footnote 16, same PDF page: United States v. Semrau, Sixth Circuit, 2012); the Supreme Court of India held involuntary BEOS tests to violate the privilege and "renders the resulting evidence inadmissible" [A/81/351, para. 9](pin:A/81/351#p4 "renders the resulting evidence inadmissible") ✓ (see [[selvi-v-state-of-karnataka]], [[brain-based-lie-detection]]). For decoding, "Whether such approaches will, at some point, be able to produce information that is sufficiently reliable to be used in the administration of justice is unknown" [A/81/351, para. 11](pin:A/81/351#p4 "Whether such approaches will, at some point, be able to produce information that is sufficiently reliable to be used in the administration of justice is unknown") ✓.

**Why reliability is the key concern.** "A key concern regarding the use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice is the reliability of neuroscientific evidence in court" [A/81/351, para. 13](pin:A/81/351#p5 "A key concern regarding the use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice is the reliability of neuroscientific evidence in court") ✓. The report names the inferential step that fails: "Particular caution is warranted when translating findings established at the group or population level into conclusions about individual persons, given intra- and inter-individual variability and the probabilistic nature of many neuroscientific findings" [A/81/351, para. 13](pin:A/81/351#p5 "Particular caution is warranted when translating findings established at the group or population level into conclusions about individual persons, given intra- and inter-individual variability and the probabilistic nature of many neuroscientific findings") ✓, worsened by "the gap between controlled laboratory conditions and real-world settings" and a lack of shared understanding "which makes it difficult for courts to assess the probative value of such evidence" [A/81/351, para. 13](pin:A/81/351#p5 "the gap between controlled laboratory conditions and real-world settings … which makes it difficult for courts to assess the probative value of such evidence") ✓. Its conclusion: "the evidentiary use of neuroscientific data remains contested. Its technical complexity, probabilistic nature and potential for misinterpretation pose significant risks" [A/81/351, para. 47](pin:A/81/351#p14 "the evidentiary use of neuroscientific data remains contested. Its technical complexity, probabilistic nature and potential for misinterpretation pose significant risks") ✓. Consumer data add a second route into court, "introduced as evidence in legal proceedings without recognition of its uniquely sensitive character, a risk amplified in counter-terrorism and national security contexts, where legal thresholds for data access and admissibility are often significantly lower" [A/81/351, para. 14](pin:A/81/351#p5 "introduced as evidence in legal proceedings without recognition of its uniquely sensitive character, a risk amplified in counter-terrorism and national security contexts, where legal thresholds for data access and admissibility are often significantly lower") ✓ (see [[neural-data]]). Two further hazards for the bench: "automation bias – the tendency to accept uncritically the outputs of technological systems" [A/81/351, para. 31](pin:A/81/351#p10 "automation bias – the tendency to accept uncritically the outputs of technological systems") ✓, and systems whose "untransparent and obscure nature" makes them a "black box" [A/81/351, para. 34](pin:A/81/351#p11 "the untransparent and obscure nature of such systems – sometimes referred to as a “black box”") ✓.

**Fair-trial conditions on admission.** Equality of arms "would require the defence to have access to the scientific expertise and proprietary data needed to interpret and challenge neurotechnology-derived evidence" [A/81/351, para. 33](pin:A/81/351#p11 "would require the defence to have access to the scientific expertise and proprietary data needed to interpret and challenge neurotechnology-derived evidence") ✓. "According to submissions and research, the right to a fair trial also depends on requiring that any neurotechnology-based evidence admitted in court meets the highest standards of scientific validation, transparency and contestability" [A/81/351, para. 33](pin:A/81/351#p11 "According to submissions and research, the right to a fair trial also depends on requiring that any neurotechnology-based evidence admitted in court meets the highest standards of scientific validation, transparency and contestability") ✓: attributed to submissions and research, not stated as law. The exclusionary rule "could apply to evidence obtained through the coercive use of neurotechnologies" [A/81/351, para. 32](pin:A/81/351#p10 "This could apply to evidence obtained through the coercive use of neurotechnologies") ✓ (see [[self-incrimination]]).

**Recommendations.** "Require rigorous independent scientific review and validation of any neurotechnology-derived evidence proposed for admission in court, including assessment, as appropriate, of its safety, validity, reliability, reproducibility, known limitations and suitability for the specific context and population in which it is applied" [A/81/351, para. 50 (f)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Require rigorous independent scientific review and validation of any neurotechnology-derived evidence proposed for admission in court, including assessment, as appropriate, of its safety, validity, reliability, reproducibility, known limitations and suitability for the specific context and population in which it is applied") ✓; "Prohibit the use of neural data obtained through torture or ill-treatment, or in violation of the rights to freedom of thought and opinion, as evidence in any proceedings" [A/81/351, para. 50 (d)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Prohibit the use of neural data obtained through torture or ill-treatment, or in violation of the rights to freedom of thought and opinion, as evidence in any proceedings") ✓; and "specialized training for law enforcement officials, prosecutors, judges and defence counsel" [A/81/351, para. 50 (j)](pin:A/81/351#p16 "specialized training for law enforcement officials, prosecutors, judges and defence counsel") ✓.

UNODC and INTERPOL note that hospital scans "have for some time been used in expert evidence in some jurisdictions to support claims related to legal insanity, risk, intent, culpability, and type of punishment" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 1](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p4 "have for some time been used in expert evidence in some jurisdictions to support claims related to legal insanity, risk, intent, culpability, and type of punishment") ✓, and that the new uses raise questions about "how standards of admissible evidence may evolve" and "the reliability of neuroscientific methods, the risk of over-reliance on expert testimony" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 2](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p5 "how standards of admissible evidence may evolve … the reliability of neuroscientific methods, the risk of over-reliance on expert testimony") ✓. "Many of the technologies under consideration have not been tested for accuracy, reliability, or safety in real-world law enforcement environments" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "Many of the technologies under consideration have not been tested for accuracy, reliability, or safety in real-world law enforcement environments") ✓, and "courts in some jurisdictions have assessed the admissibility of neuroimaging evidence on a case-by-case basis" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "courts in some jurisdictions have assessed the admissibility of neuroimaging evidence on a case-by-case basis, determining the appropriate conditions under which it can be used") ✓. The paper's rule is validation first: "Technologies should therefore not be deployed until their accuracy, safety, and feasibility have been rigorously demonstrated through independent testing and peer-reviewed research", and courts need "clear and reliable information about what these tools can - and cannot - do" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 5](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p8 "Technologies should therefore not be deployed until their accuracy, safety, and feasibility have been rigorously demonstrated through independent testing and peer-reviewed research … clear and reliable information about what these tools can - and cannot - do") ✓. It also asks for "clear procedures for maintaining the chain of custody when handling neurotechnology-related evidence" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 5](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p8 "clear procedures for maintaining the chain of custody when handling neurotechnology-related evidence") ✓ and for "developing clear rules on admissibility of evidence" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 6](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p9 "developing clear rules on admissibility of evidence") ✓.

### (d) The Australian Human Rights Commission (2025)

The AHRC's material is Australian. In R v Murray, lie detection evidence tendered by the accused "was to bolster the credibility of the accused as a witness, which was a matter for the jury to assess" [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "was to bolster the credibility of the accused as a witness, which was a matter for the jury to assess") ✓; the Lie Detector Act 1983 (NSW) "renders lie detection evidence inadmissible in court" [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "renders lie detection evidence inadmissible in court and prohibits its use to determine honesty in employment settings") ✓. The Commission concedes possible benefits only "(if the technology is accurate and sufficiently reliable)" [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "reduce the number of wrongful convictions via exculpatory evidence (if the technology is accurate and sufficiently reliable)") ✓, and its preliminary view is that, pending an ALRC inquiry, "information gained via neurotechnology should be inadmissible at trial" [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "until that time, information gained via neurotechnology should be inadmissible at trial") ✓ (see [[moratorium]]). On risk assessment it doubts accuracy: using neurotechnology "as a factor in determining a person’s chance of reoffending may not be an accurate representation of such a risk" [AHRC 2025, p. 35](pin:AHRC-2025#p35 "using neurotechnology as a factor in determining a person’s chance of reoffending may not be an accurate representation of such a risk") ✓ (see [[neuroprediction]]). It suggests a guide for judges on neurotechnology, modelled on an existing guide on AI [AHRC 2025, p. 34](pin:AHRC-2025#p34 "A similar guide focused on the possible challenges and opportunities that neurotechnology presents for Australian courts and tribunals would be a useful initiative") ✓.

### (e) Civil society

The Futures Lab submission reports accuracy claims from research, not from courts: a BCI used "to translate internal speech with 79 percent accuracy" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 2](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p3 "to translate internal speech with 79 percent accuracy onto a monitor") ✓. It reports that France admitted brain imaging in judicial proceedings, except functional imaging, by a policy "adopted prior to consensus among neuroscience experts" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 3](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p4 "This policy was adopted prior to consensus among neuroscience experts and in opposition to the recommendations of the French Parliamentary Office for the Evaluation of Scientific and Technological Choices") ✓. Its reliability point is about bias: non-diverse training data make "outputs less accurate" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 6](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p7 "making outputs less accurate and potentially harmful to people of African descent and other marginalized communities") ✓ and may yield "inaccurate or pathologizing interpretations of their mental states" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 7](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p8 "neurotechnologies may produce inaccurate or pathologizing interpretations of their mental states") ✓.

### (f) Scholarship

The library's highest accuracy figures come from clinical research with cooperating participants: speech decoding in persons with ALS "reaching accuracy levels as high as 97.5%" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3469](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p1 "successfully decoded attempted speech in individuals with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), reaching accuracy levels as high as 97.5%") ✓, while consumer devices "can achieve satisfactory accuracy, although with considerable variability between individuals" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "These devices can achieve satisfactory accuracy, although with considerable variability between individuals") ✓. Those figures describe attempted speech by volunteers, not deception by suspects; the Secretary-General's warning about the laboratory-to-courtroom gap (para. 13) is the reason they do not carry over. The authors also note that whether wearable data "should be admitted in criminal proceedings is already provoking intense debate among legal experts" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "should be admitted in criminal proceedings is already provoking intense debate among legal experts") ✓, and warn against "alarmist narratives or overhyping potential harms" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3472](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p4 "it is equally important to avoid alarmist narratives or overhyping potential harms or regulatory overreach") ✓.

## Contested claims

```contested
claim: Neuroimaging may be admitted now as corroborative, not determinative, evidence, provided it is validated and contestable.
verdict: contested
note: The Secretary-General both records courts admitting clinical neuroimaging as corroborative material and calls its evidentiary use "contested"; his recommendation presupposes admission after independent validation. UNODC and INTERPOL would deploy nothing until accuracy is demonstrated; the AHRC's preliminary view would exclude all neurotechnology-derived information in Australia until an inquiry reports. For deception detection the library is not split: no method is generally accepted.
~ c | [A/81/351, para. 7](pin:A/81/351#p3 "While the admissibility and evidentiary weight of neuroimaging remain contested, several jurisdictions permit its limited and carefully circumscribed use") ✓ | records limited corroborative use by courts while calling admissibility contested | [[a-81-351]]
+ c | [A/81/351, para. 50 (f)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Require rigorous independent scientific review and validation of any neurotechnology-derived evidence proposed for admission in court") ✓ | admission presupposed; independent validation recommended as the gate | [[a-81-351]]
- c | [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 5](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p8 "Technologies should therefore not be deployed until their accuracy, safety, and feasibility have been rigorously demonstrated through independent testing and peer-reviewed research") ✓ | no deployment in law enforcement or criminal justice until accuracy is independently demonstrated | [[unodc-interpol-2025]]
- d | [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "until that time, information gained via neurotechnology should be inadmissible at trial") ✓ | interim inadmissibility pending an ALRC inquiry (a preliminary view, Australia) | [[ahrc-2025]]
```

## Open questions

- Which standard? The Secretary-General speaks of "general acceptance" and "evidentiary standards" without naming Daubert or Frye; the library contains no admissibility test of its own. A State asked to "require rigorous independent scientific review" has no model text in the library.
- Who pays for the defence's expertise? Para. 33 says equality of arms "would require" access to expertise and proprietary data; the library does not say how, or who bears the cost.
- Exculpatory evidence: the AHRC's interim inadmissibility would also exclude tests the accused wants to tender (R v Murray); the Secretary-General's framework is written against the prosecution. Neither addresses the asymmetry.
- "Corroborative rather than determinative" describes practice; no document says what weight is permissible, or how a court keeps corroborative evidence from becoming decisive in effect.
- Consent and reliability are independent: a freely consented test is still probabilistic. See [[consent-in-custody]].

## Related

- [[brain-based-lie-detection]] (the technique with no general acceptance)
- [[self-incrimination]] (the exclusionary rule for article 7 evidence)
- [[consent-in-custody]] (consent does not settle reliability)
- [[neuroprediction]] (group-level correlations applied to individuals)
- [[neural-data]] (consumer data as evidence; lower thresholds in security contexts)
- [[moratorium]] (the AHRC's interim inadmissibility)
- [[iccpr-art-7]] (the exclusion trigger) and [[iccpr-art-14-3-g]] (compulsion)
- [[general-comment-32]] (who relies on paras. 6, 13, 30, 33, 39 and 41) and [[ccpr-c-gc-32]] (what it says)
- [[selvi-v-state-of-karnataka]] (inadmissibility of involuntary BEOS results)
- [[a-81-351]], [[unodc-interpol-2025]], [[ahrc-2025]], [[futures-lab-2026]], [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (source pages)
- [[what-should-states-do-now]] (recommendation 50 (f) among the asks)

frontmatter.title: The privilege against self-incrimination

pages.body:
# The privilege against self-incrimination

**One-liner.** Article 14(3)(g) of the ICCPR guarantees that no one charged with a criminal offence is compelled to testify against himself or to confess guilt. The Human Rights Committee reads this as the absence of any direct or indirect physical or undue psychological pressure, with exclusion of evidence obtained contrary to article 7. The Secretary-General and the Australian Human Rights Commission apply that reading to brain-based lie detection; the Committee itself has never addressed neurotechnology.

Terms this page covers: self-incrimination, article 14(3)(g), "not to be compelled to testify against oneself or to confess guilt", the right to silence (to remain silent), confession, the exclusionary rule. The UN reports say "privilege against self-incrimination"; the AHRC adds "right to remain silent".

## What the library says

### (a) Treaty text

Article 14(3)(g) entitles everyone charged with a criminal offence "not to be compelled to testify against himself or to confess guilt" ([ICCPR art. 14(3)(g)](https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-mechanisms/instruments/international-covenant-civil-and-political-rights), not in the library). The provision has its own page: [[iccpr-art-14-3-g]].

### (b) The Human Rights Committee, General Comment No. 32 (2007)

The Committee's standard is broad. The guarantee "must be understood in terms of the absence of any direct or indirect physical or undue psychological pressure from the investigating authorities on the accused, with a view to obtaining a confession of guilt" [General Comment No. 32, para. 41](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p13 "must be understood in terms of the absence of any direct or indirect physical or undue psychological pressure from the investigating authorities on the accused, with a view to obtaining a confession of guilt") ✓. Where the pressure amounts to treatment contrary to article 7, the same paragraph adds an evidentiary rule: "Domestic law must ensure that statements or confessions obtained in violation of article 7 of the Covenant are excluded from the evidence", and "the burden is on the State to prove that statements made by the accused have been given of their own free will" [General Comment No. 32, para. 41](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p13 "Domestic law must ensure that statements or confessions obtained in violation of article 7 of the Covenant are excluded from the evidence … the burden is on the State to prove that statements made by the accused have been given of their own free will") ✓. Forcing a confession under duress "violates both article 7 of the Covenant … and article 14, paragraph 3 (g) prohibiting compulsion to testify against oneself or confess guilt" [General Comment No. 32, para. 60](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p17 "violates both article 7 of the Covenant … and article 14, paragraph 3 (g) prohibiting compulsion to testify against oneself or confess guilt") ✓. The exclusion holds in emergencies too: "no statements or confessions or, in principle, other evidence obtained in violation of this provision may be invoked as evidence in any proceedings covered by article 14, including during a state of emergency" [General Comment No. 32, para. 6](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p2 "no statements or confessions or, in principle, other evidence obtained in violation of this provision may be invoked as evidence in any proceedings covered by article 14, including during a state of emergency") ✓. Disclosure to the defence must cover "indications that a confession was not voluntary" [General Comment No. 32, para. 33](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p10 "other evidence that could assist the defence (e.g. indications that a confession was not voluntary)") ✓.

General Comment No. 32 says nothing about neurotechnology, lie detection or neural data. Every application below is a report's, not the Committee's. See [[general-comment-32]] (who relies on it) and [[ccpr-c-gc-32]] (what it says).

A neighbouring guarantee is not the same thing. Under articles 18(2) and 17, "no one can be compelled to reveal his thoughts or adherence to a religion or belief" [General Comment No. 22, para. 3](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p2 "no one can be compelled to reveal his thoughts or adherence to a religion or belief") ✓. That protects thought as such, not testimony in a criminal charge; see [[freedom-of-thought]].

### (c) The Secretary-General (A/81/351) and UNODC–INTERPOL 2025

The Secretary-General applies the Committee's standard to neurotechnology: "The coercive use of brain-based lie detection could call into question the privilege against self-incrimination, protected under article 14 (3) (g) of the Covenant" [A/81/351, para. 32](pin:A/81/351#p10 "The coercive use of brain-based lie detection could call into question the privilege against self-incrimination, protected under article 14 (3) (g) of the Covenant") ✓. The report calls the privilege "an absolute guarantee" and states that "any direct or indirect physical or psychological pressure on the accused with a view to obtaining a confession of guilt is prohibited" [A/81/351, para. 32](pin:A/81/351#p10 "This privilege is an absolute guarantee and any direct or indirect physical or psychological pressure on the accused with a view to obtaining a confession of guilt is prohibited") ✓ (its footnote 62, on the same PDF page, cites General Comment No. 32). Two things are the report's own: the word "absolute", which para. 41 of the General Comment does not use, and the dropping of "undue" before "psychological pressure".

The report then relies on a domestic court: the Supreme Court of India "held that the involuntary administration of brain electrical oscillation signature profiling tests, a form of brain-based lie detection, violates the constitutional protection against self-incrimination" [A/81/351, para. 32](pin:A/81/351#p10 "held that the involuntary administration of brain electrical oscillation signature profiling tests, a form of brain-based lie detection, violates the constitutional protection against self-incrimination") ✓ (its footnote 63, on PDF p. 11, cites the judgment of 5 May 2010, paras. 215–224); see [[selvi-v-state-of-karnataka]]. On the exclusionary rule the report keeps a conditional: "statements or other evidence obtained in violation of the prohibition of torture or ill-treatment may not be invoked as evidence in any proceedings. This could apply to evidence obtained through the coercive use of neurotechnologies" [A/81/351, para. 32](pin:A/81/351#p10 "statements or other evidence obtained in violation of the prohibition of torture or ill-treatment may not be invoked as evidence in any proceedings. This could apply to evidence obtained through the coercive use of neurotechnologies") ✓.

Earlier, the report lists the privilege among four concerns raised by deception detection, "consent, coercion, reliability, and the privilege against self-incrimination" [A/81/351, para. 9](pin:A/81/351#p4 "raise serious concerns regarding consent, coercion, reliability, and the privilege against self-incrimination") ✓, and notes that after the Indian judgment "voluntary use appears to have continued in practice" [A/81/351, para. 9](pin:A/81/351#p4 "voluntary use appears to have continued in practice") ✓. Its recommendations ask States to "Prohibit the compulsory or coercive use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice, including brain-based deception detection" [A/81/351, para. 50 (c)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Prohibit the compulsory or coercive use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice, including brain-based deception detection") ✓ and to "Prohibit the use of neural data obtained through torture or ill-treatment, or in violation of the rights to freedom of thought and opinion, as evidence in any proceedings" [A/81/351, para. 50 (d)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Prohibit the use of neural data obtained through torture or ill-treatment, or in violation of the rights to freedom of thought and opinion, as evidence in any proceedings") ✓. The second ground of exclusion (freedom of thought and opinion) goes beyond the Committee's article 7 rule; it is a recommendation, not a restatement.

UNODC and INTERPOL list the privilege among the due process rights "at stake" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "Due process rights are also at stake, including the right to appear before a competent judicial authority, the presumption of innocence, the privilege against self-incrimination, and the right to appeal") ✓, and leave a question open rather than answer it: "Can courts legally order a criminal defendant, even in narrow circumstances, to cooperate with law enforcement in the use of neurotechnologies?" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 5](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p8 "Can courts legally order a criminal defendant, even in narrow circumstances, to cooperate with law enforcement in the use of neurotechnologies?") ✓.

### (d) The Australian Human Rights Commission (2025)

The AHRC restates the standard and applies it to pressure to take a test: "The use of neurotechnology as a means of lie detection may threaten this human right if alleged offenders are pressured into complying with neurotechnological tests" [AHRC 2025, p. 31](pin:AHRC-2025#p31 "Under international human rights law all people charged with a criminal offence have a right not to be compelled to testify against themselves or to confess guilt … The use of neurotechnology as a means of lie detection may threaten this human right if alleged offenders are pressured into complying with neurotechnological tests") ✓. It folds the right to silence into the privilege and adds Australian law: "The right to remain silent and not to selfincriminate is a right afforded to anyone charged with a criminal offence. This right is found in art 14.3(g) ICCPR" [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "The right to remain silent and not to selfincriminate is a right afforded to anyone charged with a criminal offence. This right is found in art 14.3(g) ICCPR") ✓. The words it then quotes, evidence "obtained through methods of coercion or oppression in defiance of the will of the accused", are a quotation from its own sources (its endnote 160, on PDF p. 78, cites Ligthart 2022 and Ibrahim and Others v. the United Kingdom), not from the Covenant or the Committee. Its distinctive contribution is the indirect-pressure scenario: a reduced sentence or immunity offered for consent [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "if an accused was offered the opportunity for a reduced sentence or some level of immunity in exchange for consenting to the use of neurotechnology during questioning by police, it would be difficult to argue that any consent given was entirely voluntary") ✓, developed on [[consent-in-custody]]. On trial processes it pairs the privilege with the presumption of innocence: "Both of these rights require that no direct or indirect physical or psychological pressure be exerted by authorities to secure a confession or testimony" [AHRC 2025, p. 33](pin:AHRC-2025#p33 "Both of these rights require that no direct or indirect physical or psychological pressure be exerted by authorities to secure a confession or testimony") ✓.

### (e) Civil society

The Futures Lab submission does not name the privilege. Its nearest point is a warning that policing use "could expand into brain-reading of suspects or witnesses" [Futures Lab 2026, p. 6](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p7 "its use in policing could expand into brain-reading of suspects or witnesses") ✓.

### (f) Scholarship

Szoszkiewicz and Yuste tie the privilege to consumer wearables rather than to interrogation: whether their data should be admitted in criminal proceedings "is already provoking intense debate among legal experts … underlining the urgent need to strengthen protections for the right against self-incrimination in the era of neurotechnology" [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "is already provoking intense debate among legal experts … underlining the urgent need to strengthen protections for the right against self-incrimination in the era of neurotechnology") ✓. Prainsack et al. do not discuss it.

## Open questions

- Is the output of a brain-based test "testimony" or a "confession" at all? No document in the library discusses the distinction between testimonial and physical evidence; the Secretary-General reports the Indian holding without its reasoning.
- The Committee speaks of "the accused" and "investigating authorities"; the reports speak of suspects, detainees and interrogation. Whether the guarantee attaches before charge is not discussed.
- Does a suspect's consent remove compulsion? See [[consent-in-custody]] and [[can-a-suspect-consent-to-lie-detection]].
- Exculpatory use: the AHRC's R v Murray example concerns a test tendered by the accused; the privilege does not answer that case. See [[reliability-and-admissibility]].

## Related

- [[iccpr-art-14-3-g]] (the provision itself)
- [[general-comment-32]] (who in the library relies on para. 41) and [[ccpr-c-gc-32]] (what the General Comment says)
- [[brain-based-lie-detection]] (the technique the privilege is applied to)
- [[consent-in-custody]] (whether consent removes compulsion)
- [[reliability-and-admissibility]] (where the exclusionary rule meets the reliability question)
- [[iccpr-art-7]] (the article 7 trigger for exclusion)
- [[freedom-of-thought]] (the separate guarantee not to reveal one's thoughts)
- [[selvi-v-state-of-karnataka]] (the domestic case the Secretary-General relies on)
- [[a-81-351]], [[unodc-interpol-2025]], [[ahrc-2025]], [[futures-lab-2026]], [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (source pages)
- [[can-a-suspect-consent-to-lie-detection]] (the question page)

pages.body:
# A/HRC/57/61, Human Rights Council Advisory Committee report on neurotechnology (2024)

**Stub: this document is in the library's inbox and has not been ingested.** Nothing on this page quotes or pins A/HRC/57/61. What follows is what four ingested documents say about it, pinned to them. The live Ingest will read the report passage by passage, write `sources/a-hrc-57-61.md`, and rewrite this page from the text; the list at the end is what that reading should check.

**What it is.** From the library's metadata: "Impact, opportunities and challenges of neurotechnology with regard to the promotion and protection of all human rights: report of the Human Rights Council Advisory Committee", symbol A/HRC/57/61, dated 8 August 2024, 23 PDF pages ([docs.un.org/en/A/HRC/57/61](https://docs.un.org/en/A/HRC/57/61); in the library's inbox, not yet ingested). The Advisory Committee is an expert body of the Human Rights Council, not a treaty body: register (c), a UN soft-law report. The Secretary-General reports a follow-up mandate [A/81/351, para. 46](pin:A/81/351#p14 "The Human Rights Council has tasked its Advisory Committee with drafting guidelines on applying existing human rights standards throughout the neurotechnology life cycle for consideration at its sixty-fourth session") ✓ (footnote 83, same PDF page: Human Rights Council resolution 58/6).

## In the library

**A/81/351 (c)** relies on it more than on any other UN text: five paragraphs cite it by symbol, and nine footnotes. In the text, the Secretary-General attributes to the Committee a view on neuromodulation of offenders [A/81/351, para. 29](pin:A/81/351#p10 "The Human Rights Council Advisory Committee is of the view that the use of neuromodulation techniques intended to alter the brain activity of offenders to reduce aggression or impulsivity may constitute treatment contrary to articles 7 or 10 of the Covenant when imposed without genuinely free and informed consent") ✓; a finding on who is most exposed [A/81/351, para. 37](pin:A/81/351#p12 "The Human Rights Council Advisory Committee has identified “groups experiencing structural discrimination and marginalized people or those in positions of socioeconomic disadvantage” as being particularly vulnerable to negative impacts of the use of neurotechnology in the administration of justice") ✓ (citing its para. 37); a phrase on remedies [A/81/351, para. 36](pin:A/81/351#p12 "potentially rendering the right to a remedy “illusory, inaccessible or ineffective” and raising accountability issues") ✓ (citing its para. 72); a statement of what the technology can do [A/81/351, para. 22](pin:A/81/351#p8 "While neurotechnology is not capable at present of “mind-reading”, it is reportedly capable of inferring emotions and internal reactions based on neural data") ✓; and an assessment of national regulation [A/81/351, para. 42](pin:A/81/351#p13 "At the national level, the regulatory response to the human rights challenges posed by neurotechnology is still nascent and uneven") ✓.

In footnotes (read in the PDF; not in the passages) A/81/351 also cites the report for: the prior reports it builds on (footnote 1, PDF p. 2, on para. 1); neuroprediction research (footnote 19, p. 4, on para. 10); neurostimulation for aggression (footnote 22, p. 5, on para. 12); the debate on new frameworks or existing law (footnote 29, p. 6, on para. 16); the UN texts on neurotechnology (footnote 30, p. 6, on para. 17); consumer data collection (footnote 48, p. 9, on para. 25); the Special Rapporteur's principles (footnote 52, p. 9, on para. 27); the Selvi case as degrading treatment (footnote 55, p. 9, on para. 28); and recognition as a person before the law (footnote 68, p. 11, on para. 35).

**UNODC–INTERPOL 2025 (c)** cites it once in the text, on discrimination [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "As the UN Human Rights Council Advisory Committee has highlighted, the potential for the discriminatory use of neurotechnologies – particularly in relation to groups that have been marginalized, subjected to structural discrimination, or are socioeconomically disadvantaged – is a key concern") ✓. Its footnotes 21 and 23 (PDF p. 7) cite "A/HRC/57/61, pp. 76-78" and "p. 37"; the report has 23 pages, so these look like paragraph numbers. A footnote on PDF p. 4 (not in the passages) says the Committee's report uses the term "neurodata" rather than "neural data".

**AHRC 2025 (d)** cites it under a name of its own [AHRC 2025, p. 33](pin:AHRC-2025#p33 "The UN Human Rights Advisory Committee has observed that any misuse of the technology to this degree would represent a violation of art 7 ICCPR") ✓, where "this degree" is neurotechnology [AHRC 2025, p. 33](pin:AHRC-2025#p33 "forcibly used to extract information from suspects") ✓. There is no "UN Human Rights Advisory Committee": the body is the Human Rights Council Advisory Committee, and the AHRC's own endnote 170 (PDF p. 79) cites it correctly, as A/HRC/57/61 of 8 August 2024, paras. 34–35. Other endnotes (PDF pp. 74, 77, 78, 81, 84) cite paras. 4, 18, 27, 36 and 47. Separately, the Commission describes a Council-commissioned report without a symbol [AHRC 2025, p. 9](pin:AHRC-2025#p9 "The UN Human Rights Council adopted a resolution to commission a report on neurotechnology and human rights. The report was released in September 2024") ✓; the library's date for A/HRC/57/61 is 8 August 2024.

**Szoszkiewicz and Yuste 2025 (f)** attribute to it a recommendation [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "the UN Human Rights Council Advisory Committee recommended developing General Comments on the freedom of thought and mental integrity for persons with disabilities") ✓.

## What to check at ingest

Each claim above is a second-hand attribution. Against the text, verify:

1. Para. 37 (per A/81/351): the quoted phrase on structurally discriminated and marginalized groups, and whether UNODC–INTERPOL's "p. 37" is the same paragraph.
2. Para. 72 (per A/81/351): the phrase "illusory, inaccessible or ineffective" on remedies.
3. The view that neuromodulation of offenders without genuinely free and informed consent "may constitute" treatment contrary to articles 7 or 10 (A/81/351 para. 29): find the paragraph and the Committee's own verb.
4. Paras. 34–35 (per AHRC endnote 170): whether forcible extraction of information "would represent a violation of art 7" is the Committee's wording or the AHRC's strengthening of it.
5. The "not capable at present of mind-reading" but "inferring emotions" statement (A/81/351 para. 22).
6. The recommendation of General Comments on freedom of thought and on mental integrity for persons with disabilities (Szoszkiewicz and Yuste): to which bodies, in what terms.
7. The "nascent and uneven" assessment of national regulation (A/81/351 para. 42), and what the report says of the United States, Chile and others.
8. Whether the report uses "neurodata" (UNODC–INTERPOL's footnote) and how it defines it, against the UNESCO definition A/81/351 adopts.
9. The date: 8 August 2024 (metadata, AHRC endnotes, UNODC–INTERPOL footnotes) against the AHRC's "released in September 2024".
10. Whether the report takes a side on new rights versus existing rights (A/81/351 footnote 29 cites it on that debate), and what it says of Selvi (footnote 55).

## Related

- [[a-81-351]] (its main reporter: five paragraphs and nine footnotes)
- [[unodc-interpol-2025]], [[ahrc-2025]], [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (the other reporters)
- [[neuromodulation-of-offenders]] and [[consent-in-custody]] (the para. 29 view)
- [[discrimination]] (the para. 37 finding, cited by two documents)
- [[iccpr-art-7]] (the article both A/81/351 and the AHRC attach to it)
- [[freedom-of-thought]] (the General Comment it is said to have recommended)
- [[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]] and [[regulatory-landscape]] (footnote 29; para. 42)
- [[selvi-v-state-of-karnataka]] (footnote 55 pairs the two)
- [[unesco-recommendation-2025]] (the other UN-level instrument known second-hand)

pages.title: California's neural data law

frontmatter.title: California's neural data law

pages.body:
# California's neural data law

**What it is.** A 2024 amendment to California's consumer privacy statute that adds neural data to its protected personal information. A/81/351 names the bill in footnote 79 (PDF p. 14) as "State of California, Senate Bill No. 1223 (2024)"; AHRC 2025 names the statute amended, the California Consumer Privacy Act 2018; Futures Lab 2026 quotes the definition and, in its footnote 11 (PDF p. 5), dates the bill's approval to 28 September 2024. It is the domestic law of one state of the United States, reported by four library documents of registers (c), (d), (e) and (f). The statute is not in the library, and this page carries the registers of the reports.

## In the library

The Secretary-General's single sentence groups California with Colorado and Montana [A/81/351, para. 45](pin:A/81/351#p14 "California, Colorado and Montana have extended sensitive data protections to neural data") ✓.

The Australian Human Rights Commission names the statute and the technique [AHRC 2025, p. 25](pin:AHRC-2025#p25 "California has now amended the California Consumer Privacy Act 2018 to extend existing consumer protections to an individual’s neural data") ✓.

Futures Lab gives the definition, the one place in the library where a statutory definition of neural data is quoted [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "The California law grants consumers privacy rights regarding personal information and neural data. In this law, neural data is defined as “information that is generated by measuring the activity of a consumer’s central or peripheral nervous system, and that is not inferred from nonneural information.”") ✓.

Szoszkiewicz and Yuste place it with the other two states as an extension of existing consumer legislation [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "Colorado, California and Montana now explicitly include neurotechnology and neural data in their statutory definitions, and apply to these data existing consumer legislation for personal sensitive data") ✓, and read the voting record as a sign of consensus [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "all legislative efforts worldwide have been unanimous or nearly unanimous, reflecting emerging bipartisan agreement") ✓.

**The definition against the others.** California's definition, as Futures Lab quotes it, excludes data "inferred from nonneural information". The definition the Secretary-General adopts from UNESCO covers structure as well as activity and is silent on inference [A/81/351, para. 5](pin:A/81/351#p3 "qualitative and quantitative data about the structure, activity and function of the nervous system gathered through neurotechnology") ✓. Szoszkiewicz and Yuste report that legal definitions sometimes go the other way [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "“Neural data” is generally defined as information generated by measuring activity in the central or peripheral nervous systems, sometimes extending to inferences drawn from that data") ✓. Which definition a State adopts decides whether inferences about a person drawn from other data count as neural data; the library records the options, not a preferred one.

**Where the reports differ.** As for [[colorado-neural-data-law]]: Futures Lab counts California and Colorado as [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "currently the only states to have passed legislation on neural data privacy") ✓, while A/81/351 (para. 45) and Szoszkiewicz and Yuste (p. 3471) add Montana. Prefer the (c) count, dated August 2026.

**What the library does not say.** The text of the Act; what rights "sensitive personal information" status gives a consumer in California; whether the law binds State agencies, prosecutors or courts. Every report places it in the consumer market; nothing in the library applies it to the administration of justice.

## Related

- [[colorado-neural-data-law]] (the companion law; the two definitions differ)
- [[neural-data]] (the definitional question: inference in or out)
- [[unesco-recommendation-2025]] (the source of the definition A/81/351 uses)
- [[regulatory-landscape]] (state laws without a federal law)
- [[is-neural-data-special]] (sensitive within an existing scheme, not a new category)
- [[a-81-351]], [[ahrc-2025]], [[futures-lab-2026]], [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (the reporting documents)

frontmatter.title: Chile Supreme Court, 2023 (neural data, Emotiv)

pages.body:
# Chile Supreme Court, 2023 (neural data, Emotiv)

**What it is.** A 2023 ruling of the Supreme Court of Chile on a consumer brain-monitoring device, applying the country's 2021 constitutional amendment on brain activity and the data derived from it. A/81/351 names it in a footnote as "Supreme Court of Chile, Girardi v. Emotiv Inc., Judgment, 9 August 2023" (footnote 75, PDF p. 13); Futures Lab 2026 calls it Girardi v. Emotiv Inc. in its text. It is domestic law, reported by three library documents of registers (c), (e) and (f). The judgment itself is not in the library, and this page carries the registers of the reports.

## In the library

The Secretary-General gives the holding in one sentence and its significance in another [A/81/351, para. 43](pin:A/81/351#p13 "In Chile, in 2023, the Supreme Court applied the 2021 constitutional amendment, to protect brain activity and derived data, holding unlawful a company’s practices involving a portable brain-monitoring device. The ruling was among the first globally to address neural data under the rights to mental privacy and physical and mental integrity") ✓. Footnote 75, on the same PDF page, names the amending law (Act No. 21.383 of 2021, amending article 19 of the Constitution) and the judgment.

Futures Lab, a civil-society submission, is the only document that gives facts. The purchaser was a senator, and the dispute was about access to one's own data [Futures Lab 2026, p. 6](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p7 "Senator Guido Girardi Lavin purchased a device from U.S.-based company Emotiv and later found that the terms of service restricted non-subscribers’ access to their neural data") ✓; the remedy went beyond the data [Futures Lab 2026, p. 6](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p7 "ordering the deletion of collected neural data and the suspension of sales until public health certification is obtained") ✓. The submission reads the case as a lesson about consent and prior assessment [Futures Lab 2026, p. 2](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p3 "demonstrates that commercialization cannot rely solely on click-through consent") ✓.

Szoszkiewicz and Yuste, in a journal article, add that the ruling was unanimous and tie it to the amendment's wording [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "Chile’s pioneering 2021 constitutional amendment, which protects “cerebral activity and the information drawn from it”—that is, brain data—as a constitutional right. This amendment led to a 2023 unanimous ruling by Chile’s Supreme Court ordering a company to delete a consumer’s neural data, as its collection violated mental privacy protections") ✓.

The Australian Human Rights Commission mentions the amendment but not the ruling [AHRC 2025, p. 25](pin:AHRC-2025#p25 "Chile has worked to introduce neural protections into its national legal system via constitutional amendment") ✓.

**Where the reports differ.** They agree on the year, the court, the device and the deletion order. They differ in what they add. A/81/351 (c) states the legal ground (the amendment; mental privacy and physical and mental integrity) and no order beyond "unlawful". Futures Lab (e) gives the facts and a second order, the suspension of sales pending public health certification, which no other document mentions. Szoszkiewicz and Yuste (f) add "unanimous" and frame the ground as mental privacy alone. None quotes the judgment. The library cannot say which account is complete.

**What the library does not say.** The Court's reasoning; the text of the constitutional provision beyond the phrase Szoszkiewicz and Yuste quote; whether the case bears on the administration of justice at all, since every report places it in the consumer market. Read it as a neural-data case, not a criminal-justice one.

## Related

- [[a-81-351]], [[futures-lab-2026]], [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (the three reports; [[ahrc-2025]] for the amendment only)
- [[neural-data]] and [[mental-privacy]] (the rights the ruling is reported to rest on)
- [[regulatory-landscape]] (Chile among national responses)
- [[is-neural-data-special]] (a court treating neural data as constitutionally protected)
- [[iccpr-art-17]] (the Covenant counterpart of the privacy ground)

pages.title: Colorado's neural data law

frontmatter.title: Colorado's neural data law

pages.body:
# Colorado's neural data law

**What it is.** A 2024 amendment to Colorado's consumer privacy law that brings neural data within the state's category of sensitive data. Two documents name the bill: A/81/351, in footnote 79 (PDF p. 14), as "State of Colorado, House Bill No. 24-1058 (2024)", and AHRC 2025 as House Bill 24-1058; Futures Lab 2026 refers to "the Colorado Privacy Act". It is the domestic law of one state of the United States, reported by four library documents of registers (c), (d), (e) and (f). The statute is not in the library, and this page carries the registers of the reports.

## In the library

The Secretary-General lists Colorado among three states, against the absence of a federal law [A/81/351, para. 45](pin:A/81/351#p14 "While the United States has no federal neurotechnology-specific laws, California, Colorado and Montana have extended sensitive data protections to neural data") ✓. Footnote 79, on the same PDF page, gives the three bills: Colorado House Bill No. 24-1058 (2024), California Senate Bill No. 1223 (2024) and Montana Senate Bill No. 163 (2025).

The Australian Human Rights Commission cites it as an overseas model [AHRC 2025, p. 25](pin:AHRC-2025#p25 "in the US, Colorado signed House Bill 24-1058 to define and protect neural data") ✓.

Futures Lab is the only document to describe what the law covers, and quotes its definition [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "The Colorado Privacy Act regulates “biological, genetic, biochemical, physiological, or neural properties, compositions, or activities or of an individual’s body or bodily function” as sensitive data that is to be protected from business use") ✓. Its footnote 12, on the same PDF page, dates the bill: approved 17 April 2024. The submission's point is the absence of a national rule [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "California and Colorado demonstrate that there is no national standard on which biological data qualifies for privacy protections") ✓, reached by revising an existing law [Futures Lab 2026, p. 7](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p8 "States such as California and Colorado have revised their existing privacy laws and added neural data protections into their legislation") ✓.

Szoszkiewicz and Yuste describe the same technique, a definition added to existing consumer legislation [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "Colorado, California and Montana now explicitly include neurotechnology and neural data in their statutory definitions, and apply to these data existing consumer legislation for personal sensitive data") ✓.

**Where the reports differ: how many states.** Futures Lab says two [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "California and Colorado are currently the only states to have passed legislation on neural data privacy, while a dozen others have legislation pending") ✓; A/81/351 (para. 45) and Szoszkiewicz and Yuste (p. 3471) say three, adding Montana, whose bill A/81/351 dates to 2025. Futures Lab itself says something larger four pages on [Futures Lab 2026, p. 8](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p9 "At least eight U.S. states have enacted legislation to protect neurorights, addressing concerns about cognitive liberty and biometric data") ✓, citing an advocacy web page (its footnote 40, PDF p. 9). The counts cannot be reconciled from the library: "neural data privacy" and "neurorights" may be counted differently, and the submission's two statements sit uneasily together. Prefer the (c) count, dated August 2026, and cite the bills footnote 79 names.

**What the library does not say.** The text of the Act; what "sensitive data" protection requires in Colorado (consent, limits on sale, enforcement); whether the law reaches State actors, courts or law enforcement, since every report places it in the consumer market. Nothing in the library applies it to the administration of justice.

## Related

- [[california-neural-data-law]] (the companion amendment, with a different definition)
- [[neural-data]] (Colorado's definition against UNESCO's and California's)
- [[regulatory-landscape]] (the United States: state laws, no federal law)
- [[is-neural-data-special]] (a legislature treating neural data as sensitive, not as a new category)
- [[mental-privacy]] (the interest the laws are reported to protect)
- [[a-81-351]], [[ahrc-2025]], [[futures-lab-2026]], [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (the reporting documents)

pages.body:
# General Comment No. 22 as an authority in the library

**What it is.** General Comment No. 22 (1993) of the Human Rights Committee on article 18 of the ICCPR, document CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4, register (b): treaty-body interpretation, not treaty text. [[ccpr-c-21-rev-1-add-4]] reads the document; this page records who in the library relies on it, and for what. It was written before neurotechnology was a question and does not mention it.

## In the library

**The paragraphs that travel.** Two. [General Comment No. 22, para. 1](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p1 "is far-reaching and profound; it encompasses freedom of thoughts on all matters") ✓, with non-derogability, [General Comment No. 22, para. 1](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p1 "this provision cannot be derogated from, even in time of public emergency") ✓; and [General Comment No. 22, para. 3](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p2 "It does not permit any limitations whatsoever on the freedom of thought and conscience") ✓, [General Comment No. 22, para. 3](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p2 "In accordance with articles 18 (2) and 17, no one can be compelled to reveal his thoughts") ✓.

**The Secretary-General (c)** relies on both, attributing them to "the Human Rights Committee" without naming the General Comment in the text: [A/81/351, para. 20](pin:A/81/351#p7 "The Human Rights Committee has affirmed that the freedom of thought, conscience and religion is “far-reaching and profound; it encompasses freedom of thought on all matters”, and that the freedom of thought and conscience “does not permit any limitations”") ✓ (footnote 36, on the same PDF page, cites General Comment No. 22, paras. 1 and 3), and [A/81/351, para. 21](pin:A/81/351#p7 "“no one can be compelled to reveal his thoughts”") ✓ (footnote 40 cites para. 3). What it draws from them is its own: that decoding and coercive neuromodulation [A/81/351, para. 20](pin:A/81/351#p7 "could thus have a profound impact on the freedom of thought") ✓. One small drift: the Committee wrote "thoughts on all matters"; the report writes "thought".

**The AHRC (d)** quotes the same two paragraphs, again without naming the General Comment in the text: [AHRC 2025, p. 28](pin:AHRC-2025#p28 "The right contained in art 18 ICCPR is ‘far reaching and profound’") ✓ (endnote 112, PDF p. 77, cites General Comment No. 22, para. 1) and [AHRC 2025, p. 39](pin:AHRC-2025#p39 "The right to freedom of thought is ‘far-reaching and profound; it encompasses freedom of thought on all matters’. As provided for under arts 18.2 and 17 ICCPR, ‘no one shall be compelled to reveal [their] thoughts’") ✓ (endnotes 248 and 249, PDF p. 81, cite paras. 1 and 3). The AHRC then asks for more than General Comment No. 22 gives: [AHRC 2025, p. 70](pin:AHRC-2025#p70 "the adoption of a general comment on article 18 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights") ✓ on freedom of thought and neurotechnologies.

**General Comment No. 34 (b)** is the only library document that names General Comment No. 22 in its text, and for a different point, the meaning of "morals": [General Comment No. 34, para. 32](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p8 "The Committee observed in general comment No. 22, that “the concept of morals derives from many social, philosophical and religious traditions") ✓.

**Finding.** No report in the library names General Comment No. 22 in its running text; two cite it in notes and carry its words as "the Human Rights Committee". UNODC–INTERPOL, the Futures Lab and the two journal articles do not use it. When a page needs the Committee's words, pin the General Comment, not the report that quotes it.

## Related

- [[ccpr-c-21-rev-1-add-4]] (the source page: what the General Comment says)
- [[iccpr-art-18]] (the article it interprets)
- [[freedom-of-thought]] (the concept that borrows its two paragraphs)
- [[general-comment-34]] (the sister page on article 19; it names this General Comment)
- [[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]] (the AHRC's request for a new general comment)
- [[a-81-351]], [[ahrc-2025]] (the reports that rely on it)

pages.body:
# General Comment No. 32 as an authority in the library

**What it is.** General Comment No. 32 (2007) of the Human Rights Committee on article 14 of the ICCPR, document CCPR/C/GC/32, register (b): treaty-body interpretation, not treaty text. [[ccpr-c-gc-32]] reads the document; this page records who in the library relies on it, and for what. It does not mention neurotechnology.

## In the library

**The paragraph that travels.** [General Comment No. 32, para. 41](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p13 "This safeguard must be understood in terms of the absence of any direct or indirect physical or undue psychological pressure from the investigating authorities on the accused, with a view to obtaining a confession of guilt") ✓, with the exclusionary rule and the burden of proof: [General Comment No. 32, para. 41](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p13 "statements or confessions obtained in violation of article 7 of the Covenant are excluded from the evidence … the burden is on the State to prove that statements made by the accused have been given of their own free will") ✓. The same rule is stated for every article 14 proceeding in [General Comment No. 32, para. 6](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p2 "no statements or confessions or, in principle, other evidence obtained in violation of this provision may be invoked as evidence in any proceedings covered by article 14") ✓.

**The Secretary-General (c)** restates para. 41 without naming it in the text: [A/81/351, para. 32](pin:A/81/351#p10 "This privilege is an absolute guarantee and any direct or indirect physical or psychological pressure on the accused with a view to obtaining a confession of guilt is prohibited") ✓ (footnote 62, on the same PDF page, cites General Comment No. 32). Two differences from the Committee's text: the word "undue" before "psychological pressure" is gone, and "absolute guarantee" is the report's phrase. The General Comment does not call the privilege absolute; what it says is that [General Comment No. 32, para. 6](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p2 "Deviating from fundamental principles of fair trial, including the presumption of innocence, is prohibited at all times") ✓. For the exclusionary rule the report cites the Convention against Torture, article 15, and General Comment No. 20 (footnote 64, PDF p. 11), not this General Comment: [A/81/351, para. 32](pin:A/81/351#p10 "under the exclusionary rule, statements or other evidence obtained in violation of the prohibition of torture or ill-treatment may not be invoked as evidence in any proceedings") ✓. The application to brain-based lie detection is the report's own.

**The AHRC (d)** uses the same formula twice, and sources it to the Advisory Committee rather than the Human Rights Committee: [AHRC 2025, p. 31](pin:AHRC-2025#p31 "This means there can be no direct or indirect physical or psychological pressure to secure a confession or testimony") ✓ (endnote 145, PDF p. 78, cites A/HRC/57/61, para. 36) and [AHRC 2025, p. 33](pin:AHRC-2025#p33 "Both of these rights require that no direct or indirect physical or psychological pressure be exerted by authorities to secure a confession or testimony") ✓ (endnote 176, PDF p. 79, same citation). "Undue" is dropped here too. See [[a-hrc-57-61]], which is in the inbox.

**General Comment No. 34 (b)** is the only library document that names General Comment No. 32 in its text: [General Comment No. 34, para. 18](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p4 "The Committee, in general comment No. 32 on article 14, set out the various entitlements to information that are held by those accused of a criminal offence") ✓.

**Finding.** The Committee's formula on compulsion appears in two reports, three times, and neither report names its source in the text; both drop "undue". UNODC–INTERPOL, the Futures Lab and the journal articles name the privilege but not the General Comment. For the Committee's words, pin para. 41 itself.

## Related

- [[ccpr-c-gc-32]] (the source page: what the General Comment says)
- [[iccpr-art-14-3-g]] (the guarantee para. 41 interprets)
- [[iccpr-art-7]] (the exclusionary rule's other anchor)
- [[self-incrimination]], [[brain-based-lie-detection]] (where the formula is applied)
- [[general-comment-22]], [[general-comment-34]] (sister pages)
- [[a-81-351]], [[ahrc-2025]] (the reports that rely on it)
- [[a-hrc-57-61]] (the AHRC's stated source, in the inbox)
