pages.body:
# General Comment No. 34 as an authority in the library

**What it is.** General Comment No. 34 (2011) of the Human Rights Committee on article 19 of the ICCPR, document CCPR/C/GC/34, register (b): treaty-body interpretation, not treaty text. [[ccpr-c-gc-34]] reads the document; this page records who in the library relies on it, and for what. It does not mention neurotechnology.

## In the library

**The paragraphs that travel.** On opinion: [General Comment No. 34, para. 9](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p2 "Paragraph 1 of article 19 requires protection of the right to hold opinions without interference. This is a right to which the Covenant permits no exception or restriction") ✓ and [General Comment No. 34, para. 9](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p2 "All forms of opinion are protected, including opinions of a political, scientific, historic, moral or religious nature") ✓. On restricting expression: [General Comment No. 34, para. 21](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p5 "when a State party imposes restrictions on the exercise of freedom of expression, these may not put in jeopardy the right itself. The Committee recalls that the relation between right and restriction and between norm and exception must not be reversed") ✓.

**The Secretary-General (c)** restates para. 9 as "the Human Rights Committee", without naming the General Comment in the text: [A/81/351, para. 23](pin:A/81/351#p8 "According to the Human Rights Committee, this right is one to which the Covenant permits no exception or restriction, and protects all forms of opinion, including political, scientific, historical, moral and religious opinions. Harassment, intimidation or stigmatization of a person on account of opinions held is forbidden") ✓ (footnote 44, on the same PDF page, cites article 19 and General Comment No. 34, with no paragraph number). The step to neurotechnology is the report's, and it sources it to a Special Rapporteur: [A/81/351, para. 23](pin:A/81/351#p8 "Forced neurological interventions, indoctrination programmes or threats of violence designed to compel individuals to form particular opinions or change their opinion would violate this freedom (see A/73/348)") ✓ (A/73/348 is not in the library).

**The AHRC (d)** draws on three paragraphs through its endnotes, naming the Committee but not the General Comment in the text. On the value of expression: [AHRC 2025, p. 19](pin:AHRC-2025#p19 "‘the foundation stone for every free and democratic society’") ✓ (endnote 53, PDF p. 75, cites para. 2; compare [General Comment No. 34, para. 2](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p1 "They constitute the foundation stone for every free and democratic society") ✓). For brain-computer interfaces as a means of expression, endnote 55 cites para. 12. On restrictions: [AHRC 2025, p. 20](pin:AHRC-2025#p20 "the UN Human Rights Committee has highlighted that, when a State party imposes restrictions on the exercise of freedom of expression, these may not put in jeopardy the right itself") ✓ (endnote 61 cites para. 21), applied to access: [AHRC 2025, p. 20](pin:AHRC-2025#p20 "where Government law or policy denies, or places insurmountable barriers to accessing neurotechnology that is essential for some people to freely communicate, this could constitute a restriction on freedom of expression") ✓.

**A correction this General Comment supplies.** The AHRC places "security of the person" in [AHRC 2025, p. 33](pin:AHRC-2025#p33 "art 19.1 ICCPR which provides that everyone has the right to ’hold opinions without interference’") ✓. Para. 9 shows that the phrase belongs to article 19(1); security of person is article 9(1). See [[iccpr-art-9]].

**Not quoted.** No library document quotes [General Comment No. 34, para. 10](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p3 "Any form of effort to coerce the holding or not holding of any opinion is prohibited") ✓, although A/81/351 para. 23 discusses forced interventions on opinion.

**Finding.** No report names General Comment No. 34 in its running text; both cite it in notes. UNODC–INTERPOL, the Futures Lab and the journal articles do not use it.

## Related

- [[ccpr-c-gc-34]] (the source page: what the General Comment says)
- [[iccpr-art-9]] (the AHRC mix-up this General Comment resolves)
- [[iccpr-art-18]] (thought and opinion, the forum internum)
- [[freedom-of-thought]] (where opinion joins thought in the reports)
- [[general-comment-22]], [[general-comment-32]] (sister pages)
- [[a-81-351]], [[ahrc-2025]] (the reports that rely on it)

pages.title: ICCPR article 14(3)(g) (not to be compelled to testify against oneself)

frontmatter.title: ICCPR article 14(3)(g) (not to be compelled to testify against oneself)

pages.body:
# ICCPR article 14(3)(g) (not to be compelled to testify against oneself)

**What it is.** Article 14(3) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966), register (a), binding treaty text: "In the determination of any criminal charge against him, everyone shall be entitled to the following minimum guarantees, in full equality: … (g) Not to be compelled to testify against himself or to confess guilt." Source: [ICCPR art. 14(3)(g)](https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-mechanisms/instruments/international-covenant-civil-and-political-rights), (a) treaty text, not in the library. It is a criminal-charge guarantee, and the wrong it names is compulsion.

## In the library

**The Human Rights Committee (b).** General Comment No. 32 is the authority: [General Comment No. 32, para. 41](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p13 "This safeguard must be understood in terms of the absence of any direct or indirect physical or undue psychological pressure from the investigating authorities on the accused, with a view to obtaining a confession of guilt") ✓; statements obtained contrary to article 7 are excluded and [General Comment No. 32, para. 41](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p13 "the burden is on the State to prove that statements made by the accused have been given of their own free will") ✓; and [General Comment No. 32, para. 60](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p17 "to force them to make or sign, under duress, a confession admitting guilt violates both article 7 … and article 14, paragraph 3 (g)") ✓. See [[general-comment-32]] for how the reports reuse this formula.

**The Secretary-General (c).** [A/81/351, para. 32](pin:A/81/351#p10 "The coercive use of brain-based lie detection could call into question the privilege against self-incrimination, protected under article 14 (3) (g) of the Covenant. This privilege is an absolute guarantee") ✓ (footnote 62, on the same PDF page, cites General Comment No. 32). The report then records that the Supreme Court of India [A/81/351, para. 32](pin:A/81/351#p10 "held that the involuntary administration of brain electrical oscillation signature profiling tests, a form of brain-based lie detection, violates the constitutional protection against self-incrimination") ✓ (see [[selvi-v-state-of-karnataka]]). Earlier it lists the privilege among the [A/81/351, para. 9](pin:A/81/351#p4 "serious concerns regarding consent, coercion, reliability, and the privilege against self-incrimination") ✓ and notes that, despite that judgment, [A/81/351, para. 9](pin:A/81/351#p4 "voluntary use appears to have continued in practice") ✓.

**UNODC and INTERPOL (c).** Among the due process rights at stake: [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "the presumption of innocence, the privilege against self-incrimination, and the right to appeal") ✓.

**The Australian Human Rights Commission (d).** [AHRC 2025, p. 31](pin:AHRC-2025#p31 "Under international human rights law all people charged with a criminal offence have a right not to be compelled to testify against themselves or to confess guilt. This means there can be no direct or indirect physical or psychological pressure to secure a confession or testimony") ✓ (endnotes 144 and 145, PDF p. 78, cite article 14(3)(g) and A/HRC/57/61, not General Comment No. 32); [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "This right is found in art 14.3(g) ICCPR") ✓. Its contribution is the inducement case: [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "if an accused was offered the opportunity for a reduced sentence or some level of immunity in exchange for consenting to the use of neurotechnology during questioning by police, it would be difficult to argue that any consent given was entirely voluntary") ✓. See [[consent-in-custody]].

**Scholarship (f).** Szoszkiewicz and Yuste raise the privilege for consumer wearables that reach the courtroom: [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "underlining the urgent need to strengthen protections for the right against self-incrimination in the era of neurotechnology") ✓. Prainsack et al. and the Futures Lab submission (e) do not mention it.

## Related

- [[self-incrimination]] (the concept page)
- [[general-comment-32]] (the Committee's formula as an authority, and how the reports alter it)
- [[ccpr-c-gc-32]] (what General Comment No. 32 says)
- [[iccpr-art-7]] (ill-treatment and the exclusionary rule)
- [[brain-based-lie-detection]] (the technology the privilege is applied to)
- [[consent-in-custody]] (inducement and voluntariness)
- [[selvi-v-state-of-karnataka]] (the domestic judgment A/81/351 relies on)
- [[a-81-351]], [[ahrc-2025]], [[unodc-interpol-2025]], [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (the documents pinned here)

pages.title: ICCPR article 17 (privacy)

frontmatter.title: ICCPR article 17 (privacy)

pages.body:
# ICCPR article 17 (privacy)

**What it is.** Article 17 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966), register (a), binding treaty text: "1. No one shall be subjected to arbitrary or unlawful interference with his privacy, family, home or correspondence, nor to unlawful attacks on his honour and reputation. 2. Everyone has the right to the protection of the law against such interference or attacks." Source: [ICCPR art. 17](https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-mechanisms/instruments/international-covenant-civil-and-political-rights), (a) treaty text, not in the library. The AHRC reproduces paragraph 1 in a text box [AHRC 2025, p. 21](pin:AHRC-2025#p21 "No one shall be subjected to arbitrary or unlawful interference with his privacy, family, home or correspondence") ✓.

## In the library

**The Human Rights Committee (b).** The Committee's reading of article 17, General Comment No. 16 (1988), is cited in A/81/351's footnotes 47 and 51 (PDF p. 9) but is not in the library. Two General Comments that are held touch the article: [General Comment No. 22, para. 3](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p2 "In accordance with articles 18 (2) and 17, no one can be compelled to reveal his thoughts or adherence to a religion or belief") ✓, and [General Comment No. 34, para. 18](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p4 "As the Committee observed in its general comment No. 16, regarding article 17 of the Covenant, every individual should have the right to ascertain in an intelligible form, whether, and if so, what personal data is stored in automatic data files, and for what purposes") ✓.

**The Secretary-General (c).** The fullest treatment. [A/81/351, para. 24](pin:A/81/351#p8 "Articles 17 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and article 16 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child protect individuals from arbitrary or unlawful interference with their privacy. Neurotechnology introduces new threats to privacy by significantly increasing the level of possible interference") ✓, with the Committee's test for an arbitrary interference, [A/81/351, para. 24](pin:A/81/351#p8 "interpreted broadly to include elements of inappropriateness, injustice, lack of predictability and due process of law, as well as elements of reasonableness, necessity and proportionality") ✓ (footnote 47, on the same PDF page, cites General Comment No. 16). It extends the right to neural data: [A/81/351, para. 25](pin:A/81/351#p9 "the right to privacy protects personal data, communications and the integrity of private life. This protection would include neural data") ✓, and the Committee's requirements for personal data, [A/81/351, para. 26](pin:A/81/351#p9 "the gathering and holding of personal information must be regulated by law … These requirements would also apply to neural data") ✓. The extension is the Secretary-General's, not the Committee's.

**UNODC and INTERPOL (c).** Without an article number: [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "Brain activity is among the most intimate forms of personal information, and any attempt to monitor, decode or manipulate it … without genuine consent would represent a profound intrusion into human dignity, autonomy, and privacy") ✓.

**The Australian Human Rights Commission (d).** [AHRC 2025, p. 21](pin:AHRC-2025#p21 "The right to privacy is a cornerstone right that underpins freedoms of association, thought and expression") ✓; on memory recovery, [AHRC 2025, p. 33](pin:AHRC-2025#p33 "a real risk of breaching the right to privacy and freedom of thought as protected by arts 17 and 18 ICCPR") ✓; and, pairing the two articles as General Comment No. 22 does, [AHRC 2025, p. 39](pin:AHRC-2025#p39 "As provided for under arts 18.2 and 17 ICCPR, ‘no one shall be compelled to reveal [their] thoughts’") ✓. Its domestic question, whether neural data counts as personal or sensitive information under Australia's Privacy Act, [AHRC 2025, p. 25](pin:AHRC-2025#p25 "needs to be clarified to ensure the human right to privacy is not diminished by legislative uncertainty") ✓, does not travel.

**Civil society (e).** The Futures Lab cites the Universal Declaration, not the Covenant: [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "Articles 12 and 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) which protect privacy and freedom of thought, conscience, and religion") ✓.

**Scholarship (f).** Szoszkiewicz and Yuste do not name article 17; their claim is that [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "Unlike conventional privacy, mental privacy demands a tailored regulatory framework") ✓. Prainsack et al. do not mention privacy.

## Related

- [[mental-privacy]] (the concept the reports build on article 17)
- [[neural-data]] (what A/81/351 brings under the article)
- [[iccpr-art-18]] (paired with article 17 in General Comment No. 22, para. 3)
- [[ccpr-c-21-rev-1-add-4]], [[ccpr-c-gc-34]] (the two General Comments that mention article 17)
- [[a-81-351]], [[ahrc-2025]], [[unodc-interpol-2025]], [[futures-lab-2026]], [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (the documents pinned here)

pages.title: ICCPR article 18 (freedom of thought, conscience and religion)

frontmatter.title: ICCPR article 18 (freedom of thought, conscience and religion)

pages.body:
# ICCPR article 18 (freedom of thought, conscience and religion)

**What it is.** Article 18(1) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966), register (a), binding treaty text, opens: "Everyone shall have the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion." Paragraph 2: "No one shall be subject to coercion which would impair his freedom to have or to adopt a religion or belief of his choice." Paragraph 3 allows limitations only on the freedom to manifest a religion or belief. Source: [ICCPR art. 18](https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-mechanisms/instruments/international-covenant-civil-and-political-rights), (a) treaty text, not in the library. The AHRC reproduces paragraph 1 in a text box [AHRC 2025, p. 28](pin:AHRC-2025#p28 "Everyone shall have the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion") ✓. The library uses the article for the forum internum: thought itself, which paragraph 3 does not reach.

## In the library

**The Human Rights Committee (b).** General Comment No. 22 (1993) is the reading: [General Comment No. 22, para. 1](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p1 "far-reaching and profound; it encompasses freedom of thoughts on all matters") ✓ and [General Comment No. 22, para. 1](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p1 "this provision cannot be derogated from, even in time of public emergency") ✓; [General Comment No. 22, para. 3](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p2 "It does not permit any limitations whatsoever on the freedom of thought and conscience") ✓ and [General Comment No. 22, para. 3](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p2 "In accordance with articles 18 (2) and 17, no one can be compelled to reveal his thoughts or adherence to a religion or belief") ✓; on coercion, [General Comment No. 22, para. 5](pin:CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4#p2 "Article 18 (2) bars coercions that would impair the right to have or adopt a religion or belief, including the use of threat of physical force or penal sanctions") ✓. General Comment No. 34 ties opinion to thought: [General Comment No. 34, para. 5](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p1 "the relationship of opinion and thought (article 18)") ✓. Neither mentions neurotechnology. See [[general-comment-22]] for who relies on these paragraphs.

**The Secretary-General (c).** [A/81/351, para. 20](pin:A/81/351#p7 "Neurotechnologies used to infer mental states, memory or recognition … could reveal information that the person has not chosen to disclose. Coercive neuromodulation technologies can alter brain activity and shape how thoughts occur. Such technologies could thus have a profound impact on the freedom of thought, recognized in article 18") ✓ (footnote 36, on the same PDF page, cites General Comment No. 22, paras. 1 and 3). It takes the "four pillars" of freedom of thought from experts and finds that [A/81/351, para. 22](pin:A/81/351#p8 "Neurotechnology may potentially affect all four pillars of freedom of thought") ✓, and recommends barring neural data obtained [A/81/351, para. 50 (d)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "in violation of the rights to freedom of thought and opinion, as evidence in any proceedings") ✓.

**UNODC and INTERPOL (c).** Listed among the rights to secure: [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "individuals’ rights to privacy, freedom of thought, bodily integrity, non-discrimination") ✓.

**The Australian Human Rights Commission (d).** [AHRC 2025, p. 28](pin:AHRC-2025#p28 "The right contained in art 18 ICCPR is ‘far reaching and profound’ and captures freedom of thought on all matters and personal convictions") ✓, and [AHRC 2025, p. 28](pin:AHRC-2025#p28 "Freedom of thought is considered part of an individual’s forum internum (internal realm) and is non-derogable") ✓. On coercion it applies paragraph 2 itself: [AHRC 2025, p. 29](pin:AHRC-2025#p29 "Protection against coercion is enshrined in art 18(2) ICCPR … This would protect people from being subject to the nonconsensual use of neurotechnology devices that may alter thought or neural patterns or behaviours") ✓; the Committee has not said this. Its Recommendation 4: [AHRC 2025, p. 70](pin:AHRC-2025#p70 "The United Nations Human Rights Committee provide guidance on freedom of thought and neurotechnologies through the adoption of a general comment on article 18") ✓.

**Civil society (e).** The Futures Lab cites the Universal Declaration: [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "Articles 12 and 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) which protect privacy and freedom of thought, conscience, and religion") ✓.

**Scholarship (f).** Szoszkiewicz and Yuste, without an article number: [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "intrusions on mental privacy may, in some instances, amount to a violation of the freedom of thought and conscience, an absolute right protected under international human rights law") ✓. Prainsack et al. do not mention it.

## Related

- [[freedom-of-thought]] (the concept page, with the four pillars)
- [[general-comment-22]] (who relies on the Committee's reading)
- [[ccpr-c-21-rev-1-add-4]] (what General Comment No. 22 says)
- [[ccpr-c-gc-34]] (opinion, the article's neighbour in the forum internum)
- [[iccpr-art-17]] (paired with article 18 in General Comment No. 22, para. 3)
- [[mental-privacy]] (how the article is reached through neural data)
- [[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]] (the AHRC's call for a new general comment)
- [[a-81-351]], [[ahrc-2025]], [[unodc-interpol-2025]], [[futures-lab-2026]], [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] (the documents pinned here)

pages.title: ICCPR article 7 (torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment)

frontmatter.title: ICCPR article 7 (torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment)

pages.body:
# ICCPR article 7 (torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment)

**What it is.** Article 7 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966), register (a), binding treaty text: "No one shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. In particular, no one shall be subjected without his free consent to medical or scientific experimentation." Source: [ICCPR art. 7](https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-mechanisms/instruments/international-covenant-civil-and-political-rights), (a) treaty text, not in the library. The AHRC reproduces the words in a text box [AHRC 2025, p. 33](pin:AHRC-2025#p33 "no one shall be subjected without his free consent to medical or scientific experimentation") ✓. Two limbs matter here: the prohibition of ill-treatment, and free consent to experimentation.

## In the library

**The Human Rights Committee (b).** No General Comment on article 7 is in the library; the reports' footnotes cite General Comment No. 20 (1992), which is not held. General Comment No. 32, on article 14, reads article 7 into the law of evidence: [General Comment No. 32, para. 6](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p2 "as article 7 is also non-derogable in its entirety, no statements or confessions or, in principle, other evidence obtained in violation of this provision may be invoked as evidence in any proceedings covered by article 14") ✓, and where exclusion is claimed [General Comment No. 32, para. 41](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p13 "the burden is on the State to prove that statements made by the accused have been given of their own free will") ✓. The Committee says nothing about neurotechnology; every application below is the report's own.

**The Secretary-General (c).** The first limb, applied to investigation and custody: [A/81/351, para. 28](pin:A/81/351#p9 "brain-based lie detection, decoding … coercive interrogation techniques, and neuromodulation, applied in detention or investigative contexts, may result in mental or physical suffering contravening the protection provided under articles 7 and 10 (1)") ✓ (its footnote 53, on the same PDF page, cites General Comment No. 20). Neuromodulation of offenders, reported in the Advisory Committee's own verb: [A/81/351, para. 29](pin:A/81/351#p10 "may constitute treatment contrary to articles 7 or 10 of the Covenant when imposed without genuinely free and informed consent") ✓ (the view is attributed to [[a-hrc-57-61]], which is in the inbox and is not quoted here). The second limb: [A/81/351, para. 29](pin:A/81/351#p10 "Article 7 of the Covenant “expressly prohibits medical or scientific experimentation without the free consent of the person concerned”") ✓ (footnote 57 cites General Comment No. 20, para. 7). Evidence: [A/81/351, para. 32](pin:A/81/351#p10 "under the exclusionary rule, statements or other evidence obtained in violation of the prohibition of torture or ill-treatment may not be invoked as evidence in any proceedings. This could apply to evidence obtained through the coercive use of neurotechnologies") ✓. The report recommends that States [A/81/351, para. 50 (d)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Prohibit the use of neurotechnology as a means of torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment") ✓.

**UNODC and INTERPOL (c).** The paper lists [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "the prohibition of torture, inhuman and degrading treatment") ✓ among the rights institutions must secure, and names the coercive offer: [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "“offered” the use of these technologies in ways that are coercive, or under the guise of moral-enhancement") ✓.

**The Australian Human Rights Commission (d).** On memory recovery: [AHRC 2025, p. 33](pin:AHRC-2025#p33 "if neurotechnology is forcibly used to extract information from suspects they may breach the prohibition of torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. The UN Human Rights Advisory Committee has observed that any misuse of the technology to this degree would represent a violation of art 7 ICCPR") ✓. The body it calls "the UN Human Rights Advisory Committee" is the Human Rights Council Advisory Committee ([[a-hrc-57-61]]); its endnote 170 (PDF p. 79) cites A/HRC/57/61, paras. 34–35.

**Civil society (e) and scholarship (f).** The Futures Lab submission and the two journal articles do not invoke article 7.

## Related

- [[general-comment-32]] (the exclusionary rule and the burden of proof as an authority)
- [[ccpr-c-gc-32]] (what General Comment No. 32 says)
- [[iccpr-art-14-3-g]] (the privilege that article 7 backs with exclusion)
- [[neuromodulation-of-offenders]] (the Advisory Committee's "may constitute" view, as reported)
- [[consent-in-custody]] (free consent under the second limb)
- [[reliability-and-admissibility]] (exclusion as an evidence rule)
- [[a-81-351]], [[unodc-interpol-2025]], [[ahrc-2025]] (the reports pinned here)
- [[a-hrc-57-61]] (in the inbox; cited by two reports, never pinned)

pages.title: ICCPR article 9 (liberty and security of person)

frontmatter.title: ICCPR article 9 (liberty and security of person)

pages.body:
# ICCPR article 9 (liberty and security of person)

**What it is.** Article 9(1) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966), register (a), binding treaty text: "Everyone has the right to liberty and security of person. No one shall be subjected to arbitrary arrest or detention. No one shall be deprived of his liberty except on such grounds and in accordance with such procedure as are established by law." The article's later paragraphs cover arrest, judicial control and review of detention. Source: [ICCPR art. 9](https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-mechanisms/instruments/international-covenant-civil-and-political-rights), (a) treaty text, not in the library.

## In the library

**The Human Rights Committee (b).** The library holds no General Comment on article 9. The Committee's reading, General Comment No. 35 (2014), is cited by A/81/351 (footnotes 66 and 67, PDF p. 11) and by the AHRC (endnote 169), but it is not held. General Comment No. 32 names article 9 only in passing: [General Comment No. 32, para. 31](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p9 "Notice of the reasons for an arrest is separately guaranteed in article 9, paragraph 2 of the Covenant") ✓, and on delay, [General Comment No. 32, para. 61](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p17 "If someone suspected of a crime and detained on the basis of article 9 of the Covenant is charged with an offence but not brought to trial") ✓ both articles 9(3) and 14(3)(c) may be violated.

**The Secretary-General (c).** The one developed treatment in the library: [A/81/351, para. 34](pin:A/81/351#p11 "Neurotechnologies claiming to assess the risk of recidivism, and the use of brain-based deception technologies to determine whether a person should be detained, may lead to arbitrary detention under article 9") ✓. The report glosses the two interests, [A/81/351, para. 34](pin:A/81/351#p11 "liberty of person, meaning freedom from confinement of the body, and security of person, meaning freedom from injury to the body and the mind") ✓ (footnote 66, on the same PDF page, cites General Comments No. 35 and No. 20), states the individuation rule, [A/81/351, para. 34](pin:A/81/351#p11 "the decision to detain, or continue to detain, a person must be based on reasons specific to that individual") ✓, and adds that [A/81/351, para. 34](pin:A/81/351#p11 "Detention based on neural data may also be considered arbitrary, when the right to challenge confinement is undermined by the untransparent and obscure nature of such systems") ✓. See [[neuroprediction]] and [[brain-based-lie-detection]].

**The Australian Human Rights Commission (d): an error to quarantine.** The AHRC writes: [AHRC 2025, p. 33](pin:AHRC-2025#p33 "The protection of the mind and mental integrity is also alluded to in the right to security of the person in art 19.1 ICCPR which provides that everyone has the right to ’hold opinions without interference’. The UN Human Rights Committee notes that security of the person includes ‘freedom of injury to the body and the mind, or bodily or mental integrity’") ✓. Two articles are run together. Security of person is article 9(1); "hold opinions without interference" is article 19(1), as General Comment No. 34 states: [General Comment No. 34, para. 9](pin:CCPR/C/GC/34#p2 "Paragraph 1 of article 19 requires protection of the right to hold opinions without interference") ✓ (see [[ccpr-c-gc-34]]). The Committee quotation that follows is about article 9: the AHRC's own endnotes 168 and 169 (PDF p. 79) cite "ICCPR art 9.1" and General Comment No. 35, para. 3. Read the sentence with its endnotes, not its body text; the same gloss, correctly placed, is in A/81/351 para. 34 above (the AHRC's quotation also reads "freedom of injury" where A/81/351 has "freedom from injury"). The AHRC invokes article 9 once more, for soldiers coerced into using neurotechnology, [AHRC 2025, p. 49](pin:AHRC-2025#p49 "This may have implications for the right to personal integrity under art 1 UDHR and art 9 ICCPR") ✓, a military setting outside the administration of justice.

**Nothing else.** UNODC–INTERPOL, the Futures Lab submission and the two journal articles do not name article 9. The nearest is UNODC–INTERPOL's list of due process rights, [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "the right to appear before a competent judicial authority") ✓, with no article number.

## Related

- [[ahrc-2025]] (the source page for the report that misplaces security of person)
- [[a-81-351]] (the only developed treatment of article 9 in the library)
- [[ccpr-c-gc-34]] and [[general-comment-34]] (where "hold opinions without interference" belongs)
- [[neuroprediction]] (risk assessment and preventive detention)
- [[brain-based-lie-detection]] (deception detection in detention decisions)
- [[iccpr-art-7]] (bodily and mental integrity, which A/81/351 para. 34 also places under article 7)
- [[ccpr-c-gc-32]] (the two passing mentions of article 9)

pages.title: Selvi v. State of Karnataka (Supreme Court of India, 2010)

frontmatter.title: Selvi v. State of Karnataka (Supreme Court of India, 2010)

pages.body:
# Selvi v. State of Karnataka (Supreme Court of India, 2010)

**What it is.** A judgment of the Supreme Court of India on brain-based lie detection, which A/81/351 cites in its footnotes as "Supreme Court of India, Selvi v. State of Karnataka, Judgment, 5 May 2010" (footnote 17, PDF p. 4; footnote 63, PDF p. 11, adds "paras. 215–224"). It is domestic law. The judgment is not in the library: the wiki knows it only through the Secretary-General's report, a (c) document, and this page carries that register. Nothing here is a reading of the judgment itself.

## In the library

Only A/81/351 reports the case: twice in the text, three times in footnotes.

In its survey of brain-based deception detection, the Secretary-General reports the holding and its evidentiary consequence [A/81/351, para. 9](pin:A/81/351#p4 "The Supreme Court of India held that the involuntary administration of brain electrical oscillation signature profiling tests violates the constitutional protection against self-incrimination and renders the resulting evidence inadmissible") ✓ (its footnote 17, on the same PDF page, gives the date). The same paragraph adds that the ruling did not end the practice [A/81/351, para. 9](pin:A/81/351#p4 "However, voluntary use appears to have continued in practice") ✓.

In the fair-trial section, the case is placed next to article 14 (3) (g) of the Covenant [A/81/351, para. 32](pin:A/81/351#p10 "The Supreme Court of India, in Selvi v. State of Karnataka, held that the involuntary administration of brain electrical oscillation signature profiling tests, a form of brain-based lie detection, violates the constitutional protection against self-incrimination") ✓. The footnote to that sentence (footnote 63, printed on PDF p. 11) pinpoints paras. 215–224 of the judgment and cites alongside it a 2024 European Parliamentary Research Service study on mental privacy.

A third mention sits in a footnote to the paragraph on torture and ill-treatment. That paragraph says brain-based lie detection applied in detention or investigative contexts [A/81/351, para. 28](pin:A/81/351#p9 "may result in mental or physical suffering contravening the protection provided under articles 7 and 10 (1) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights") ✓; its footnote 55, on the same PDF page, offers Selvi as an instance that "established a landmark precedent by prohibiting coercive neuro-imaging techniques as a form of degrading treatment", adding "See also A/HRC/57/61".

**Two framings in one report.** The text (paras. 9 and 32) presents Selvi as a self-incrimination holding; footnote 55 presents it as a degrading-treatment holding. The library contains no text of the judgment and cannot say which description is the better one, or whether both hold. A reader who needs the ground of decision must open the judgment at the paragraphs footnote 63 names.

**What the library does not say.** The facts of the case; the Court's reasoning; whether the Court addressed consent given under inducement; what brain electrical oscillation signature profiling measures, beyond the report's one-line description of the technique family [A/81/351, para. 8](pin:A/81/351#p4 "These techniques measure physiological or brain responses to determine whether a person recognizes concealed or crime-related information") ✓. No other library document names the case.

## Related

- [[a-81-351]] (the only document that reports the case)
- [[brain-based-lie-detection]] (BEOS as one technique among those the report lists)
- [[self-incrimination]] (the right the text says the Court applied)
- [[iccpr-art-14-3-g]] and [[general-comment-32]] (the Covenant guarantee and the Committee's reading of "pressure")
- [[iccpr-art-7]] (the footnote-55 framing: degrading treatment)
- [[consent-in-custody]] and [[can-a-suspect-consent-to-lie-detection]] ("voluntary use appears to have continued")
- [[reliability-and-admissibility]] (the ruling renders the evidence inadmissible)

pages.title: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology (2025)

frontmatter.title: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology (2025)

pages.body:
# UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology (2025)

**What it is.** A recommendation adopted by the General Conference of UNESCO in 2025, as the Secretary-General reports [A/81/351, para. 46](pin:A/81/351#p14 "At the international level, the General Conference of UNESCO adopted its Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology in 2025, which calls for national coordinating bodies for neurotechnology, among other measures") ✓. Footnote 4 of the same report (PDF p. 2, on para. 4) dates the adoption: 11 November 2025. It is UN agency soft law, register (c). Its text is not in the library. The wiki knows it through four documents, which saw it at different stages; read each with its date.

## In the library, by date

**Szoszkiewicz and Yuste, July 2025: a draft under negotiation.** [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "UNESCO published a draft instrument in 2024, currently under intergovernmental negotiation") ✓, listed among the soft-law instruments then taking shape.

**AHRC 2025, October 2025: a draft, adoption expected.** [AHRC 2025, p. 9](pin:AHRC-2025#p9 "in 2024 it released its draft recommendation. It is expected that the recommendation will be adopted in late 2025") ✓. The Commission builds on the draft all the same: it takes its definition of neurotechnology from UNESCO [AHRC 2025, p. 8](pin:AHRC-2025#p8 "the Commission has adopted the definition set out by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) as a leading voice on the international application of neurotechnology") ✓, and relies on the draft for a worker's right of access to neural data [AHRC 2025, p. 42](pin:AHRC-2025#p42 "As noted in UNESCO’s draft recommendation on neurotechnology, workers should have a right to obtain access to comprehensible neural data collected about themselves") ✓. Its endnotes (PDF pp. 74, 76, 82 and 86, not in the passages) cite three successive texts: working documents of 17 April 2024 and 27 August 2024, and a "Draft Text of the Recommendation" of 9 April 2025.

**Futures Lab, March 2026: still "draft".** Though submitted after the adoption date A/81/351 gives, the submission speaks of a draft [Futures Lab 2026, p. 5](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p6 "Draft global standards on the ethics of neurotechnology underline that technologies must be developed and used in ways that avoid segregation, discrimination, or subordination of peoples") ✓ and [Futures Lab 2026, p. 5](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p6 "The UNESCO draft calls for gender-responsive policies to close gaps in access and leadership in neurotechnology") ✓. Its footnotes 19 and 20 (PDF p. 6) cite a 2023 MIT Media Lab article and a "Draft Global Standard" of 2023: its source predates the 2024 drafts the other documents cite. Elsewhere it counts UNESCO as guidance without a binding framework [Futures Lab 2026, p. 2](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p3 "there remains no unified international framework for neurorights, despite early leadership from countries such as Chile and guidance from organizations such as UNESCO") ✓.

**A/81/351, August 2026: adopted, and used.** Besides para. 46, the report takes both of its working definitions from the Recommendation: neurotechnology [A/81/351, para. 4](pin:A/81/351#p2 "devices, systems and procedures – encompassing both hardware and software – that directly measure, access, monitor, analyse, predict or modulate the nervous system") ✓ (footnote 4, same PDF page) and neural data [A/81/351, para. 5](pin:A/81/351#p3 "qualitative and quantitative data about the structure, activity and function of the nervous system gathered through neurotechnology") ✓ (footnote 6, same PDF page). It cites the Recommendation (footnote 65, PDF p. 11) for the standard that neurotechnology-based evidence admitted in court [A/81/351, para. 33](pin:A/81/351#p11 "meets the highest standards of scientific validation, transparency and contestability") ✓.

**The time difference, flagged.** Three documents describe a draft (July 2025, October 2025, March 2026); one describes an adopted instrument (August 2026) and dates adoption to 11 November 2025. The AHRC's expectation and the Secretary-General's report agree with each other. Futures Lab's "draft", written four months after that date on 2023 sources, is the one to handle with care: quote it for what a draft said, not for what the Recommendation says. On the definition of neurotechnology the stage makes no difference: the words the AHRC quotes from the draft [AHRC 2025, p. 8](pin:AHRC-2025#p8 "devices, systems, and procedures— encompassing both hardware and software—that directly measure, access, monitor, analyse, predict or modulate the nervous system") ✓ are those A/81/351 quotes from the adopted text.

**What the library does not say.** The Recommendation's structure or provisions beyond the two definitions, the call for national coordinating bodies, the gender-responsive policies and the evidence standard; whether it addresses the administration of justice directly.

## Related

- [[neural-data]] (the definition the wiki uses comes from here, through A/81/351)
- [[regulatory-landscape]] (the Recommendation among international instruments)
- [[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]] (a soft-law instrument, not a new right)
- [[what-should-states-do-now]] (national coordinating bodies as one ask)

pages.title: Can a suspect validly consent to brain-based lie detection?

frontmatter.title: Can a suspect validly consent to brain-based lie detection?

pages.body:
# Can a suspect validly consent to brain-based lie detection?

**Short answer.** No document in the library says consent in custody is impossible, and none says a consented test is lawful. Every document that addresses it treats such consent as suspect and conditions it: the Human Rights Committee's standard for article 14 (3) (g) reaches indirect and psychological pressure, not only force; the Secretary-General recommends prohibiting compulsory or coercive use and holding any consent to the highest evidentiary standards; UNODC and INTERPOL require consent free of undue influence, particularly in custody; the Australian Human Rights Commission doubts that consent given against an offer of leniency is voluntary and, for now, prefers a moratorium. The one ruling the library reports, Selvi, concerned involuntary administration, and the Secretary-General notes that voluntary use continued after it.

## Reasoning

**The standard (b).** The Committee reads the privilege against self-incrimination as a prohibition of pressure in all its forms [General Comment No. 32, para. 41](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p13 "This safeguard must be understood in terms of the absence of any direct or indirect physical or undue psychological pressure from the investigating authorities on the accused, with a view to obtaining a confession of guilt") ✓, and, where article 7 is in play, puts the burden on the State [General Comment No. 32, para. 41](pin:CCPR/C/GC/32#p13 "in such cases the burden is on the State to prove that statements made by the accused have been given of their own free will") ✓. The General Comment predates neurotechnology and says nothing about it; the applications below are the reports' own.

**The application (c).** The Secretary-General applies the standard to lie detection in terms of coercion [A/81/351, para. 32](pin:A/81/351#p10 "The coercive use of brain-based lie detection could call into question the privilege against self-incrimination, protected under article 14 (3) (g) of the Covenant. This privilege is an absolute guarantee and any direct or indirect physical or psychological pressure on the accused with a view to obtaining a confession of guilt is prohibited") ✓, and reports the Indian ruling on involuntary tests together with what followed it [A/81/351, para. 9](pin:A/81/351#p4 "The Supreme Court of India held that the involuntary administration of brain electrical oscillation signature profiling tests violates the constitutional protection against self-incrimination and renders the resulting evidence inadmissible. However, voluntary use appears to have continued in practice") ✓. On consent in custody the report speaks in the neuromodulation context, but in general terms [A/81/351, para. 29](pin:A/81/351#p10 "In custodial settings, the pronounced power imbalance between the State and the individual may call into question the genuineness of consent. Experts affirm that where such techniques are presented in connection with prospects such as early release or favourable parole outcomes, there is a significant risk that consent may not be fully free or voluntary") ✓. Its recommendations keep the two ideas apart: prohibit the coercive use [A/81/351, para. 50 (c)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Prohibit the compulsory or coercive use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice, including brain-based deception detection") ✓; for any other use, require consent of a demanding kind [A/81/351, para. 50 (e)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Require free, prior, informed, explicit and revocable consent for any potential use of neurotechnology in the administration of justice, accompanied by full transparency regarding risks, access to independent legal counsel of one’s own choice and effective avenues for redress. Given the constrained and coercive nature of justice settings, any consent should be subject to the highest evidentiary standards and rigorous scrutiny") ✓. The Secretary-General does not say consent is impossible; he says it must be proved to a high standard.

UNODC and INTERPOL name the risk of the "offer" [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "there is concern about the potential for neurotechnology to be used coercively, or under conditions in which individuals are “offered” the use of these technologies in ways that are coercive") ✓, set the condition [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 6](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p9 "Consent must be voluntary and informed, free of coercion or undue influence, particularly in custodial or correctional settings where power imbalances are acute") ✓, and leave the court-order question open [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 5](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p8 "Can courts legally order a criminal defendant, even in narrow circumstances, to cooperate with law enforcement in the use of neurotechnologies?") ✓.

**The inducement problem (d).** The Australian Human Rights Commission is the one document that works through an example [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "if an accused was offered the opportunity for a reduced sentence or some level of immunity in exchange for consenting to the use of neurotechnology during questioning by police, it would be difficult to argue that any consent given was entirely voluntary") ✓, and notes that pressure can come from refusal's consequences [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "indirect pressure, which may arise in informing an accused of the consequences of refusing to undergo questioning via neurotechnology") ✓. Its answer, for now, is not to refine consent but to pause [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "The Commission’s preliminary view is that a moratorium on the use of neurotechnology in criminal investigations should be imposed until the ALRC has published the findings of the recommended inquiry. Additionally, until that time, information gained via neurotechnology should be inadmissible at trial") ✓. This is an NHRI's preliminary view, addressed to Australia.

**A limit on what can be consented to (e).** Futures Lab would restrict the scope of consent until standards exist [Futures Lab 2026, p. 7](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p8 "Individuals should not be able to consent to overly broad uses of neurotechnology until clear and established neurorights are in place") ✓.

Read together: the higher the register, the more the answer is "consent is possible but must be shown to be free"; the lower, the more it is "not yet".

## What the library cannot answer

- Whether a suspect's consent, once given freely, makes the result admissible: A/81/351 ties inadmissibility to coercion and ill-treatment (para. 32), not to consent, and no document says a consented result is admissible.
- Whether the Committee's "undue psychological pressure" covers an offer of leniency: the General Comment does not say, and only the AHRC (d) argues it.
- What Selvi says about consented tests: the library reports the holding on involuntary administration only ([[selvi-v-state-of-karnataka]]).
- Whether a test the suspect asks for, to clear themselves, raises the same issues: no document addresses it.

## Related

- [[consent-in-custody]] (the concept, with its contested card)
- [[self-incrimination]] and [[iccpr-art-14-3-g]] (the right)
- [[general-comment-32]] / [[ccpr-c-gc-32]] (the standard pinned above)
- [[brain-based-lie-detection]] (what is being consented to)
- [[selvi-v-state-of-karnataka]] (the involuntary case)
- [[moratorium]] (the AHRC's answer)
- [[iccpr-art-7]] (the burden-shift and exclusion limb)
- [[a-81-351]], [[unodc-interpol-2025]], [[ahrc-2025]], [[futures-lab-2026]] (the documents pinned)

pages.title: Is neural data different from other personal data?

frontmatter.title: Is neural data different from other personal data?

pages.body:
# Is neural data different from other personal data?

**Short answer.** On sensitivity, every register in the library says yes: the Secretary-General reports a "broad consensus" that neural data are highly sensitive and need heightened protection, and the UN agency paper, the NHRI, the civil-society submission and the scholarship say the same in their own words. The documents part on what follows. The laws they report (California, Colorado, Montana, Brazil) and the Secretary-General's recommendation put neural data inside an existing category, sensitive personal data, at its highest level. Szoszkiewicz and Yuste argue it must be treated as "fundamentally distinct", with a tailored framework. Prainsack and others answer a different question: governance should turn on public value and collective control, not on the category of the data.

## Reasoning

**Sensitive, by consensus (c).** [A/81/351, para. 5](pin:A/81/351#p3 "There is broad consensus that neural data are highly sensitive, providing unprecedented access to internal mental states, and that they require heightened ethical and legal protection") ✓ (its footnote 7, on the same PDF page, cites A/HRC/58/58, Szoszkiewicz and Yuste 2025, and Genser, Damianos and Yuste 2024; footnote 6 takes the definition from the UNESCO Recommendation). The report gives reasons [A/81/351, para. 25](pin:A/81/351#p9 "Neural data are uniquely revealing since they are capable of disclosing certain aspects of identity and personality") ✓ and [A/81/351, para. 25](pin:A/81/351#p9 "Neural data is biometric in character and may reportedly be re-identified across data sets and yield insights that were not foreseeable at the time of collection") ✓. UNODC and INTERPOL agree on the premise [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 4](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p7 "Brain activity is among the most intimate forms of personal information") ✓.

**What follows, for the Secretary-General: an existing category, at its top.** [A/81/351, para. 50 (b)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Recognize neural data as highly sensitive personal data subject to the highest level of legal protection; impose clear limitations on its collection, processing, sale, storage, retention, reuse and sharing") ✓. Article 17 is the frame: the Committee's requirements for personal data [A/81/351, para. 26](pin:A/81/351#p9 "would also apply to neural data and other information retrieved through the use of neurotechnologies") ✓. This is existing law applied, with a justice-specific worry that consumer data may reach courts [A/81/351, para. 14](pin:A/81/351#p5 "without recognition of its uniquely sensitive character") ✓.

**The laws as reported (c, d, e, f): the same move.** Three US states, as the library reports them, added neural data to statutory definitions of sensitive data ([[california-neural-data-law]], [[colorado-neural-data-law]]) [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "apply to these data existing consumer legislation for personal sensitive data") ✓; Brazil did likewise [A/81/351, para. 43](pin:A/81/351#p13 "In Brazil, neural data is classified as sensitive personal data") ✓. The AHRC frames the Australian question the same way [AHRC 2025, p. 23](pin:AHRC-2025#p23 "a key consideration will be whether neural data is classified as ‘personal information’ or ‘sensitive information’") ✓. Futures Lab wants more at the international level [Futures Lab 2026, p. 4](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p5 "specific international standards must be established to recognize the highly sensitive and personal nature of bio- and neurotechnologies") ✓.

**A category of its own (f).** Szoszkiewicz and Yuste go further than the laws they describe. The gap is that outside medicine the data are [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "not classified as sensitive information when collected outside medical contexts by consumer products") ✓; the reason neural data differ is that they [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "also reflect subconscious and involuntary activity, exposing information that individuals may not consciously recognize") ✓; and the conclusion is categorical [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3470](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p2 "Unlike conventional privacy, mental privacy demands a tailored regulatory framework. As it can reveal the most intimate aspects of a person, neural data must be treated as fundamentally distinct, with enhanced safeguards") ✓. Yet their proposal builds on data protection rather than replacing it [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3469](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p1 "We propose strengthening existing data protection regulations with a broad approach to safeguard neural data") ✓.

**A different answer: not category, governance (f).** Prainsack and others, writing about health data generally, argue that individual control is the wrong lever [Prainsack et al. 2022, p. e773](pin:Prainsack-et-al-2022#p1 "regulatory frameworks that seek to prevent harm mostly by strengthening the control that individuals have over their data are not enough") ✓ and that the test should be public value against risk [Prainsack et al. 2022, p. e773](pin:Prainsack-et-al-2022#p1 "Data use that creates little or no public value but poses substantial risks should be prohibited") ✓. On that view the question "is neural data special?" matters less than "what is this use for, and who bears the risk?". Szoszkiewicz and Yuste take the idea up as one option for neural data [Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025, p. 3471](pin:Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025#p3 "would treat neural data as a shared resource that serves the public good") ✓.

## What the library cannot answer

- Whether "highly sensitive personal data" in existing data-protection law gives the protection the Secretary-General and the scholarship call for: no document tests a statute against neural data.
- Whether inferences drawn from non-neural data count: the California definition excludes them, the UNESCO definition as quoted is silent, and Szoszkiewicz and Yuste report both practices ([[neural-data]]).
- Whether neural data obtained in criminal investigations falls under data-protection law at all, rather than criminal procedure: the US laws and the Chilean ruling, as reported, are consumer cases.

## Related

- [[neural-data]] (the concept, with the contested card on a category of its own)
- [[mental-privacy]] (why the data are said to be different)
- [[data-solidarity]] (Prainsack and others' governance answer)
- [[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]] (the same disagreement at the level of rights)
- [[regulatory-landscape]], [[california-neural-data-law]], [[colorado-neural-data-law]], [[chile-supreme-court-2023]], [[unesco-recommendation-2025]] (the instruments reported)
- [[iccpr-art-17]] (the Covenant frame A/81/351 uses)
- [[a-81-351]], [[unodc-interpol-2025]], [[ahrc-2025]], [[futures-lab-2026]], [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]], [[prainsack-et-al-2022]] (the documents pinned)

pages.title: What does the library ask States to do now?

frontmatter.title: What does the library ask States to do now?

pages.body:
# What does the library ask States to do now?

**Short answer.** Four documents make recommendations, and they ask different things of different addressees. The Secretary-General (c) asks Member States for ten measures: regulate, treat neural data as highly sensitive, prohibit coercive use, exclude tainted evidence, require demanding consent, validate evidence, protect vulnerable groups, respect Indigenous rights, hold business to account, and train. UNODC and INTERPOL (c) ask law enforcement and justice institutions not to deploy until accuracy and safety are demonstrated, and to build frameworks, oversight and harmonized standards. The Australian Human Rights Commission (d) asks its own Attorney-General for an inquiry with a moratorium meanwhile, and asks the Human Rights Committee for a General Comment on article 18. Futures Lab (e) asks the United Nations for new global standards and the United States for a federal framework. None is an obligation; each is a recommendation in its author's register.

## Reasoning, by register

**(c) The Secretary-General, to Member States.** The premise is that the law exists but needs clarifying [A/81/351, para. 48](pin:A/81/351#p15 "International human rights law provides an applicable framework to address the risks of neurotechnology, but further clarification and consistent application are needed") ✓, with a request that UN mechanisms provide guidance within their mandates. The recommendations ("I recommend that Member States") open with regulation [A/81/351, para. 50 (a)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Establish regulatory frameworks, consistent with international human rights law and relevant international standards and guidance provided by United Nations human rights mechanisms, governing the development, deployment and use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice") ✓; then data [A/81/351, para. 50 (b)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Recognize neural data as highly sensitive personal data subject to the highest level of legal protection") ✓; a prohibition [A/81/351, para. 50 (c)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Prohibit the compulsory or coercive use of neurotechnologies in the administration of justice, including brain-based deception detection, predictive applications, decoding applications to “read” thoughts, intentions or memories, neuromodulation and arbitrary or unlawful cognitive surveillance and monitoring") ✓; an exclusionary rule [A/81/351, para. 50 (d)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Prohibit the use of neural data obtained through torture or ill-treatment, or in violation of the rights to freedom of thought and opinion, as evidence in any proceedings") ✓; consent [A/81/351, para. 50 (e)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Require free, prior, informed, explicit and revocable consent for any potential use of neurotechnology in the administration of justice") ✓; validation of evidence [A/81/351, para. 50 (f)](pin:A/81/351#p15 "Require rigorous independent scientific review and validation of any neurotechnology-derived evidence proposed for admission in court") ✓; safeguards for groups [A/81/351, para. 50 (g)](pin:A/81/351#p16 "Ensure enhanced safeguards for children, detainees, persons with disabilities, women, older persons, persons belonging to particular racial or ethnic groups") ✓; Indigenous Peoples [A/81/351, para. 50 (h)](pin:A/81/351#p16 "Ensure that the development and deployment of neurotechnology respects the rights of Indigenous Peoples, including the requirement of free, prior and informed consent") ✓; business [A/81/351, para. 50 (i)](pin:A/81/351#p16 "Urge all business enterprises involved in neurotechnology to take all steps to meet their responsibility to respect human rights") ✓; and training [A/81/351, para. 50 (j)](pin:A/81/351#p16 "specialized training for law enforcement officials, prosecutors, judges and defence counsel") ✓.

**(c) UNODC and INTERPOL, to law enforcement and justice institutions.** A background paper, by its own account [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 3](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p6 "This background paper shares some preliminary thoughts on the field of neurotechnology and its significance for law enforcement and the criminal justice system") ✓, not a list of recommendations to States. Its first ask is a precondition [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 5](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p8 "Technologies should therefore not be deployed until their accuracy, safety, and feasibility have been rigorously demonstrated through independent testing and peer-reviewed research") ✓; then frameworks, consent, data protection and oversight [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 6](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p9 "establishing clear legal and ethical frameworks to protect human rights, ensuring voluntary and informed consent from individuals, implementing robust data protection and cybersecurity measures, and maintaining independent oversight") ✓; rules on evidence [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 6](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p9 "developing clear rules on admissibility of evidence, establishing independent mechanisms for oversight and accountability") ✓; and cooperation [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 6](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p9 "international cooperation and harmonization of standards will be essential to addressing regulatory gaps") ✓. Its next step is its own [UNODC–INTERPOL 2025, p. 6](pin:UNODC-INTERPOL-2025#p9 "a Technology Assessment will be developed to provide more comprehensive guidance") ✓.

**(d) The Australian Human Rights Commission, to Australia and to the Human Rights Committee.** Recommendation 6 is addressed to the Attorney-General [AHRC 2025, p. 70](pin:AHRC-2025#p70 "refer to the Australian Law Reform Commission an inquiry to consider the potential application of neurotechnology in the criminal justice system, and examine in what circumstances (if any) it can be appropriately used. Until this work is completed there should be a moratorium on the use of neurotechnology in the criminal justice system") ✓, with an interim evidentiary position in the body text [AHRC 2025, p. 32](pin:AHRC-2025#p32 "until that time, information gained via neurotechnology should be inadmissible at trial") ✓. Recommendation 4 is addressed to a treaty body [AHRC 2025, p. 70](pin:AHRC-2025#p70 "The United Nations Human Rights Committee provide guidance on freedom of thought and neurotechnologies through the adoption of a general comment on article 18 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights") ✓. Both are an NHRI's recommendations; the moratorium is for one country's criminal justice system.

**(e) Futures Lab, to the United Nations and the United States.** [Futures Lab 2026, p. 2](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p3 "the United Nations should establish global standards grounded in human dignity, cognitive liberty, and equality") ✓, restated as new standards with monitoring meanwhile [Futures Lab 2026, p. 7](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p8 "the United Nations needs to develop new human rights standards that reflect the emerging and rapidly evolving nature of neurotechnology. Until such standards are established, the use of neurotechnology, particularly in legal responses to violations of neurorights, should be subject to careful monitoring") ✓; and, at home, [Futures Lab 2026, p. 8](pin:FuturesLab-2026#p9 "the United States must implement a federal framework grounded in human rights law using the EU model") ✓.

**Side by side.** All four want validation before use, consent, oversight and a rule on evidence. They differ on the pause: the Secretary-General prohibits coercive use and regulates the rest; UNODC and INTERPOL make deployment wait for demonstrated accuracy; the AHRC suspends all use in criminal justice pending an inquiry; Futures Lab monitors pending new standards. And they differ on where guidance should come from: existing mechanisms (A/81/351 para. 48; AHRC Recommendation 4, a General Comment) or new standards (Futures Lab). That second difference is the one on [[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]].

## What the library cannot answer

- What any State has done in response: the reports describe laws and rulings that predate them ([[regulatory-landscape]]).
- Whether the Human Rights Committee has taken up Recommendation 4, or whether the Advisory Committee's guidelines have been adopted (A/81/351 para. 46 reports the mandate only; [[a-hrc-57-61]] is not yet ingested).
- How a moratorium would be defined in law: the AHRC gives the scope ("criminal justice system", "criminal investigations") but no instrument.

## Related

- [[regulatory-landscape]] (what exists), [[moratorium]] (the pause, with its contested card)
- [[consent-in-custody]], [[reliability-and-admissibility]], [[neural-data]], [[discrimination]] (the subjects of 50 (b) to (g))
- [[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]] (guidance from existing mechanisms, or new standards)
- [[general-comment-22]] (the Committee's existing reading of article 18, which Recommendation 4 would extend)
- [[a-81-351]], [[unodc-interpol-2025]], [[ahrc-2025]], [[futures-lab-2026]] (the four documents)
- [[unesco-recommendation-2025]] (an instrument already adopted, calling for national coordinating bodies)

# Index

**40 pages** · 9 sources · 14 concepts · 14 entities · 3 questions · 707 pins, all ✓ verified · 6 contested cards · built 2 November 2026.

The catalog of the wiki: read it first on every Ask, update it on every Ingest. One line per page: what it is, the registers its pins draw on, and how many verified pins it carries. Companions: `WIKI.md` (the rules), `log.md` (what was done, when), `TENSIONS.md` (open disagreements).

## Sources

One page per library document read into the wiki, highest register first. In the inbox, not yet ingested: A/HRC/57/61 ([[a-hrc-57-61]]).

- [[ccpr-c-21-rev-1-add-4]] — General Comment No. 22 (1993): freedom of thought unconditional and non-derogable; no one compelled to reveal thoughts · (b) · ✓5
- [[ccpr-c-gc-32]] — General Comment No. 32 (2007): no direct or indirect physical or undue psychological pressure; evidence obtained contrary to article 7 excluded · (b) · ✓11
- [[ccpr-c-gc-34]] — General Comment No. 34 (2011): holding opinions permits no exception or restriction; no coercion to hold or not hold an opinion · (b) · ✓9
- [[a-81-351]] — Secretary-General's 2026 report: maps uses, applies Covenant rights, surveys regulation, recommends States prohibit coercive use of neurotechnology · (c) · ✓31
- [[unodc-interpol-2025]] — UNODC–INTERPOL background paper from the law-enforcement side: uses, rights at stake, validation-first safeguards, questions for submissions · (c) · ✓23
- [[ahrc-2025]] — Australian NHRI: the neurorights debate settling on existing rights; asks for an article 18 general comment; moratorium and inadmissibility · (d) · ✓38
- [[futures-lab-2026]] — Civil-society submission asking the UN for new neurotechnology standards, framed in UDHR terms; US state laws, Girardi v. Emotiv · (e) · ✓20
- [[prainsack-et-al-2022]] — Two-page Lancet Digital Health Comment: individual control is not enough; data solidarity's three pillars, for health data · (f) · ✓8
- [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]] — EMBO Reports article co-written by the workshop's trainer: neural data uniquely sensitive; Chile, US states, EU compared; agency, solidarity, precaution · (f) · ✓18

## Concepts

- [[brain-based-lie-detection]] — Brain measurements used to infer deception or recognition of crime details; also called deception detection, brain fingerprinting, BEOS · (b)(c)(d)(e)(f) · ✓32
- [[consent-in-custody]] — Consent to neurotechnology in detention, interrogation or sentencing: a necessary gate for the UN reports, unreliable for the NHRI · (b)(c)(d)(e)(f) · ✓32
- [[data-solidarity]] — Governing data collectively by public value, not only by consent; proposed for health data, applied to neural data by one article · (f) · ✓10
- [[discrimination]] — Who bears the risk: every register expects neurotechnology in justice to fall hardest on marginalised and vulnerable groups · (b)(c)(d)(e)(f) · ✓20
- [[freedom-of-thought]] — Article 18's forum internum, protected without limitation, and the four 'pillars' the reports apply to brain decoding · (b)(c)(d)(e)(f) · ✓26
- [[mental-privacy]] — Protection of mental activity and the data that reveal it, where article 17 privacy meets article 18 thought · (b)(c)(d)(e)(f) · ✓23
- [[moratorium]] — Only the AHRC asks for a moratorium; the UN reports prohibit coercive uses and regulate the rest · (b)(c)(d)(e)(f) · ✓21
- [[neural-data]] — Data about the nervous system gathered by neurotechnology: highly sensitive for all; a category of its own for few · (b)(c)(d)(e)(f) · ✓34
- [[neuromodulation-of-offenders]] — Stimulating offenders' brains to reduce aggression or impulsivity: possible treatment contrary to articles 7 or 10 · (b)(c)(d)(f) · ✓19
- [[neuroprediction]] — Brain measurements to predict reoffending for sentencing or parole: biological determinism for the SG and the AHRC · (b)(c)(d)(e) · ✓17
- [[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]] — Neurorights or existing rights, clarified? UN reports and the NHRI lean to existing rights; civil society asks for new standards · (b)(c)(d)(e)(f) · ✓19
- [[regulatory-landscape]] — What law and guidance exist: a few national data laws, international soft law, almost nothing written for police, courts and prisons · (c)(d)(e)(f) · ✓18
- [[reliability-and-admissibility]] — Is brain-based evidence reliable, and may a court admit it? Corroborative use recorded; validation demanded first · (b)(c)(d)(e)(f) · ✓51
- [[self-incrimination]] — Article 14(3)(g) and General Comment No. 32's no-pressure standard, applied by the reports to brain-based tests · (b)(c)(d)(e)(f) · ✓22

## Entities

- [[a-hrc-57-61]] — Stub: the Human Rights Council Advisory Committee's 2024 report, in the inbox; what other documents say it says · (c) · ✓11 · stub
- [[california-neural-data-law]] — California's 2024 consumer-privacy amendment adding neural data, as four library documents report it · (c)(d)(e)(f) · ✓8
- [[chile-supreme-court-2023]] — Chile's Supreme Court applies the 2021 neurorights amendment to a consumer brain device (Girardi v. Emotiv) · (c)(e)(f) · ✓6
- [[colorado-neural-data-law]] — Colorado's 2024 amendment bringing neural data into sensitive data, as four library documents report it · (c)(d)(e)(f) · ✓8
- [[general-comment-22]] — General Comment No. 22 as an authority: who in the library relies on it, for the forum internum · (b) · ✓11
- [[general-comment-32]] — General Comment No. 32 as an authority: the no-pressure standard and the exclusionary rule, as the reports use them · (b) · ✓9
- [[general-comment-34]] — General Comment No. 34 as an authority: holding opinions without interference, as the reports use it · (b) · ✓11
- [[iccpr-art-14-3-g]] — Not to be compelled to testify against oneself or confess guilt: the treaty text and its readings in the library · (a) · ✓12
- [[iccpr-art-17]] — Privacy: the article the library reads as reaching neural data · (a) · ✓14
- [[iccpr-art-18]] — Freedom of thought, conscience and religion: the forum internum and its application to neurotechnology · (a) · ✓17
- [[iccpr-art-7]] — Torture and ill-treatment: coercive extraction of information, neuromodulation of offenders, excluded evidence · (a) · ✓11
- [[iccpr-art-9]] — Liberty and security of person; the AHRC's mistaken 'art 19.1' recorded here · (a) · ✓10
- [[selvi-v-state-of-karnataka]] — India's Supreme Court (2010): involuntary brain-based lie detection violates the protection against self-incrimination · (c) · ✓5
- [[unesco-recommendation-2025]] — UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology: adopted in 2025, a draft in the older documents · (c) · ✓12

tensions:
# Tensions

The register of open disagreements in the wiki. One `###` entry per contested card (the card itself, with its pins and authority ladder, is on the page named in `card:`), then discrepancies of fact between documents, which need no card: one document is simply out of date or wrong. Status: `open` (the documents split), `leaning` (the weight lies on one side, by the authority ladder), `settled` (the library resolves it). Updated on every Ingest.

## Contested claims

### do-existing-rights-suffice
title: Do existing rights suffice, or are new neurorights needed?
status: leaning
card: [[new-rights-vs-existing-rights]]
poles: existing rights, interpreted and clarified (A/81/351 para. 48; AHRC 2025 p. 30) || new UN standards (Futures Lab 2026 p. 7)
where: [[a-81-351]], [[ahrc-2025]], [[futures-lab-2026]], [[szoszkiewicz-yuste-2025]], [[freedom-of-thought]]
note: no treaty body has spoken; the AHRC asks the Human Rights Committee for a general comment on article 18. A/HRC/57/61 (inbox) will add the Advisory Committee's view.

### neural-data-own-category
title: Do neural data need a legal category of their own?
status: leaning
card: [[neural-data]]
poles: the top tier of existing sensitive-data law (A/81/351 para. 50 (b); AHRC 2025 p. 22) || specific standards for neural data (Futures Lab 2026 p. 4; Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025 p. 3470)
where: [[mental-privacy]], [[is-neural-data-special]], [[regulatory-landscape]], [[colorado-neural-data-law]], [[california-neural-data-law]]

### consent-to-lie-detection
title: Can a suspect's consent make brain-based lie detection lawful?
status: leaning
card: [[consent-in-custody]]
poles: consent as a necessary gate, under the highest scrutiny (A/81/351 para. 50 (e); UNODC–INTERPOL 2025 p. 6) || consent in custody cannot be relied on (AHRC 2025 p. 32; Futures Lab 2026 p. 7)
where: [[self-incrimination]], [[brain-based-lie-detection]], [[can-a-suspect-consent-to-lie-detection]], [[general-comment-32]]

### moratorium-or-safeguards
title: Suspend neurotechnology in criminal justice, or regulate it with safeguards?
status: open
card: [[moratorium]]
poles: a moratorium until assessed (AHRC 2025 Recommendation 6, p. 70) || prohibit coercive uses, regulate the rest (A/81/351 para. 50 (c), (f)); no deployment until validated (UNODC–INTERPOL 2025 p. 5); monitoring (Futures Lab 2026 p. 7)
where: [[ahrc-2025]], [[a-81-351]], [[unodc-interpol-2025]], [[what-should-states-do-now]]
note: the AHRC's own scope varies: "criminal investigations" (p. 32) against "the criminal justice system" (Recommendation 6, p. 70).

### neuroprediction-in-sentencing
title: Can neuroprediction have a legitimate role in sentencing and parole?
status: leaning
card: [[neuroprediction]]
poles: promise, if regulated with participation (Futures Lab 2026 p. 3) || statistical risk is not a reason specific to the individual (A/81/351 para. 34); prohibit coercive predictive uses (para. 50 (c))
where: [[discrimination]], [[neuromodulation-of-offenders]], [[ahrc-2025]]

### neuroimaging-as-evidence
title: May neuroimaging be admitted now as corroborative evidence?
status: open
card: [[reliability-and-admissibility]]
poles: admitted as corroborative, after independent validation (A/81/351 paras. 7, 50 (f)) || nothing deployed until accuracy is demonstrated (UNODC–INTERPOL 2025 p. 5); interim inadmissibility (AHRC 2025 p. 32)
where: [[brain-based-lie-detection]], [[selvi-v-state-of-karnataka]], [[regulatory-landscape]]

## Discrepancies between documents

### us-state-laws-count
title: How many US states protect neural data by law?
status: open
poles: California, Colorado and Montana (A/81/351 para. 45; Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025 p. 3471) || California and Colorado, "the only states" (Futures Lab 2026 p. 4) || "at least eight" (Futures Lab 2026 p. 8)
where: [[regulatory-landscape]], [[colorado-neural-data-law]], [[california-neural-data-law]], [[futures-lab-2026]]
note: the library holds none of these laws; the submission contradicts itself.

### unesco-recommendation-status
title: Is the UNESCO Recommendation adopted or a draft?
status: settled
poles: adopted in 2025 (A/81/351 para. 46) || a draft under negotiation (Szoszkiewicz & Yuste 2025 p. 3471; AHRC 2025 p. 9; Futures Lab 2026 p. 5)
where: [[unesco-recommendation-2025]], [[regulatory-landscape]]
note: a difference of date, not of view: the latest document (August 2026) reports the adoption.

### the-word-undue
title: How strict is the self-incrimination standard?
status: settled
poles: "direct or indirect physical or undue psychological pressure" (General Comment No. 32 para. 41) || the same without "undue", and called "an absolute guarantee" (A/81/351 para. 32; AHRC 2025 pp. 31, 33)
where: [[self-incrimination]], [[ccpr-c-gc-32]], [[a-81-351]], [[iccpr-art-14-3-g]]
note: quote the Committee's own words; the reports' stricter wording is theirs.

### security-of-person-article
title: Which ICCPR article protects security of the person?
status: settled
poles: article 9 (the treaty; see [[iccpr-art-9]]) || "art 19.1 ICCPR" (AHRC 2025 p. 33)
where: [[ahrc-2025]], [[iccpr-art-9]], [[ccpr-c-gc-34]]
note: an error in the AHRC report; article 19(1) protects holding opinions.

### decoding-capability
title: Can neurotechnology read thoughts today?
status: open
poles: "used to decode human thought in the form of words into text on a screen" (UNODC–INTERPOL 2025 p. 1) || not capable at present of "mind-reading" (A/81/351 para. 22)
where: [[unodc-interpol-2025]], [[a-81-351]], [[brain-based-lie-detection]], [[mental-privacy]]
